Which of the following is NOT a defining characteristic of jerk nystagmus? A.Nomenclature based on direction of the slow phase B.Consisting of a fast and slow phase C.Characterized by amplitude and velocity D.Rhythmic High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Nystagmus is a disorder marked by excessive eye movements that are rhythmic. Jerk nystagmus has clear fast and slow phase. By convention the nystagmus is always named based on the direction of the fast phase. Pendular nystagmus is an exception to the fast and slow phase rule because pendular nystagmus consists of two phases with equal velocity and amplitude. Nystagmoid movements such as square wave jerks and superior oblique myokymia are not rhythmic and therefore do not fit these definitions. Because they look grossly similar to nystagmus on examination, however, they are sometimes referred to as nystagmoid movements. What is the most common structural etiology causing downbeat nystagmus? A.Posterior fossa meningioma B.Chiari type I malformation C.Spinal cord and/or brainstem syrinx D.Cerebellar hemangioma High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Downbeat nystagmus (DBN) is the result of abnormal drift of the eyes upward followed by a corrective downward fast saccade. Most pathology causing DBN localizes to the cervicomedullary junction (CVMJ) or cerebellum. MRI of the brain is warranted for evaluation of DBN because structural lesions of the CVMJ or cerebellum including Arnold-Chiari malformation, mass lesions (meningioma or hemangioma), and syrinx are causes of DBN and may be amenable to surgical intervention. When interpreting the MRI, careful attention should be paid to evaluating for cerebellar tonsil herniation through the foramen magnum (Arnold-Chiari type I malformation) because this is the most common structural etiology of DBN and the DBN may be reversible following neuro-surgical decompression. What is the standard "cycle" time required for periodic alternating nystagmus to pass from the static (nystagmus free) phase through two nystagmus phases in different directions and back to a static phase? A.5-10 seconds B.15-45 seconds C.1-2 minutes D.2-4 minutes High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) is a form of bilateral, horizontal jerk nystagmus that alternates fast phase directions following a reliable time cycle (usually 2-4 minutes). The cycle begins with a static phase devoid of nystagmus and is followed by crescendo then decrescendo jerk nystagmus to one side. A return to the static phase occurs after which there is a crescendo / decrescendo jerk nystagmus to the opposite side. The cycle then terminates with another static phase. PAN may be congenital or acquired. When acquired it is usually caused by posterior fossa pathology of the brainstem or cerebellum (especially the vermis of the cerebellum). Because of the reliability of the short cycle and the importance of diagnosis, all patients with horizontal jerk nystagmus should be observed for a minimum of 2 minutes to ensure that the diagnosis of PAN is not missed. One of the greatest concerns in missing the diagnosis of PAN is that the null point in patients with PAN can alternate depending on the direction of the jerk nystagmus. For this reason, Kestenbaum surgery or Kestenbaum variants used to shift the null point to primary gaze should be avoided in these patients unless it is clear that the patient always maintains the same null point throughout the PAN cycle. A 17-year-old female presents with a complaint of intermittent blurred vision for the past 2 years and inability to “focus.” Friends and family have noticed her eyes shaking at times. She has a past medical history of anxiety for which she takes Cymbalta and no past ocular history. Her exam is notable for the eye movement abnormality noted in the video below. She already underwent an MRI of the brain with and without IV contrast ordered by her primary care physician 2 months and this was unremarkable. Note that the patient was pharmacologically dilated at the time of the video. (there is a missing video) What is the next best step in the management of this patient? A.Reassurance with no further work-up B.Referral for breast and pelvic examination by an OBGYN C.MRI of the orbits with and without IV contrast D.Order serum paraneoplastic antibody panel ‘ High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: This video depicts a textbook example of volitional nystagmus or voluntary nystagmus (VN). VN can be performed by a surprisingly high number of individuals (up to 8% of the general population in one study). While for most it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work-ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high-frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is usually (though not always) horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and / or convergence movements. The video clearly shows short bursts of low amplitude, high frequency “shimmering” horizontal nystagmus. At one point the patient actually stops to forcefully squeeze her eyelids- a sign that she is exerting considerable effort to produce the effect. Notice her eyelids are virtually always fluttering at the same time as her horizontal nystagmus. While not shown on the video, she did not exhibit the nystagmus on smooth pursuit motility testing which is characteristic of volitional nystagmus. The main differential diagnoses in this case would be acquired horizontal pendular nystagmus and ocular flutter neither of which would be so dramatically intermittent nor associated with eyelid fluttering. In the case of acquired ocular flutter, the differential diagnosis is essentially identical to opsoclonus and would include post-infectious autoimmune cases, paraneoplastic, and cerebellar / brainstem disease that would be seen on MRI (e.g. multiple sclerosis or neoplasm or inflammation). If the patient had ocular flutter with a clean MRI brain, paraneoplastic causes could be considered and a work-up would include body imaging for malignancy, paraneoplastic antibodies, a careful female examination to assess for breast or ovarian cancer, and consideration of dedicated breast imaging if body imaging negative. This patient’s young age and 2 year history of symptoms would be unusual for paraneoplastic disease. MRI of the orbits would not provide any additional insight in this case.

question: Which of the following types of nystagmus is associated with hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI?
explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is classically vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. One OQ user brought to our attention this excellent website showing the characteristic changes of inferior olivary hypertrophy: http://radiopaedia.org/articles/hypertrophic-olivary-degeneration What is the correct description of latent nystagmus (LN)? A.Under monocular conditions, bilateral jerk nystagmus occurs with the fast phase beating towards the viewing eye B.Under monocular conditions, bilateral jerk nystagmus occurs with the fast phase beating towards the occluded eye C.Under monocular conditions, there is unilateral jerk nystagmus of the viewing eye with the fast phase beating towards the viewing eye. D.Under monocular conditions, there is unilateral jerk nystagmus of the viewing eye with the fast phase beating towards the occluded eye. High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Latent nystagmus (LN) is a form of nystagmus that develops early in life and mostly likely occurs from early disruption of binocular vision. For that reason it is very common in children with infantile strabismus. LN is generally asymptomatic for most patients (unless it becomes manifest) but can result in poor visual acuity results on monocular vision testing. The nystagmus is a BILATERAL jerk nystagmus that generally only manifests upon occlusion of one eye. The fast phase of the nystagmus beats towards the viewing eye. Some may think of LN as monocular because it is observed clinically when one eye is covered but the occluded eye also has nystagmus. When testing vision in children with LN, optical blurring of one eye is preferable to occlusion because it does not incite as much nystagmus in the viewing eye thus allowing a more accurate acuity measurement. Which of the following is actually a misnomer in that it does not meet the definition of a true nystagmus? A.Periodic alternating nystagmus B.Congenital nystagmus C.Convergence-retraction nystagmus D.Downbeat nystagmus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Nystagmus is an abnormal rhythmic oscillation of the eyes with a slow phase in which the eye drifts from its intended target and a fast phase marked by a quick corrective saccade back to the target. This abnormal eye movement is not rhythmic, does not have a fast or slow phase, and doesn't involve an abnormal drift from fixation. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is most easily elicited by a holding a down going OKN drum or OKN strip in front of the patient. The patient will momentarily follow one target downward before a fast upward "catch-up" saccade occurs to find the next target. The convergence- retraction nystagmus occurs simultaneously with the attempted fast upward saccade. What is the standard "cycle" time required for periodic alternating nystagmus to pass from the static (nystagmus free) phase through two nystagmus phases in different directions and back to a static phase? A 17-year-old female presents with a complaint of intermittent blurred vision for the past 2 years and inability to “focus.” Friends and family have noticed her eyes shaking at times. She has a past medical history of anxiety for which she takes Cymbalta and no past ocular history. Her exam is notable for the eye movement abnormality noted in the video below. She already underwent an MRI of the brain with and without IV contrast ordered by her primary care physician 2 months and this was unremarkable. question: What is the correct description of latent nystagmus (LN)?

options.A: Under monocular conditions, bilateral jerk nystagmus occurs with the fast phase beating towards the viewing eye
options.B: Under monocular conditions, bilateral jerk nystagmus occurs with the fast phase beating towards the occluded eye
options.C: Under monocular conditions, there is unilateral jerk nystagmus of the viewing eye with the fast phase beating towards the viewing eye.
options.D: Under monocular conditions, there is unilateral jerk nystagmus of the viewing eye with the fast phase beating towards the occluded eye.

explanation: Latent nystagmus (LN) is a form of nystagmus that develops early in life and mostly likely occurs from early disruption of binocular vision. For that reason it is very common in children with infantile strabismus. LN is generally asymptomatic for most patients (unless it becomes manifest) but can result in poor visual acuity results on monocular vision testing. The nystagmus is a BILATERAL jerk nystagmus that generally only manifests upon occlusion of one eye. The fast phase of the nystagmus beats towards the viewing eye. Some may think of LN as monocular because it is observed clinically when one eye is covered but the occluded eye also has nystagmus. When testing vision in children with LN, optical blurring of one eye is preferable to occlusion because it does not incite as much nystagmus in the viewing eye thus allowing a more accurate acuity measurement. Which of the following types of nystagmus is caused by a lesion of the central tegmental tract? A.Oculopalatal myoclonus B.Periodic alternating nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.See-saw nystagmus High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is very unique and is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. Which of the following is actually a misnomer in that it does not meet the definition of a true nystagmus? A.Periodic alternating nystagmus B.Congenital nystagmus C.Convergence-retraction nystagmus D.Downbeat nystagmus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Nystagmus is an abnormal rhythmic oscillation of the eyes with a slow phase in which the eye drifts from its intended target and a fast phase marked by a quick corrective saccade back to the target. In pendular nystagmus, the fast phase and slow phase have the same velocity but it is still considered a true nystagmus. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is one component of the dorsal midbrain syndrome (aka Parinaud's syndrome) and is marked by abnormal co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on attempted up-gaze. This abnormal eye movement is not rhythmic, does not have a fast or slow phase, and doesn't involve an abnormal drift from fixation. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is most easily elicited by a holding a down going OKN drum or OKN strip in front of the patient. The patient will momentarily follow one target downward before a fast upward "catch-up" saccade occurs to find the next target. The convergence- retraction nystagmus occurs simultaneously with the attempted fast upward saccade. Which of the following diseases is NOT associated with vascular compression induced neuropathy by an aberrant, ectatic, or dilated intracranial artery compressing on a cranial nerve? A.Benign essential blepharospasm B.Superior oblique myokymia C.Trigeminal neuralgia D.Hemifacial spasm High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: As the resolution and availability of neuro-imaging improves, more neurological diseases have been found to arise from vascular compression of intracranial nerves. Superior oblique myokymia is a disease marked by episodic paroxysmal contraction of the superior oblique on one side causing a "jumping" of vision in one eye and binocular diplopia. In at least some cases, MRI has shown vascular compression of the 4th nerve on the affected side. Trigeminal neuralgia is a pain disorder marked by severe unilateral paroxysmal shooting pain in the trigeminal nerve distribution that is usually transient (lasting seconds or less). It can have multiple etiologies but vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve is a well established cause; some patients with severe trigeminal neuralgia are treated surgically by microvascular decompression with placement of a sponge between the superior cerebellar artery and the trigeminal nerve. Hemifacial spasm is generally a unilateral disorder marked by abnormal spasms of the facial muscles supplied by CN7. Hemifacial spasm has numerous causes including stroke, demyelination, tumors, AVMs, and idiopathic disease. MRI studies now show that many cases previously thought to be idiopathic, however, are actually caused by vascular compression of the facial nerve root by the distal branches of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, or vertebral artery. In severe cases refractory to medication and/or botox, microvascular decompression surgery (similar to that performed for trigeminal neuralgia) can be performed and has been successful in the past. Benign essential blepharospasm is generally a bilateral disease with pronounced episodic contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscles. There is some evidence that benign essential blepharospasm is related to underlying basal ganglia dysfunction but many patients also have a functional or stress related component. Symptoms may be exacerbated by corneal surface disease such as dry eye. The MRI in benign essential blepharospasm patients is virtually always normal and does not suggest a vascular compressive etiology. Which of the following history and exam features are NOT helpful in distinguishing voluntary (or self-induced) nystagmoid movements from other involuntary forms of nystagmus and nystagmoid movements? A.Associated facial grimacing and eyelid flutter B.Disappearance of oscillations with distraction C.Associated convergence movements D.Lack of oscillopsia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The most common functional neuro-ophthalmic complaints probably involve vision loss but functional or voluntary nystagmoid movements can present to your clinic as well. The diagnosis of volitional nystagmoid movements can usually be made easily in the clinic by looking for associated facial grimacing or eyelid flutter. Distracting the patient by having them perform tasks often breaks a cycle of oscillations. Usually the eye movements are low amplitude and associated with convergence movements so it is nearly impossible for the patient to maintain the performance when testing far lateral gaze on motility exam. It requires a great deal of effort to sustain volitional oscillations for more than a few seconds so it is helpful when attacks are noted to last only a few seconds. Oscillopsia is the sensation that the visual field is moving and is much more commonly described by patients with acquired nystagmus and nystagmoid eye movements. Its presence or absence on history, however, is not helpful in diagnosing voluntary nystagmoid eye movements. 16-month-old boy presents to your eye clinic because his parents noted his right eye "shaking" for the past month. Your exam shows fix, follow, intermittent maintain "FF(M)" vision OD and fix, follow, and maintain "FFM" vision OS. The pupil exam shows a trace APD OD. Motility is full and alignment is orthophoric based on alternate cover testing. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +2.00 OD and -1.00 OS. External exam reveals a fine shimmering vertical nystagmus in the right eye with no nystagmus seen in the left eye. No head bobbing or torticollis is seen. Slit lamp exam and fundus exam is unremarkable. What is the next most appropriate step in the care of this patient? A.Prescribe glasses and follow-up in 3 months for re-evaluation B.Order an MRI of the brain and orbits under sedation C.Observe with repeat examination in 3 months D.Patch the left eye 6 hours daily and return in 3 month High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Monocular nystagmus in a child should immediately raise concerns for an optic nerve glioma. A monocular, small amplitude vertical nystagmus has been referred to as the Heimann- Bielschowsky phenomenon and may occur in association with any cause of decreased vision including amblyopia. This patient does have anisometropia which could cause amblyopia and account for his mild decrease in vision OD. The APD in the right eye is highly concerning for organic pathology, however. Severe amblyopia can result in a mild APD but in this situation organic pathology (such as a glioma) of the optic nerve, chiasm, or tract must be excluded. Spasmus nutans, a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding, can closely resemble Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon and vice-versa so most clinicians (and the BCSC) suggest scanning all patients with spasmus nutans. The parents of a 4-year-old boy with torticollis and vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye since 1 year of age come to your clinic for a second opinion. The patient was diagnosed with spasmus nutans by another provider at presentation 3 years ago after a reportedly normal MRI. By matching Allen pictures, the patient has 20/100 vision OD and 20/50 vision OS. His visual field is full to confrontation with finger count techniques, motility normal, and alignment orthophoric by alternate cover testing. The patient was uncooperative for pupillary testing so it was difficult to assess for an APD although his pupils reacted to light bilaterally. External exam confirms a monocular vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye and torticollis with a right head tilt. His penlight anterior segment exam is grossly normal and dilated fundus exam reveals trace pallor of the right optic nerve. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +1.00 sphere in both eyes. What is the next best step in the care of this patient? A.Order an MRI of the brain and orbits under sedation B.Reassure the parents and have the patient follow-up in one year C.Prescribe glasses and have the patient follow-up in one year D.Initiate patching for 6 hours daily in the left eye. High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Spasmus nutans is a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding. The nystagmus is frequently referred to as "shimmering" due to its high frequency low amplitude nature. The nystagmus is usually horizontal and bilateral although it may be unilateral, vertical, or rotary. It usually presents within the first 2 years of life and then resolves within 1-2 years. Spasmus nutans can closely resemble Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon and vice-versa so most clinicians (and the BCSC) suggest scanning all patients with spasmus nutans to rule out an anterior optic pathway glioma. This patient appropriately underwent an MRI at the time of diagnosis which was normal. After 3 years, however, his nystagmus and torticollis have not resolved which is alarming. Also, this patient has unexplained decreased visual acuity in the right eye along with optic nerve pallor increasing concern for optic nerve pathology such as an anterior optic pathway glioma. When spasmus nutans does not recover as expected or is associated with additional neurological deficits then repeat neuro-imaging is warranted. Which of the following is NOT a recognized cause of downbeat nystagmus? A.Arnold-Chiari type I malformation B.Demyelination the cerebellum and/or medulla C.Migraine D.Magnesium deficiency High Yield: Yes Your Answer: D Correct Answer: C Explanation: Downbeat nystagmus (DBN) is the result of abnormal drift of the eyes upward followed by a corrective downward fast saccade. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of congenital nystagmus? A.Presence of a null point B.Predominantly a conjugate, vertical nystagmus C.Manifests with either pendular or jerk nystagmus D.Intensifies with viewing of objects at distance High Yield: Yes Your Answer: D Correct Answer: B Explanation: Congenital nystagmus is a highly tested topic. This is a well- known mnemonic published in multiple review books. The mnemonic is not great but don't shoot the messenger. Instead of more criticisms about this mnemonic, I'd like to tap into the wisdom of the group and see if users can generate a better one. Thanks! question: Which of the following is actually a misnomer in that it does not meet the definition of a true nystagmus?
explanation: Nystagmus is an abnormal rhythmic oscillation of the eyes with a slow phase in which the eye drifts from its intended target and a fast phase marked by a quick corrective saccade back to the target. This abnormal eye movement is not rhythmic, does not have a fast or slow phase, and doesn't involve an abnormal drift from fixation. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is most easily elicited by a holding a down going OKN drum or OKN strip in front of the patient. The patient will momentarily follow one target downward before a fast upward "catch-up" saccade occurs to find the next target. The convergence- retraction nystagmus occurs simultaneously with the attempted fast upward saccade. Superior oblique myokymia is a disease marked by episodic paroxysmal contraction of the superior oblique on one side causing a "jumping" of vision in one eye and binocular diplopia. Trigeminal neuralgia is a pain disorder marked by severe unilateral paroxysmal shooting pain in the trigeminal nerve distribution that is usually transient (lasting seconds or less). It can have multiple etiologies but vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve is a well established cause; some patients with severe trigeminal neuralgia are treated surgically by microvascular decompression with placement of a sponge between the superior cerebellar artery and the trigeminal nerve. Hemifacial spasm is generally a unilateral disorder marked by abnormal spasms of the facial muscles supplied by CN7. Benign essential blepharospasm is generally a bilateral disease with pronounced episodic contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscles. There is some evidence that benign essential blepharospasm is related to underlying basal ganglia dysfunction but many patients also have a functional or stress related component. Symptoms may be exacerbated by corneal surface disease such as dry eye. The MRI in benign essential blepharospasm patients is virtually always normal and does not suggest a vascular compressive etiology. question: The parents of a 4-year-old boy with torticollis and vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye since 1 year of age come to your clinic for a second opinion. The patient was diagnosed with spasmus nutans by another provider at presentation 3 years ago after a reportedly normal MRI. By matching Allen pictures, the patient has 20/100 vision OD and 20/50 vision OS. His visual field is full to confrontation with finger count techniques, motility normal, and alignment orthophoric by alternate cover testing. The patient was uncooperative for pupillary testing so it was difficult to assess for an APD although his pupils reacted to light bilaterally. External exam confirms a monocular vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye and torticollis with a right head tilt. His penlight anterior segment exam is grossly normal and dilated fundus exam reveals trace pallor of the right optic nerve. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +1.00 sphere in both eyes. What is the next best step in the care of this patient?

options.A: Order an MRI of the brain and orbits under sedation
options.B: Reassure the parents and have the patient follow-up in one year
options.C: Prescribe glasses and have the patient follow-up in one year
options.D: Initiate patching for 6 hours daily in the left eye.

explanation: Spasmus nutans is a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding. The nystagmus is frequently referred to as "shimmering" due to its high frequency low amplitude nature. The nystagmus is usually horizontal and bilateral although it may be unilateral, vertical, or rotary. It usually presents within the first 2 years of life and then resolves within 1-2 years. Spasmus nutans can closely resemble Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon and vice-versa so most clinicians (and the BCSC) suggest scanning all patients with spasmus nutans to rule out an anterior optic pathway glioma. This patient appropriately underwent an MRI at the time of diagnosis which was normal. After 3 years, however, his nystagmus and torticollis have not resolved which is alarming. Also, this patient has unexplained decreased visual acuity in the right eye along with optic nerve pallor increasing concern for optic nerve pathology such as an anterior optic pathway glioma. When spasmus nutans does not recover as expected or is associated with additional neurological deficits then repeat neuro-imaging is warranted. question: Which of the following is NOT a defining characteristic of jerk nystagmus?

options.A: Nomenclature based on direction of the slow phase
options.B: Consisting of a fast and slow phase

explanation: Nystagmus is a disorder marked by excessive eye movements that are rhythmic. Jerk nystagmus has clear fast and slow phase. By convention the nystagmus is always named based on the direction of the fast phase. Pendular nystagmus is an exception to the fast and slow phase rule because pendular nystagmus consists of two phases with equal velocity and amplitude. Nystagmoid movements such as square wave jerks and superior oblique myokymia are not rhythmic and therefore do not fit these definitions. A.Posterior fossa meningioma B.Chiari type I malformation C.Spinal cord and/or brainstem syrinx D.Cerebellar hemangioma High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Downbeat nystagmus (DBN) is the result of abnormal drift of the eyes upward followed by a corrective downward fast saccade. Most pathology causing DBN localizes to the cervicomedullary junction (CVMJ) or cerebellum. MRI of the brain is warranted for evaluation of DBN because structural lesions of the CVMJ or cerebellum including Arnold-Chiari malformation, mass lesions (meningioma or hemangioma), and syrinx are causes of DBN and may be amenable to surgical intervention. A.5-10 seconds B.15-45 seconds C.1-2 minutes D.2-4 minutes High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) is a form of bilateral, horizontal jerk nystagmus that alternates fast phase directions following a reliable time cycle (usually 2-4 minutes). A return to the static phase occurs after which there is a crescendo / decrescendo jerk nystagmus to the opposite side. The cycle then terminates with another static phase. PAN may be congenital or acquired. When acquired it is usually caused by posterior fossa pathology of the brainstem or cerebellum (especially the vermis of the cerebellum). Because of the reliability of the short cycle and the importance of diagnosis, all patients with horizontal jerk nystagmus should be observed for a minimum of 2 minutes to ensure that the diagnosis of PAN is not missed. For this reason, Kestenbaum surgery or Kestenbaum variants used to shift the null point to primary gaze should be avoided in these patients unless it is clear that the patient always maintains the same null point throughout the PAN cycle. question: Which of the following descriptive terms of nystagmus is correctly defined below?

options.A: Dissociated nystagmus: the amplitude of oscillations differs in each eye
options.B: Disconjugate nystagmus: nystagmus in one eye only
options.C: Null point: the point of gaze where there is no nystagmus
options.D: Disjunctive: nystagmus in one eye only

explanation: Nystagmus terminology can be confusing and standardized tests may take advantage of that confusion. Dissociated nystagmus is a nystagmus where the amplitude of the wave form differs in each eye (for instance the nystagmus is much more pronounced in the right eye than the left). Disconjugate nystagmus (also known as disjunctive nystagmus) occurs when the direction of nystagmus differs between two eyes (for instance a right beating nystagmus in the right eye and a left beating nystagmus in the left eye). A null point is the point of gaze where the nystagmus is least severe. The nystagmus is usually not absent in the null point but dampened. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of spasmus nutans? A.Resolution after 1-2 years B.Onset within the first 2 years of life C.High amplitude horizontal, vertical, or rotary nystagmus D.Abnormal head posturing and nodding High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Spasmus nutans is a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding. The nystagmus is frequently referred to as "shimmering" due to its high frequency low amplitude nature. The nystagmus is usually horizontal and bilateral although it may be unilateral, vertical, or rotary. It usually presents within the first 2 years of life and then resolves within 1-2 years. Aside from an increased incidence of strabismus, spasmus nutans is not associated with other neurological deficits or diseases. Spasmus nutans can closely resemble Heimann- Bielschowsky phenomenon and vice-versa so most clinicians (and the BCSC) suggest scanning all patients with spasmus nutans to rule out an anterior optic pathway glioma. A variety of links have been suggested by OQ users to show spasmus nutans. I believe this link to the University of Utah's NOVEL page is probably the best example and also provides excellent additional didactic narration regarding spasmus nutans. LINK Convergence retraction nystagmus is NOT associated with which of the following exam findings? A.Bilateral superior eyelid retraction B.Lateral gaze palsy C.Abnormal convergence D.Pupillary light-near dissociation High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: Convergence-retraction nystagmus is one component of the dorsal midbrain syndrome (aka Parinaud's syndrome) and is marked by abnormal co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on attempted up-gaze. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is most easily elicited by a holding a down going OKN drum or OKN strip in front of the patient. The patient will momentarily follow one target downward before a fast upward "catch-up" saccade occurs to find the next target. The convergence- retraction nystagmus occurs simultaneously with the attempted fast upward saccade. Other features of dorsal midbrain syndrome include limitation of conjugate upgaze, mid-dilated pupils with light-near dissociation (meaning the pupils constrict more to near than to light), and bilateral superior eyelid retraction (Collier's sign). Other findings associated with dorsal midbrain syndrome but not major components include convergence spasm, convergence insufficiency / paresis, accommodative insufficiency, and skew deviation. Rarely do all of the features of dorsal midbrain syndrome occur in the same patient; the defining and most commonly exhibited characteristic of the syndrome is upgaze palsy. A 20-year-old male comes to see you for vertical binocular diplopia and difficulty focusing after removal of a cerebellar tumor. The relevant portion of his exam is shown in the video below. What is the best term for this patient’s horizontal eye movements? ( video missing ) A.Volitional nystagmus B.Horizontal jerk nystagmus C.Square wave jerks D.Ocular flutter High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient with a clear cause for cerebellar dysfunction shows exam findings typical of square wave jerks (SWJs). For those astute observers, the patient also had a right hypertropia (which can barely be appreciated in the video) related to a skew deviation following his cerebellar tumor excision. SWJs are a type of saccadic intrusion. Unlike nystagmus, square wave jerks lack a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees) although amplitudes can be greater than 5 degrees in which case the name “macrosquare wave jerks” may be used. Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause (or "intersaccadic interval") and then a quick return to fixation. That intersaccadic interval is characteristically 200 msec when mapped with eye movement tracings. Interestingly the term square wave jerk arises from the square waveform on eye movement tracings (see reference links below for examples). SWJs can be physiologic but when there are more than 9 per minute it is typically pathologic. Common causes include cerebellar disease, Parkinson’s disease, and supranuclear palsy. An astute eye care provider will look for signs and inquire about symptoms of Parkinsonism in any patient exhibiting frequent SWJs. If there are additional concerns for Parkinsonism then referral to a Neurologist with experience in movement disorders is indicated. While it might be easy to mistake abundant SWJs for horizontal pendular nystagmus, the intersaccadic interval (time where eyes fixate without moving) is seen only in SWJs. There is clearly no fast phase / slow phase present in this case so jerk nystagmus is not a consideration. Ocular flutter is a sustained horizontal saccadic intrusion without intersaccadic intervals and has a broad differential diagnosis identical to that of opsoclonus. Volitional nystagmus, or voluntary nystagmus, is a skill that up to 8% of the general population can perform. While for some it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work-ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high- frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is usually (but not always) horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than a few seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and convergence movements. One way to fish out voluntary nystagmus is to see if the nystagmus stops as you have the patient follow your finger on motility testing. References: 1. http://www.dizziness-and-balance.com/practice/nystagmus/SWJ.htm 2. http://www.neuroophthalmology.ca/textbook/e-figures/square-wave-jerks-waveforms What is the most accurate means to quantify the severity of an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the clinic? A.The time required for release of the pupil upon swinging a light to the abnormal eye B.The speed and extent of reactivity of the pupil to light in the abnormal eye C.The visual acuity in the abnormal eye D.Neutral density filters High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Many clinicians do not quantify the severity of an APD in practice preferring instead to only document its presence. Some clinicians will comment on whether an APD is questionable, subtle, or brisk. Some clinicians will measure the severity of an APD by using neutral density filters. In a patient with a right APD, neutral density filters are held over the left eye starting with the least dense filter (usually 0.3 log units). The swinging flashlight test is then performed with the filter covering the left eye. If the right pupil still dilates immediately when the flashlight is swung from the left eye to the right eye then the APD is still present. The density of the filter over the left eye is increased to 0.6 log units and the swinging flashlight test is repeated. This continues until the APD has been "neutralized." If too strong of a filter is placed over the better eye then the APD will actually reverse. The density of the filter required to neutralize the APD defines the severity of the APD. The advantage of grading an APD is that it allows an additional objective means (along with visual acuity, color vision, and visual fields) to follow a patient for possible progression of optic nerve pathology. If only the presence of an APD is documented then it is impossible to know if the APD gets worse over time. Approximately what percentage of eyes affected by demyelinating optic neuritis demonstrate optic disc edema? A.35% B.55% C.75% D.95% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The optic neuritis treatment trial (ONTT) showed that most optic nerves (65%) in demyelinating optic neuritis were normal appearing. Also, the ONTT found that eyes with peripapillary optic nerve hemorrhages had a markedly reduced risk of developing multiple sclerosis compared to all eyes with optic neuritis. Which of the following types of nystagmus usually has a delayed onset presenting months to years following an inciting stroke of the brainstem? A.Oculopalatal myoclonus B.Periodic alternating nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.See-saw nystagmus High Yield: Yes Your Answer: C Correct Answer: A Explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is very unique and is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) (answer choice B) is a peculiar form of nystagmus with a cyclical transition of right beating to left beating jerk nystagmus. For a short period in the middle of the cycle there may be no apparent or minimal nystagmus and there can even be shift null points depending on where in the cycle the patient is. A complete PAN cycle usually lasts around 4 minutes. PAN may be acquired from a lesion of the cerebellum (particularly the nodulus or uvulua) or may be congenital. Acquired PAN often improves with baclofen (high yield testing point). Upbeat nystagmus (UBN) (answer choice C) is characterized by a slow drift down followed by a corrective fast saccade up. UBN localizes to the brainstem (typically the medulla) and the anterior cerebellar vermis. Common causes include thiamine deficiency (which often starts as UBN and transitions to DBN with time), demyelination, stroke, and cerebellar degeneration. See-saw nystagmus (SSN)(answer choice D) is characterized by rhythmic alternating of one eye elevating and incyclotorting while the other eye simultaneously depresses and excylotorts followed by the reverse movement. SSN is highly localizable to the midbrain and parasellar region. It is not unusual for SSN patients to exhibit bitemporal hemianopic field defects and bilateral optic atrophy because the parasellar lesion causing the nystagmus also results in disruption of the nearby visual pathways. Hence SSN is a rare example of when both nystagmus and visual field defects can be caused by one lesion.

( video missing ) A.Volitional nystagmus B.Horizontal jerk nystagmus C.Square wave jerks D.Ocular flutter High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient with a clear cause for cerebellar dysfunction shows exam findings typical of square wave jerks (SWJs). For those astute observers, the patient also had a right hypertropia (which can barely be appreciated in the video) related to a skew deviation following his cerebellar tumor excision. SWJs are a type of saccadic intrusion. Unlike nystagmus, square wave jerks lack a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees) although amplitudes can be greater than 5 degrees in which case the name “macrosquare wave jerks” may be used. Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause (or "intersaccadic interval") and then a quick return to fixation. That intersaccadic interval is characteristically 200 msec when mapped with eye movement tracings. Interestingly the term square wave jerk arises from the square waveform on eye movement tracings (see reference links below for examples). SWJs can be physiologic but when there are more than 9 per minute it is typically pathologic. Common causes include cerebellar disease, Parkinson’s disease, and supranuclear palsy. An astute eye care provider will look for signs and inquire about symptoms of Parkinsonism in any patient exhibiting frequent SWJs. If there are additional concerns for Parkinsonism then referral to a Neurologist with experience in movement disorders is indicated. While it might be easy to mistake abundant SWJs for horizontal pendular nystagmus, the intersaccadic interval (time where eyes fixate without moving) is seen only in SWJs. There is clearly no fast phase / slow phase present in this case so jerk nystagmus is not a consideration. Ocular flutter is a sustained horizontal saccadic intrusion without intersaccadic intervals and has a broad differential diagnosis identical to that of opsoclonus. Volitional nystagmus, or voluntary nystagmus, is a skill that up to 8% of the general population can perform. While for some it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work-ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high- frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is usually (but not always) horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than a few seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and convergence movements. One way to fish out voluntary nystagmus is to see if the nystagmus stops as you have the patient follow your finger on motility testing. The swinging flashlight test is then performed with the filter covering the left eye. Which of the following types of nystagmus usually has a delayed onset presenting months to years following an inciting stroke of the brainstem? A.Oculopalatal myoclonus B.Periodic alternating nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.See-saw nystagmus High Yield: Yes Your Answer: C Correct Answer: A Explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is very unique and is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) (answer choice B) is a peculiar form of nystagmus with a cyclical transition of right beating to left beating jerk nystagmus. For a short period in the middle of the cycle there may be no apparent or minimal nystagmus and there can even be shift null points depending on where in the cycle the patient is. A complete PAN cycle usually lasts around 4 minutes. PAN may be acquired from a lesion of the cerebellum (particularly the nodulus or uvulua) or may be congenital. Acquired PAN often improves with baclofen (high yield testing point). Upbeat nystagmus (UBN) (answer choice C) is characterized by a slow drift down followed by a corrective fast saccade up. UBN localizes to the brainstem (typically the medulla) and the anterior cerebellar vermis. Common causes include thiamine deficiency (which often starts as UBN and transitions to DBN with time), demyelination, stroke, and cerebellar degeneration. See-saw nystagmus (SSN)(answer choice D) is characterized by rhythmic alternating of one eye elevating and incyclotorting while the other eye simultaneously depresses and excylotorts followed by the reverse movement. SSN is highly localizable to the midbrain and parasellar region. It is not unusual for SSN patients to exhibit bitemporal hemianopic field defects and bilateral optic atrophy because the parasellar lesion causing the nystagmus also results in disruption of the nearby visual pathways. Hence SSN is a rare example of when both nystagmus and visual field defects can be caused by one lesion.

question: Convergence retraction nystagmus is NOT associated with which of the following exam findings?
explanation: Convergence-retraction nystagmus is one component of the dorsal midbrain syndrome (aka Parinaud's syndrome) and is marked by abnormal co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on attempted up-gaze. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is most easily elicited by a holding a down going OKN drum or OKN strip in front of the patient. The patient will momentarily follow one target downward before a fast upward "catch-up" saccade occurs to find the next target. The convergence- retraction nystagmus occurs simultaneously with the attempted fast upward saccade. Other features of dorsal midbrain syndrome include limitation of conjugate upgaze, mid-dilated pupils with light-near dissociation (meaning the pupils constrict more to near than to light), and bilateral superior eyelid retraction (Collier's sign). Other findings associated with dorsal midbrain syndrome but not major components include convergence spasm, convergence insufficiency / paresis, accommodative insufficiency, and skew deviation. Rarely do all of the features of dorsal midbrain syndrome occur in the same patient; the defining and most commonly exhibited characteristic of the syndrome is upgaze palsy. question: Which of the following types of nystagmus usually has a delayed onset presenting months to years following an inciting stroke of the brainstem?
explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is very unique and is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) (answer choice B) is a peculiar form of nystagmus with a cyclical transition of right beating to left beating jerk nystagmus. For a short period in the middle of the cycle there may be no apparent or minimal nystagmus and there can even be shift null points depending on where in the cycle the patient is. A complete PAN cycle usually lasts around 4 minutes. PAN may be acquired from a lesion of the cerebellum (particularly the nodulus or uvulua) or may be congenital. question: A 60-year-old Caucasian male comes in for a routine glasses check. His eye exam is essentially normal and he is getting ready to leave when he mentions that his chin has been numb for the last month. He denies any trauma and has no explanation for his symptoms. He has normal cranial nerve function except for subjective numbness in the chin region. What would be the most appropriate line of questioning considering his symptoms?

options.A: Ask about risk factors for and symptoms of diabetes
options.B: Ask about history of alcohol use
options.C: Take a detailed family history of neurological disease
options.D: Inquire about prior history of cancer

explanation: "Numb chin syndrome" or mental nerve neuropathy is highly concerning for malignancy. The most common associated malignancies affecting the mental nerve are lymphoma and metastatic breast carcinoma but many other malignancies have been reported to cause this syndrome including: osteosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, plasmacytoma, metastatic lung cancer, and metastatic prostate cancer. Sarcoidosis has also been described as a cause of mental nerve neuropathy.

question: Which of the following is NOT associated with palinopsia?

options.A: Medications including topiramate, clomiphene, and trazodone

explanation: Palinopsia is a phenomenon marked by the persistence or recurrence of images following removal of the stimulus from the visual field. The most common cause is a lesion of the parieto- occipital region (usually the non-dominant, right side of brain) with an associated contralateral hemi-field visual field defect. In this instance, the phenomenon usually occurs within the blind portion of the visual field. Also associated are topiramate, clomiphene, trazodone, and prior use of hallucinogenic drugs (especially LSD and mushrooms). Episodic migraine associated palinopsia has been described as well. There are isolated reports of palinopsia related to epileptiform activity in the parieto-occipital region although most neuro-ophthalmologists do not believe that palinopsia in most cases is a seizure-related phenomenon. Papilledema has not been associated with palinopsia. Vision can subjectively take on what color in digoxin toxicity? A.Yellow / Green B.Red / orange C.Blue D.Brown High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Chromatopsia is the illusion of vision exhibiting an abnormal color. Digoxin toxicity-related chromatopsia is usually described as a yellow (i.e. "xanthopsia") or yellowish green hue throughout the visual field. It is typically reversible with cessation or decreased dose of the drug. These visual effects can occur despite "normal" serum level of digoxin on lab testing. ERG may reveal cone dysfunction in these patients. Sildenafil (Viagra) has been reported to result in a blue chromatopsia and this illusion may be a harbinger of an underlying risk in certain individuals for more serious ocular pathology such as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) due to sildenafil (and related erectile dysfunction (ED) drugs). The exact association between ED drugs and NAION is still quite controversial. Which of the following is true of focal occipital lobe seizures? A.They typically last for 1-2 seconds B.In children, they are usually associated with structural lesions such as tumors C.They typically manifest with unformed hallucinations or positive visual phenomena D.They usually occur without other motor signs of seizures The Patient with Illusions, Hallucinations, and Disorders of Higher Cortical Function High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: Occipital lobe seizures are usually a form of benign self-limited epilepsy in children (in other words not associated with a structural lesion of the brain) while in adults there is often a clearly identifiable structural lesion on imaging. Seizure activity of the primary visual cortex typically results in unformed positive visual phenomena such as binocular flashing lights and geometric shapes in the contralateral hemifield of the seizure focus. They usually last 1-2 minutes but can last hours and even days. They usually are associated with other signs such as rapid bilateral eyelid blinking, eye flutter, or eye deviation. Complex visual hallucinations are more typical of temporal lobe seizures or parietal lobe seizures (which are very rare). What is the name of the "nystagmus-like" eye movement that is not a true nystagmus but rather a type of saccadic intrusion? It lacks a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Usually witnessed when a patient is fixating, it results in horizontal shifting away from fixation followed by a brief pause and then returns back to fixation. A.Opsoclonus B.Square-wave jerk C.Superior oblique myokymia D.Ocular dysmetria Topic: The Patient with Illusions, Hallucinations, and Disorders of Higher Cortical Function High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Square-wave jerks (SWJs) are a "nystagmoid" eye movement that is not a true nystagmus but rather a type of saccadic intrusion. It lacks a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause and then a quick return to fixation. They are often seen in normal patients but when there are more than 9 square-wave jerks per minute the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease or progressive supranuclear palsy should be considered (both commonly exhibit numerous square-wave jerks). Superior oblique myokymia is a high frequency monocular oscillation caused by spontaneous firing of the superior oblique muscle. Opsoclonus is also known as saccadomania and is a dramatic bilateral eye movement disorder marked by involuntary multidirectional saccades without an intersaccadic quiet interval. Ocular dysmetria is a over shoot or undershoot of the eyes upon refixation to a new target and is loosely suggestive of cerebellar pathology. which of the following is NOT a classic feature of Balint syndrome? A.Object agnosia B.Optic ataxia C.Ocular apraxia D.Simultagnosia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Balint syndrome is due to bilateral parieto-occipital lesions. The classic triad includes optic ataxia, acquired ocular motor apraxia, and simultagnosia although most cases of Balint syndrome do not clearly demonstrate all three findings. The underlying etiology is usually either bilateral strokes or cortical dysfunction from a variant of Alzheimer's disease which predominately affects the parieto-occipital region known as posterior cortical atrophy (or the visual variant of Alzheimer's disease). Optic ataxia is essentially acquired poor hand-eye coordination caused by a disconnect between vision and motor functions. There are many other causes of poor hand-eye coordination so this is not that helpful in making a diagnosis of Balint syndrome. Ocular apraxia is difficulty initiating saccades. Simultagnosia is the most prevalent component of the Balint syndrome triad and is also arguably the most useful sign to look for on examination. It is the failure to understand the entire meaning of a picture despite retaining the ability to recognize isolated objects within the picture. In other words, patients with simultagnosia can not "see the forest through the trees." Simultagnosia is often tested for by using the "cookie theft picture" and asking the patient to give an account of what is happening in the picture. Object agnosia is the inability to visually recognize objects despite being able to recognize objects based on touch or description. Hallucinations and illusions are related but clearly distinct subjective visual phenomena with differing etiologies. Which of the following is associated with hallucinations as opposed to illusions? A.Metamorphopsia B.Pulfrich phenomenon C.Micropsia D.Photopsias High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Illusions are an optical or cortical distortion of an object seen in reality. Metamorphopsia describes an abnormal subjective curvature or waviness to objects that in reality are straight. It usually occurs as a result of macular disease such as macular degeneration or epiretinal membrane. The Pulfrich phenomenon is the illusion that an object moving perpendicular to a person's line of sight is actually moving toward them or away from them. Theoretically, it could be seen in any disease affecting the conduction of visual information in one optic nerve more than the other. It is usually described in patients who have partially recovered following a bout of optic neuritis. Micropsia is the illusion that objects appear smaller than they should and is indicative of macular pathology, parietal lobe pathology, or an unusual migraine headache related phenomenon known as the "Alice in Wonderland" effect. Photopsias associated with cancer associated retinopathy, MEWDS, AZOOR, birdshot chorioretinopathy, and PVD are all simple, unformed hallucinations because they do not arise from distortion of an object in reality. A 78-year-old man presents six months following a stroke. He is left with a right-sided visual field defect but retains 20/20 vision in both eyes. The patient’s greatest complaint is difficulty with reading. When given a sample text to read, the patient cannot form any of the words, and instead reads each letter individually. The patient otherwise speaks and writes fluidly, and easily comprehends the examiners commands. The patient’s lesion localizes best to which of the following? A.Left occipital lobe B.Left parietal lobe C.Left occipitotemporal lobe D.Right optic nerve High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The patient has alexia (inability to read) without agraphia (inability to write) which localizes to a lesion of the left occipital lobe, with ipsilateral involvement of the splenium of the corpus callosum and adjacent periventricular white matter. The disrupted pathway that is responsible for the deficit is shown in the image. The left angular gyrus converts written to spoken language and receives visual input from the occipital lobe. If a lesion of the left occipital lobe occurs, visual information can only be received from the right occipital lobe via outflow from the corpus callosum and periventricular white matter. Simultaneous involvement of the outflow tract and left occipital lobe will therefore leave patients with alexia and a right homonymous hemianopsia. However, patients will be able to write, speak, repeat, and comprehend without difficulty. The cause of the lesion is most commonly a posterior cerebral artery distribution stroke. The video shows an example of a patient with a new hemorrhagic stroke involving the left occipital-parietal lobe and splenium of the corpus callosum. He is able to write words that are prompted to him but is immediately unable to read back. Less commonly, patients can present with alexia without agraphia with a preserved visual field. This may be possible if the lesion spares the striate cortex of the left occipital lobe, but still interferes with the transfer of information from the left and right occipital lobes to the left angular gyrus. WRONG ANSWERS: • B. The parietal lobe is involved in the “where” pathway of higher cortical visual function that involves spatial recognition of objects. Right parietal lesions can result in left sided hemineglect and difficulty with localization of objects in the left visual field. Less commonly, left parietal lesions can result in right sided neglect, but this tends to be less severe and recovers more quickly. • C. The occipitotemporal lobe is involved in the “what” pathway of higher cortical visual function that involves object recognition. Lesions of this pathway can lead to visual agnosia (difficulty with object recognition), hemiachromatopsia (loss of color perception in one hemifield), and prosopagnosia (difficulty with facial recognition). • D. A right optic nerve lesion would not be expected to produce a hemifield defect. Numerous (> 9 per minute) square-wave jerks can be a sign of what disease? A.Parkinson's disease B.Occipital lobe stroke C.Lead poisoning D.Alzheimer's disease High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Square-wave jerks (SWJs) are a "nystagmoid" eye movement that is not a true nystagmus but rather a type of saccadic intrusion. It lacks a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause and then a quick return to fixation. SWJs are often seen in normal patients but when there are more than 9 per minute, the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease or progressive supranuclear palsy should be considered (both commonly exhibit numerous square-wave jerks).

question: A 14-month-old child presents to your clinic after his mom noted his eyes "shaking" since about 3 months of age. He is small for his age and is significantly delayed in meeting all of his milestones. His mom fears that he does not see well. On examination you note fixation with intermittent following in both eyes. His pupils react to light and do not show an afferent pupillary defect. He has grossly full motility in both eyes and no strabismus. He does have prominent pendular nystagmus. The macula, vessels, and peripheral retina examination is normal in both eyes. His optic nerves are displayed above along with a recent MRI section demonstrating an important finding. What is the next most appropriate step?
explanation: This child has septo-optic dysplasia (SOD) which is a congenital disease characterized by midline brain development abnormalities and unilateral or bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia. Vision can range from near normal to severely impaired. Nystagmus is frequently present and develops around age 1-4 months when the pathways required for normal fixation typically mature. All children with optic nerve hypoplasia should have an MRI of the brain and an endocrine evaluation because anomalies in brain development and hypopituitarism are common. Growth hormone (GH) deficiency is the most common endocrinopathy found in approximately 70% of children with SOD while hypothyroidism, adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency, and diabetes insipidus are less common. Any disease with a highly effective treatment (hormone replacement in this instance), is high yield on standardized tests so commit these facts to memory. An ERG would not be helpful in this case because the patient's optic nerves are hypoplastic and can explain the patient's poor vision and nystagmus. There is no need to look for a retina etiology. There are only isolated reports of familial SOD so genetic counseling is not necessary. An FA would have no utility in this situation. The coronal section of a T1-weighted MRI above demonstrates the absence of a septum pellucidum. As you may recall from medical school neuro-anatomy, the septum pellucidum is a thin, vertical membrane separating the left and right lateral ventricles of the brain. The structure itself has no known function and it is not rare to find normal individuals with an absent septum pellucidum on MRI. In some individuals, however, agenesis of the septum pellucidum is a sign of septo-optic dysplasia (aka "de Morsier syndrome") supported in this patient by his hypoplastic optic nerves. Responding to a request from our users, below you can see a modified version of this patient's optic nerves to better highlight the pathology. The inner green circle indicates the margin of this patient's actual hypoplastic optic nerve consisting of retinal ganglion cell axons, the area from the inner green circle to the outer black circle is a region of retinal atrophy in the location of the intended scleral canal (in other words where the optic nerve was supposed to have inserted if it were of normal size). This finding is sometimes referred to as the "double ring" sign. The optic nerve hypoplasia in this case is more obvious in the left eye (center image). It is not unusual for there to be asymmetry in the degree of optic nerve hypoplasia in any one given patient- some patients with SOD may even have one completely normal appearing optic nerve. Which of the following is least likely to occur with a diagnosis of optic disc drusen (ODD)? A.slowly-progressive nasal visual field defects respecting the horizontal meridian B.permanent decreased central visual acuity C.peripapillary choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM) formation D.transient visual obscurations (TVOs) Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Optic disc drusen are proteinaceous nodules that can be calcified. They usually remain buried deep in the optic nerve early in life and then extrude themselves over time. As they surface at the entrance of the nerve fiber layer to the optic disc, they are theorized to block axoplasmic flow. This cessation of axonal function may lead to the "nerve fiber layer type" progressive visual field defects exhibited in ODD. Because they disrupt normal architecture of the retina and nerve head, they can be associated with CNVM formation. A small percentage of patients (< 10%) may suffer transient visual obscurations lasting seconds believed to be due to transient ischemia of the nerve head (episodes similar to TVOs from papilledema). Decreased central visual acuity is a harbinger of other pathology unrelated to ODD and should prompt a work-up for compressive lesions. Rarely, ODD is associated with non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy.

question: A 75-year-old veteran with a 60 pack-year history of smoking and alcohol abuse comes in with a complaint of 2 years of progressive vision loss. Which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient taking into account the visual field shown above? (note that the right eye shows similar fields and nerve appearance)
explanation: The visual field presented is a Goldmann visual field demonstrating a central scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows severe disc edema related to elevated intracranial pressure. Papilledema is associated with enlargement of the blind spot in the early stages and nerve fiber layer defects in the later stages. Central vision is typically spared until the late stages in papilledema similar to glaucoma. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated central visual field defect. Image D shows mild to moderate temporal pallor which can be associated with many different visual field defects including isolated central visual field defects.

question: in the axial cut of the FLAIR sequence MRI shown above, what structure does the tip of arrow "A" touch?
explanation: The superior ophthalmic vein begins superonasally in the orbit at the junction of the supratrochlear, supraorbital, and angular veins. It then passes posterolaterally in the superior portion of the orbit (superior to the optic nerve and inferior to the superior rectus muscle) before exiting the orbit at the superior orbital fissure and draining into the cavernous sinus. The importance of this structure should not be underestimated since enlargement of the SOV is an indicator of poor venous drainage through the cavernous sinus. SOV enlargement is a prominent feature in anteriorly draining carotid cavernous fistulas and in cavernous sinus thrombosis. Cranial nerves can be seen on MRI but would not be nearly as prominent as the SOV seen here (this SOV is not pathologically enlarged). Arrow "B" points to the left optic nerve. Arrow "C' points to the left optic tract. Arrow "D' points to the midbrain (identifiable by the “mickey mouse” sign).

question: What is the diagnosis in this case?
explanation: This is a classic presentation and video of ocular neuromyotonia of the right abducens nerve. Ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) is a rare diagnosis which can cause episodic diplopia. Most commonly associated with previous skull-base radiation treatment, the onset of this disease is usually months-to-years after the radiation treatment. The diplopia episodes last from seconds to minutes and are generally very stereotypical involving the same cranial nerve innervating the same muscles every episode. ONM can affect any muscle innervated by any ocular motor cranial nerve (CN III, IV, or VI) and the diplopia is often triggered by activation of the involved nerve or muscle as in this case. In other words, this patient with right abducens involved ONM triggers his episodes by looking to the right and increasing innervational tone to the right lateral rectus muscle. Similar to this patient, looking away from the involved muscle (thus decreasing innervational tone to the involved muscle / nerve) often helps to break an attack. This patient’s video shows a fascinating additional finding of palpebral fissure narrowing on the right side with apparent globe retraction when he attempts to look left during an attack of ONM. This occurs because ONM defies Sherrington’s law of reciprocal innervation. According to this law, when the right medial rectus contracts the right lateral rectus should relax. In this case during the attack there is simultaneous contraction of both the lateral rectus and the medial rectus leading to impaired adduction in the right eye and temporary right globe retraction into the orbit with apparent ptosis. Once the ONM episode resolves the patient’s enophthalmos and ptosis resolve. ONM is thought to occur because of ephaptic neural transmission which occurs when there is conduction of neural impulses across parallel neurons. In normal neuronal impulses, conduction between neurons occurs exclusively at synapses. When damage has occurred to the myelin of cranial nerves 3,4,or 6 then abnormal “cross-talk” between parallel neuron axons can occur leading to a pathologic increase in innervational tone in that nerve or nerve branch. The other simple way to think of it is a “short circuit” causing a transient increase in tone. ONM typically responds very well to anticonvulsant treatment (e.g. carbamazepine or gabapentin). Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an excellent consideration in any patient with intermittent diplopia. MG is a variable disease and would virtually never be expected to cause the exact same type of diplopia for 5 years. Furthermore, between episodes this patient’s alignment was completely normal. In MG, diplopia episodes typically last much longer, are more variable in quality, and are accompanied by evidence of fatigability on exam. This patient had no fatigue on prolonged upgaze and no orbicularis oculi weakness which are two of the most helpful tests on exam for patients with ocular involvement by MG. Seizures essentially never cause isolated unilateral eye movement abnormalities. Furthermore, a seizure causing recurrent bilateral eye movement abnormalities in isolation would still be extremely unlikely. Duane syndrome (DS) is a congenital eye movement disorder thought to be due to agenesis or dysgenesis of the 6th nerve nucleus and cranial nerve resulting in failure to abduct and/or adduct (depending on the subtype of Duane syndrome). DS comes in 3 forms depending on whether there is abnormal abduction (type 1), adduction (type 2), or both (type 3). While type 2 DS could cause impaired adduction with globe retraction on attempted adduction, it would result in constant rather than intermittent motility deficits and is congenital (not acquired as in this case).
