Though this clinical vignette wants you to jump to the diagnosis of pseudotumor cerebri, you MUST get neuro-imaging to exclude other causes of papilledema. These other causes include an intracranial tumor, hydrocephalus, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, and venous thrombosis. Though CT with contrast is sometimes used, MRI of the brain is preferred since it is more sensitive for detecting the various causes of increased ICP. MRV is also typically performed at the same time due to its convenience and ability to help rule-in/out venous sinus thrombosis. Finally, it is important to note that this patient is taking isotretinoin which is a vitamin A derivative medication and is a known cause of intracranial hypertension. In this case the work- up for probable papilledema needs to be completed but you would also want to stop isotretinoin. A patient has his right eye pharmacologically dilated while his left eye remains undilated. Assume that he has a known longstanding right afferent pupillary defect from prior exams. You know that to properly assess for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) you must hold a light indirectly on the _______ eye while a direct light is swung back and forth between the eyes. In this particular case the ______ pupil will dilate when direct light is swung from the _______ eye to the _______ eye. A.left; left; right; left B.left; left; left; right C.right; left; left; right D.It is not possible to assess for a RAPD in this scenario Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Dilation of one eye does not prevent the accurate assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). If one eye is dilated, simply hold a dim indirect light source to the side of the undilated eye (in this case the left eye) and perform the swinging flashlight test. If the undilated eye has a RAPD then it will dilate as expected when the flashlight is swung over from the dilated eye. If the dilated eye has a RAPD, the undilated eye will dilate when the flashlight is swung from the undilated eye to the dilated eye. Some refer to this as checking for a RAPD "by reverse" but others object to the use of this terminology calling it a misnomer. Misnomer or not, most ophthalmologists understand what is meant by assessing a RAPD "by reverse." Which of the following medications has been implicated as a cause of intracranial hypertension? A.cyclosporine B.furosemide (Lasix) C.sildenafil (Viagra) D.escitalopram (Lexapro) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: It is important to know the medicines that are associated with drug-induced intracranial hypertension. The more commonly implicated drugs include: vitamin A and vitamin A derivatives (isotretinoin), the tetracycline family of antibiotics, cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, prednisone (both the use and sudden withdrawal), and synthetic growth hormone. Lasix is actually a second-line treatment for IIH patients. Viagra has a questionable association with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. A 75-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol and cigarette use comes to your clinic today with a 2-month history of progressive visual loss in both eyes to 20/100 best corrected with associated prominent photopsias in both eyes. Exam one month ago by an outside ophthalmologist found 20/50 vision in both eyes with global depression on a reliable 24-2 Humphrey visual field. An electroretinogram (ERG) was performed a week ago and showed marked reduction in amplitude of both rod and cone function. Aside from his vision and mild vitritis OU, his ocular exam today is unremarkable (including normal pupils and fundus OU). What would be the next best step in diagnosis of this patient? A.optic nerve optical coherence tomography (OCT) B.thyroid function studies C.CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis D.fluorescein angiography (FA) High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient has a classic presentation for cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) although melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) is also a definite consideration. CAR and MAR are both paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndromes which share many similar features including progressive vision loss with photopsias and nyctalopia. Both diseases often have normal fundus findings until late in the disease course when retinal arterioles may become attenuated with thinning of the RPE and atrophy of the optic nerve. CAR tends to present with both Cone And Rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) and MAR Mostly Affects Rods although either can affect rods and/or cones (shout out to OQ user "Grimlock" for that memory aid. A late onset acquired retinal rod or cone dysfunction on ERG is highly suggestive of CAR or MAR. Vitritis (often mild as in this case) may or may not be present on exam in either MAR and CAR- both have been reported in the literature but vitritis is not required for the diagnosis. About 50% of patients with CAR have a known diagnosis of cancer at onset of ocular disease while the vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. The most common inciting malignancy in CAR is small cell carcinoma of the lung although other carcinomas of the lungs, breast, uterus, and cervix have also been associated. While new generation OCTs of the macula may show non-specific pathologic changes of the outer retina with CAR / MAR, an OCT of the optic nerve would expected to be normal in CAR / MAR and would not prove useful in this case. Patients with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) usually show signs of either eyelid retraction, eye muscle motility disturbance, strabismus, or proptosis on exam AND thyroid function tests can be low, high, or normal in patients with TAO so it is only a marginally useful test. A FA would not be expected to show any abnormalities that would aid diagnosis in this patient. An 80-year-old Veteran who enjoys his cigarettes, rum, and junk food presents with visual decline in both eyes over 1 year with an objective decline in serial measurements of VA and color vision bilaterally. Both eyes show a similar visual field and optic nerve appearance. In the context of a normal macular exam, which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient with the visual field shown above? A.Image A B.Image B C.Image C D.Image D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The visual field presented is a Humphrey automated 24-2 visual field of the left eye demonstrating a cecocentral scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history strongly suggestive of a combined nutritional optic neuropathy and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve but is the typical appearance associated with nutritional and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Generally this causes relatively symmetric bilateral central / cecocentral vision loss due to loss of the papillomacular bundle causing temporal atrophy of the optic nerve. While we all like clean diagnoses (e.g. vitamin B-12 deficiency or copper deficiency) many patients with this type of optic neuropathy have a "dirty diagnosis" full of both poisons (smoking and drinking) and vitamin deficiency from poor nutrition leading to mitochondrial failure of the retinal ganglion cells of the papillomacular bundle. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling or pallor is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows a severely swollen, hyperemic optic nerve with surrounding exudates that would be typical for a patient presenting with increased intracranial pressure (i.e. papilledema) (e.g. from pseudotumor cerebri, compressive tumor, or venous sinus thrombosis). Papilledema does not typically cause a cecocentral scotoma. Instead it causes enlarged blind spots and glaucomatous type field defects. End stage severe papilledema, like end-stage glaucoma, can cause central vision loss once the periphery is lost. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated cecocentral visual field defect. According to the Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial, what is the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement in patients with acute monocular non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.1-2% B.12-19% C.25-35% D.50-60% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a fact that must be memorized. For comparison, the rate of contralateral involvement in patients with untreated monocular vision loss from arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis is estimated to be 54-95% within weeks. OQ users have been frustrated by apparently different statistics in different "reputable sources" regarding the risk of contralateral NAION in a patient who suffers unilateral NAION. The current neuro BCSC states that "the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement is 15%." This is based on very good data from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study which found the rate to be 14.7% in 5 years.1 Different statistics quoted by review manuals may be looking at lifetime risk (rather than 5 year risk) or may be quoting smaller studies. OQ has researched this topic thoroughly and we are sticking with the current BCSC text on this question. Don't send us hateful comments if your review manual has a different statistic. 1Newman NJ, Scherer R, Langenberg P, Kelman S, Feldon S, Kaufman D, Dickersin K; Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial Research Group. The fellow eye in NAION: report from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study. Am J Ophthalmol. 2002 Sep;134(3):317-28. What is the term for vision which deteriorates in brighter light? A.hemeralopia B.photophobia C.metamorphopsia D.palinopsia High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Photophobia is a "fear of light" or sensitivity to light. While closely related to hemeralopia, or deterioration of vision in higher light environments, it is not the same. Hemeralopia is often described in patients with cone dystrophy. Metamorphopsia is a distortion of vision where straight objects appear wavy or crooked. Metamorphopsia typically is described by patients with macular disease. Palinopsia is an illusion marked by the preservation of images or "afterimages." Palinopsia can occur as an isolated visual phenomenon or in association with medications, hallucinogenic drugs, seizure disorders, and/or visual pathway lesions. A 60-year old male with no past ocular history undergoes a 6-hour cardiac bypass surgery. When he awakes from surgery he is found to have hand motion vision in both eyes. Aside from his abnormal vision, sluggish pupillary function, and pupillary light-near dissociation, his exam is unremarkable (including his dilated fundus exam). What is the most likely diagnosis? A.Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy B.Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy C.Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy D.Dorsal midbrain syndrome High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) is much rarer than anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but similarly is believed to be related to hypoperfusion of the posterior optic nerve. Usually the hypoperfusion is due to a perfect storm of contributing risk factors including anemia, hypotension, poor cardiac output, hypovolemia, and cardiopulmonary instability during surgery. Rarely PION can be related to a vasculitic process including giant cell arteritis, lupus-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa, and VZV related vasculitis. Unlike anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, PION almost always has a normal appearing optic nerve in the acute phase. Dorsal midbrain syndrome does include pupillary light-near dissociation, but has other findings not exhibited in this patient and does not typically result in sudden bilateral vision loss. As an aside, any disease process causing bilateral optic neuropathy can result in pupillary light-near dissociation. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. She reports severe left eye pain that is worse with eye movement. Her examination shows 20/20 vision in the right eye and 20/25 vision in the left eye. She has normal color vision, alignment, IOP, and motility. Her pupils show a left afferent pupillary defect. Her right eye exam is essentially normal. Confrontation fields are diffusely constricted in the left eye. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What type of optic neuropathy does this patient have? A.Demyelinating optic neuritis B.Ischemic optic neuropathy C.Optic perineuritis D.Nutritional optic neuropathy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The image shows a coronal section of a T1-weighted, fat-saturated post-contrast MRI. The MRI shows marked enhancement and slight thickening of the optic nerve sheath while the optic nerve itself shows very little enhancement. Optic nerve sheath enhancement can be seen in optic nerve sheath meningiomas and optic perineuritis (OPN). This patient’s acute presentation and pain with eye movement is suggestive of optic perineuritis. Defined by inflammation of the meninges surrounding the optic nerve, OPN is a radiologic and pathologic diagnosis. The era of MRI has enabled increased recognition of this entity while in the past these cases may have been categorized as “optic neuritis” or “atypical optic neuritis.” OPN is generally considered on the spectrum of orbital pseudotumor because in many cases there is concomitant orbital inflammation and like orbital pseudotumor it is usually idiopathic inflammation. Additional known etiologies of OPN, however, include sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, tuberculosis and syphilis. Without the MRI to aide in the diagnosis of OPN, it is virtually indistinguishable from demyelinating optic neuritis (DON). In contrast to DON, OPN has a reported slight tendency to less commonly involve the central visual field, often occurs alongside other radiographic and clinical findings of orbital inflammation, and is exquisitely steroid responsive. As we alluded to above, reasons to distinguish OPN from DON is that OPN: 1) Does not carry the same risk of future multiple sclerosis as DON; and 2) Requires a laboratory evaluation to rule-out other causes such as sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, tuberculosis and syphilis. Ingestion of which of the following substances causes an acute, bilateral toxic optic neuropathy with associated severe vision loss and disc edema? A.Ethambutol B.Ethanol C.Chloramphenicol D.Methanol High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Chronic use of ethambutol, ethanol, chloramphenicol, hydroxyquinolones, penicillamine, cisplatin, and vincristine are associated with chronic toxic optic neuropathy. Chronic toxic optic neuropathy and chronic nutritional neuropathy from B-12 / folate / thiamine classically result in diminished central visual acuity from central / cecocentral scotomas with selective loss of the papillomacular nerve fiber layer and optic nerve pallor. Methanol and ethylene glycol toxicity, however, occurs immediately with ingestion and results in devastating acute, diffuse vision loss with associated disc edema. A.A right optic nerve lesion B.A right optic tract lesion C.A right optic radiation lesion D.A right-sided lesion of the primary visual cortex High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: A lesion of the optic tract often results in an afferent pupillary defect of the contralateral eye. This is thought to occur because there are more crossed than uncrossed pupillary fibers in the optic tract. A lesion of the right optic tract results in decreased afferent input from both retinas but relatively-speaking there is a more marked reduction of afferent input from the contralateral eye. This is a simple concept yet often trips students up. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. She reports severe left eye pain that is worse with eye movement. Her examination shows 20/20 vision in the right eye and 20/25 vision in the left eye. She has normal color vision, alignment, IOP, and motility. Her pupils show a left afferent pupillary defect. Her right eye exam is essentially normal. Confrontation fields are diffusely constricted in the left eye. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What would NOT be considered in the differential for this patient’s optic neuropathy? A.Demyelinating optic neuritis associated with multiple sclerosis B.Granulomatosis with polyangiitis C.Syphilis D.Sarcoidosis High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The image shows a coronal section of a T1-weighted, fat-saturated post-contrast MRI. Additional known etiologies of OPN, however, include sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis (now renamed granulomatosis with polygangitis), tuberculosis and syphilis. question: A 60-year-old patient presents with a homonymous heminanopsia, but with normal visual acuity. Which of the following is the most common cause of this visual field defect in an adult?
explanation: While the cause is usually ischemic stroke, any patient found to have a previously undiagnosed homonymous hemianopia on routine exam must have neuro-imaging for further evaluation (preferably an MRI). Often these patients will complain of blurred vision in one eye on the side of the homonymous hemianopia instead of realizing that the vision loss is actually in both eyes. The most common cause of unilateral retrochiasmal visual loss (i.e. which would produce a homonymous hemianopsia) in adults is a stroke (~60% of cases). The other major causes of this visual field defect in adults is from trauma (~10%) and hemorrhage (~10%). In contrast, the most common cause of retrochiasmal visual loss in children is from trauma and tumors (or the surgical resection necessary for their removal). A lesion of the right optic tract might be expected to result in what finding? A.an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the left eye B.an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the right eye C.a right homonymous hemianopia (in both eyes) D.a left hemianopia in the right eye only High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Optic tract lesions classically result in a contralateral homonymous hemianopia (often incongruous) and a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. The APD is contralateral to the lesion because each tract contains more crossed than uncrossed pupillary fibers (recall there is an asymmetric decussation of all axons at the chiasm). Therefore, a lesion of the optic tract will cause more damage to fibers crossing from the contralateral eye than uncrossed fibers from the ipsilateral eye. which of the following is not a known cause of infiltrative optic neuropathy? A.lymphoma B.sarcoidosis C.varicella zoster virus (VZV) D.tuberculosis (TB) High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: Infiltrative optic neuropathy often presents acutely with devastating effects on optic nerve function (visual fields and visual acuity). Causes include optic nerve gliomas, leukemia, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, syphilis, TB, fungal infections and meningeal carcinomatosis. When VZV affects optic nerve function (often referred to as "orbital zoster") it is thought to be a vasculitis that cuts off arterial circulation to the optic nerve. Often, there are preceding or concurrent VZV skin vesicles and/or diffuse unilateral motility deficits from hypoxia of the extraocular muscles. A neurologist refers a patient to you who has been newly diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS). The neurologist wishes to start the oral medication, fingolimod (brand name: Gilenya™), as an alternative to intramuscular interferon beta-1a injections. What ocular side effect may occur with fingolimod? A.increased rate of optic neuritis B.non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy C.multiple cranial nerve palsies D.macular edema High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: D Explanation: Daily oral fingolimod demonstrated superior efficacy in the treatment of relapsing-remitting MS compared to weekly intramuscular injections of interferon beta-1a in a prospective, randomized controlled trial (N Engl J Med. 2010;362:402-15). The annualized relapse rate was lower in the fingolimod groups compared to interferon beta-1a and the MRI results corroborated these results. The only adverse ocular finding was the presence of macular edema in <1% of patients receiving fingolimod. This macular edema occurred within 4 months of receiving this medication and was asymptomatic in half of these affected patients. Which of the following tests is the most appropriate to assess if a patient's chronic vision loss may be due to an old branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) involving the macula which occured 5 years prior? A VEP is rarely useful clinically and only shows gross deficits anywhere along the afferent visual pathway from the macula to the occipital lobe. A.optic nerve optical coherence tomography (OCT) B.thyroid function studies C.CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis D.fluorescein angiography (FA) High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient has a classic presentation for cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) although melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) is also a definite consideration. CAR and MAR are both paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndromes which share many similar features including progressive vision loss with photopsias and nyctalopia. Both diseases often have normal fundus findings until late in the disease course when retinal arterioles may become attenuated with thinning of the RPE and atrophy of the optic nerve. CAR tends to present with both Cone And Rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) and MAR Mostly Affects Rods although either can affect rods and/or cones (shout out to OQ user "Grimlock" for that memory aid. A late onset acquired retinal rod or cone dysfunction on ERG is highly suggestive of CAR or MAR. Vitritis (often mild as in this case) may or may not be present on exam in either MAR and CAR- both have been reported in the literature but vitritis is not required for the diagnosis. About 50% of patients with CAR have a known diagnosis of cancer at onset of ocular disease while the vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. The most common inciting malignancy in CAR is small cell carcinoma of the lung although other carcinomas of the lungs, breast, uterus, and cervix have also been associated. While new generation OCTs of the macula may show non-specific pathologic changes of the outer retina with CAR / MAR, an OCT of the optic nerve would expected to be normal in CAR / MAR and would not prove useful in this case. Patients with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) usually show signs of either eyelid retraction, eye muscle motility disturbance, strabismus, or proptosis on exam AND thyroid function tests can be low, high, or normal in patients with TAO so it is only a marginally useful test. A FA would not be expected to show any abnormalities that would aid diagnosis in this patient. An 80-year-old Veteran who enjoys his cigarettes, rum, and junk food presents with visual decline in both eyes over 1 year with an objective decline in serial measurements of VA and color vision bilaterally. Both eyes show a similar visual field and optic nerve appearance. In the context of a normal macular exam, which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient with the visual field shown above? A.Image A B.Image B C.Image C D.Image D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The visual field presented is a Humphrey automated 24-2 visual field of the left eye demonstrating a cecocentral scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history strongly suggestive of a combined nutritional optic neuropathy and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve but is the typical appearance associated with nutritional and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Generally this causes relatively symmetric bilateral central / cecocentral vision loss due to loss of the papillomacular bundle causing temporal atrophy of the optic nerve. While we all like clean diagnoses (e.g. vitamin B-12 deficiency or copper deficiency) many patients with this type of optic neuropathy have a "dirty diagnosis" full of both poisons (smoking and drinking) and vitamin deficiency from poor nutrition leading to mitochondrial failure of the retinal ganglion cells of the papillomacular bundle. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling or pallor is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows a severely swollen, hyperemic optic nerve with surrounding exudates that would be typical for a patient presenting with increased intracranial pressure (i.e. papilledema) (e.g. from pseudotumor cerebri, compressive tumor, or venous sinus thrombosis). Papilledema does not typically cause a cecocentral scotoma. Instead it causes enlarged blind spots and glaucomatous type field defects. End stage severe papilledema, like end-stage glaucoma, can cause central vision loss once the periphery is lost. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated cecocentral visual field defect. According to the Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial, what is the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement in patients with acute monocular non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.1-2% B.12-19% C.25-35% D.50-60% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a fact that must be memorized. For comparison, the rate of contralateral involvement in patients with untreated monocular vision loss from arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis is estimated to be 54-95% within weeks. OQ users have been frustrated by apparently different statistics in different "reputable sources" regarding the risk of contralateral NAION in a patient who suffers unilateral NAION. The current neuro BCSC states that "the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement is 15%." This is based on very good data from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study which found the rate to be 14.7% in 5 years.1 Different statistics quoted by review manuals may be looking at lifetime risk (rather than 5 year risk) or may be quoting smaller studies. OQ has researched this topic thoroughly and we are sticking with the current BCSC text on this question. Don't send us hateful comments if your review manual has a different statistic. 1Newman NJ, Scherer R, Langenberg P, Kelman S, Feldon S, Kaufman D, Dickersin K; Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial Research Group. The fellow eye in NAION: report from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study. Am J Ophthalmol. 2002 Sep;134(3):317-28. What is the term for vision which deteriorates in brighter light? A.hemeralopia B.photophobia C.metamorphopsia D.palinopsia High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Photophobia is a "fear of light" or sensitivity to light. While closely related to hemeralopia, or deterioration of vision in higher light environments, it is not the same. Hemeralopia is often described in patients with cone dystrophy. Metamorphopsia is a distortion of vision where straight objects appear wavy or crooked. Metamorphopsia typically is described by patients with macular disease. Palinopsia is an illusion marked by the preservation of images or "afterimages." Palinopsia can occur as an isolated visual phenomenon or in association with medications, hallucinogenic drugs, seizure disorders, and/or visual pathway lesions. A 60-year old male with no past ocular history undergoes a 6-hour cardiac bypass surgery. When he awakes from surgery he is found to have hand motion vision in both eyes. Aside from his abnormal vision, sluggish pupillary function, and pupillary light-near dissociation, his exam is unremarkable (including his dilated fundus exam). What is the most likely diagnosis? A.Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy B.Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy C.Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy D.Dorsal midbrain syndrome High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) is much rarer than anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but similarly is believed to be related to hypoperfusion of the posterior optic nerve. Usually the hypoperfusion is due to a perfect storm of contributing risk factors including anemia, hypotension, poor cardiac output, hypovolemia, and cardiopulmonary instability during surgery. Rarely PION can be related to a vasculitic process including giant cell arteritis, lupus-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa, and VZV related vasculitis. Unlike anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, PION almost always has a normal appearing optic nerve in the acute phase. Dorsal midbrain syndrome does include pupillary light-near dissociation, but has other findings not exhibited in this patient and does not typically result in sudden bilateral vision loss. As an aside, any disease process causing bilateral optic neuropathy can result in pupillary light-near dissociation. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. She reports severe left eye pain that is worse with eye movement. Her examination shows 20/20 vision in the right eye and 20/25 vision in the left eye. She has normal color vision, alignment, IOP, and motility. Her pupils show a left afferent pupillary defect. Her right eye exam is essentially normal. Confrontation fields are diffusely constricted in the left eye. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What type of optic neuropathy does this patient have? A.Demyelinating optic neuritis B.Ischemic optic neuropathy C.Optic perineuritis D.Nutritional optic neuropathy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The image shows a coronal section of a T1-weighted, fat-saturated post-contrast MRI. The MRI shows marked enhancement and slight thickening of the optic nerve sheath while the optic nerve itself shows very little enhancement. Optic nerve sheath enhancement can be seen in optic nerve sheath meningiomas and optic perineuritis (OPN). This patient’s acute presentation and pain with eye movement is suggestive of optic perineuritis. Defined by inflammation of the meninges surrounding the optic nerve, OPN is a radiologic and pathologic diagnosis. The era of MRI has enabled increased recognition of this entity while in the past these cases may have been categorized as “optic neuritis” or “atypical optic neuritis.” OPN is generally considered on the spectrum of orbital pseudotumor because in many cases there is concomitant orbital inflammation and like orbital pseudotumor it is usually idiopathic inflammation. Additional known etiologies of OPN, however, include sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, tuberculosis and syphilis. Without the MRI to aide in the diagnosis of OPN, it is virtually indistinguishable from demyelinating optic neuritis (DON). In contrast to DON, OPN has a reported slight tendency to less commonly involve the central visual field, often occurs alongside other radiographic and clinical findings of orbital inflammation, and is exquisitely steroid responsive. As we alluded to above, reasons to distinguish OPN from DON is that OPN: 1) Does not carry the same risk of future multiple sclerosis as DON; and 2) Requires a laboratory evaluation to rule-out other causes such as sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, tuberculosis and syphilis. Ingestion of which of the following substances causes an acute, bilateral toxic optic neuropathy with associated severe vision loss and disc edema? A.Ethambutol B.Ethanol C.Chloramphenicol D.Methanol High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Chronic use of ethambutol, ethanol, chloramphenicol, hydroxyquinolones, penicillamine, cisplatin, and vincristine are associated with chronic toxic optic neuropathy. Chronic toxic optic neuropathy and chronic nutritional neuropathy from B-12 / folate / thiamine classically result in diminished central visual acuity from central / cecocentral scotomas with selective loss of the papillomacular nerve fiber layer and optic nerve pallor. Methanol and ethylene glycol toxicity, however, occurs immediately with ingestion and results in devastating acute, diffuse vision loss with associated disc edema. Which of the following would be expected to result in a left afferent pupillary defect? A.A right optic nerve lesion B.A right optic tract lesion C.A right optic radiation lesion D.A right-sided lesion of the primary visual cortex High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: A lesion of the optic tract often results in an afferent pupillary defect of the contralateral eye. This is thought to occur because there are more crossed than uncrossed pupillary fibers in the optic tract. A lesion of the right optic tract results in decreased afferent input from both retinas but relatively-speaking there is a more marked reduction of afferent input from the contralateral eye. This is a simple concept yet often trips students up. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. She reports severe left eye pain that is worse with eye movement. Her examination shows 20/20 vision in the right eye and 20/25 vision in the left eye. She has normal color vision, alignment, IOP, and motility. Her pupils show a left afferent pupillary defect. Her right eye exam is essentially normal. Confrontation fields are diffusely constricted in the left eye. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What would NOT be considered in the differential for this patient’s optic neuropathy? A.Demyelinating optic neuritis associated with multiple sclerosis B.Granulomatosis with polyangiitis C.Syphilis D.Sarcoidosis High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The image shows a coronal section of a T1-weighted, fat-saturated post-contrast MRI. question: A lesion of the right optic tract might be expected to result in what finding?

options.A: an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the left eye
options.B: an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the right eye
options.C: a right homonymous hemianopia (in both eyes)
options.D: a left hemianopia in the right eye only

explanation: Optic tract lesions classically result in a contralateral homonymous hemianopia (often incongruous) and a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. The APD is contralateral to the lesion because each tract contains more crossed than uncrossed pupillary fibers (recall there is an asymmetric decussation of all axons at the chiasm). Therefore, a lesion of the optic tract will cause more damage to fibers crossing from the contralateral eye than uncrossed fibers from the ipsilateral eye. which of the following is not a known cause of infiltrative optic neuropathy? A.lymphoma B.sarcoidosis C.varicella zoster virus (VZV) D.tuberculosis (TB) High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: Infiltrative optic neuropathy often presents acutely with devastating effects on optic nerve function (visual fields and visual acuity). Causes include optic nerve gliomas, leukemia, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, syphilis, TB, fungal infections and meningeal carcinomatosis. When VZV affects optic nerve function (often referred to as "orbital zoster") it is thought to be a vasculitis that cuts off arterial circulation to the optic nerve. Often, there are preceding or concurrent VZV skin vesicles and/or diffuse unilateral motility deficits from hypoxia of the extraocular muscles. A neurologist refers a patient to you who has been newly diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS). The neurologist wishes to start the oral medication, fingolimod (brand name: Gilenya™), as an alternative to intramuscular interferon beta-1a injections. What ocular side effect may occur with fingolimod? A.increased rate of optic neuritis B.non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy C.multiple cranial nerve palsies D.macular edema High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: D Explanation: Daily oral fingolimod demonstrated superior efficacy in the treatment of relapsing-remitting MS compared to weekly intramuscular injections of interferon beta-1a in a prospective, randomized controlled trial (N Engl J Med. 2010;362:402-15). The annualized relapse rate was lower in the fingolimod groups compared to interferon beta-1a and the MRI results corroborated these results. The only adverse ocular finding was the presence of macular edema in <1% of patients receiving fingolimod. This macular edema occurred within 4 months of receiving this medication and was asymptomatic in half of these affected patients. Which of the following tests is the most appropriate to assess if a patient's chronic vision loss may be due to an old branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) involving the macula which occured 5 years prior? A.Visual evoked potential (VEP) B.Full field electroretinogram (ERG) C.Potential acuity meter (PAM) D.Multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG) High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: A chronic branch retinal artery occlusion often shows no detectable fundoscopy findings and may have a completely normal appearing fluorescein angiography. A VEP is rarely useful clinically and only shows gross deficits anywhere along the afferent visual pathway from the macula to the occipital lobe. An abnormal VEP cannot localize the site of pathology within the visual pathway. The PAM is used to assess macular vision potential through hazy media (usually a cataract). A full field ERG is best at evaluating rod function although the stimulus frequency can be altered to evaluate gross cone function. For assessing focal retinal dysfunction within the macula, such as a small BRAO, multifocal ERG is most useful. What is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy? A.autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) B.Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) C.Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) D.Behr syndrome High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: ADOA (or Kjer's syndrome) is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy with an estimated incidence of 1 in 50,000. About 50-70% of patients with the ADOA phenotype have a mutation in the OPA1 gene on chromosome 3. The OPA1 gene codes for a GTPase that appears to have a function in mitochondrial energy production and maintenance of mitochondrial membrane integrity. LHON is a maternally-inherited disease of mitochondrial dysfunction caused by point mutations in mitochondrial DNA. Wolfram syndrome is a syndrome with a unique constellation of findings including diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, and sensorineural deafness. It is generally inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion (though can be sporadic). Behr syndrome is a variant of autosomal recessive optic atrophy associated with other neurologic abnormalities including ataxia, pyramidal and extrapyramidal dysfunction, hypertonia, intellectual disability, urinary incontinence, and pes cavus. Experts believe Behr syndrome is likely a wastebasket for many different undiagnosed diseases (and is unlikely to show up on your test). Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) has all of the following characteristics EXCEPT: A.insidious bilateral vision loss over years B.known pathogenic mutations in the OPA1 gene of chromosome 3 C.focal temporal excavation of involved optic nerves D.nerve fiber bundle type visual field defects respecting the horizontal meridian High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: ADOA typically presents in the first 10 years of life but can present much later. Patients with ADOA often offer a vague family history of color blindness, progressive glaucoma, or poor vision of unknown etiology in close family members which supports the dominant inheritance (although may be a de novo mutation). Vision is typically 20/60-20/200 upon diagnosis with many patients not realizing they have a problem until obtaining a routine eye exam. Color vision is generally diminished and old literature suggests tritanopia is most characteristic of ADOA (although more recent literature found color vision deficits of all types). The optic nerves have a characteristic temporal excavation with pallor in about half of cases and diffuse pallor in other cases. Visual fields typically show central / cecocentral depression although some demonstrate global depression. Neuro-imaging of the brain / orbits should be performed prior to the diagnosis of ADOA to rule out compressive lesions. n 18-year-old girl presents to your clinic as a referral from her optometrist for "bilateral disc swelling." The patient's only complaint is a new-onset, mild headache starting 3 weeks ago. Her medical history is significant for acne vulgaris for which she is taking isotretinoin. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU, her pupillary exam is normal, she has full ductions and versions, and her static perimetry is full OU. Her dilated exam is shown above. Which of the following represents the next best course of management? A.acetaminophen or a NSAID for her mild headaches B.oral acetazolamide for her mild headaches C.lumbar puncture D.MRI / MRV High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The fundus photo depicts bilateral disc edema with tortuous retinal vessels OU. There is perhaps a peripapillary hemorrhage at 7 o'clock on the right optic disc as well as some obscuration of the vessels as they pass over the disc rim. The differential diagnosis of disc edema can be broken down according to the most frequent causes: • Most common: papilledema, optic neuritis, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, pseudopapilledema • Somewhat common: CRVO, diabetic papillopathy • Uncommon: posterior uveitis, hypotony, malignant hypertension, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, optic nerve infiltration (e.g. sarcoidosis, lymphoma) This patient most likely has papilledema given the appearance of her discs, her relatively-intact visual function, her headache symptoms, and lack of other symptoms (e.g. no pain on eye movement). As you know, the basic definition of papilledema is optic disc swelling caused by increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Though this clinical vignette wants you to jump to the diagnosis of pseudotumor cerebri, you MUST get neuro-imaging to exclude other causes of papilledema. These other causes include an intracranial tumor, hydrocephalus, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, and venous thrombosis. Though CT with contrast is sometimes used, MRI of the brain is preferred since it is more sensitive for detecting the various causes of increased ICP. MRV is also typically performed at the same time due to its convenience and ability to help rule-in/out venous sinus thrombosis. Finally, it is important to note that this patient is taking isotretinoin which is a vitamin A derivative medication and is a known cause of intracranial hypertension. In this case the work- up for probable papilledema needs to be completed but you would also want to stop isotretinoin. A patient has his right eye pharmacologically dilated while his left eye remains undilated. Assume that he has a known longstanding right afferent pupillary defect from prior exams. You know that to properly assess for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) you must hold a light indirectly on the _______ eye while a direct light is swung back and forth between the eyes. In this particular case the ______ pupil will dilate when direct light is swung from the _______ eye to the _______ eye. A.left; left; right; left B.left; left; left; right C.right; left; left; right D.It is not possible to assess for a RAPD in this scenario Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Dilation of one eye does not prevent the accurate assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). If one eye is dilated, simply hold a dim indirect light source to the side of the undilated eye (in this case the left eye) and perform the swinging flashlight test. If the undilated eye has a RAPD then it will dilate as expected when the flashlight is swung over from the dilated eye. If the dilated eye has a RAPD, the undilated eye will dilate when the flashlight is swung from the undilated eye to the dilated eye. Some refer to this as checking for a RAPD "by reverse" but others object to the use of this terminology calling it a misnomer. Misnomer or not, most ophthalmologists understand what is meant by assessing a RAPD "by reverse." Which of the following medications has been implicated as a cause of intracranial hypertension? A.cyclosporine B.furosemide (Lasix) C.sildenafil (Viagra) D.escitalopram (Lexapro) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: It is important to know the medicines that are associated with drug-induced intracranial hypertension. The more commonly implicated drugs include: vitamin A and vitamin A derivatives (isotretinoin), the tetracycline family of antibiotics, cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, prednisone (both the use and sudden withdrawal), and synthetic growth hormone. Lasix is actually a second-line treatment for IIH patients. Viagra has a questionable association with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. She reports severe left eye pain that is worse with eye movement. Her examination shows 20/20 vision in the right eye and 20/25 vision in the left eye. She has normal color vision, alignment, IOP, and motility. Her pupils show a left afferent pupillary defect. Her right eye exam is essentially normal. Confrontation fields are diffusely constricted in the left eye. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What type of optic neuropathy does this patient have? A.Demyelinating optic neuritis B.Ischemic optic neuropathy C.Optic perineuritis D.Nutritional optic neuropathy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The image shows a coronal section of a T1-weighted, fat-saturated post-contrast MRI. The MRI shows marked enhancement and slight thickening of the optic nerve sheath while the optic nerve itself shows very little enhancement. Optic nerve sheath enhancement can be seen in optic nerve sheath meningiomas and optic perineuritis (OPN). This patient’s acute presentation and pain with eye movement is suggestive of optic perineuritis. Defined by inflammation of the meninges surrounding the optic nerve, OPN is a radiologic and pathologic diagnosis. The era of MRI has enabled increased recognition of this entity while in the past these cases may have been categorized as “optic neuritis” or “atypical optic neuritis.” OPN is generally considered on the spectrum of orbital pseudotumor because in many cases there is concomitant orbital inflammation and like orbital pseudotumor it is usually idiopathic inflammation. In contrast to DON, OPN has a reported slight tendency to less commonly involve the central visual field, often occurs alongside other radiographic and clinical findings of orbital inflammation, and is exquisitely steroid responsive. question: which of the following is not a known cause of infiltrative optic neuropathy?
explanation: Infiltrative optic neuropathy often presents acutely with devastating effects on optic nerve function (visual fields and visual acuity). Causes include optic nerve gliomas, leukemia, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, syphilis, TB, fungal infections and meningeal carcinomatosis. When VZV affects optic nerve function (often referred to as "orbital zoster") it is thought to be a vasculitis that cuts off arterial circulation to the optic nerve. Often, there are preceding or concurrent VZV skin vesicles and/or diffuse unilateral motility deficits from hypoxia of the extraocular muscles. A neurologist refers a patient to you who has been newly diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS). The neurologist wishes to start the oral medication, fingolimod (brand name: Gilenya™), as an alternative to intramuscular interferon beta-1a injections. What ocular side effect may occur with fingolimod? A.increased rate of optic neuritis B.non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy C.multiple cranial nerve palsies D.macular edema High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: D Explanation: Daily oral fingolimod demonstrated superior efficacy in the treatment of relapsing-remitting MS compared to weekly intramuscular injections of interferon beta-1a in a prospective, randomized controlled trial (N Engl J Med. 2010;362:402-15). The annualized relapse rate was lower in the fingolimod groups compared to interferon beta-1a and the MRI results corroborated these results. The only adverse ocular finding was the presence of macular edema in <1% of patients receiving fingolimod. This macular edema occurred within 4 months of receiving this medication and was asymptomatic in half of these affected patients. Which of the following tests is the most appropriate to assess if a patient's chronic vision loss may be due to an old branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) involving the macula which occured 5 years prior? A.Visual evoked potential (VEP) B.Full field electroretinogram (ERG) C.Potential acuity meter (PAM) D.Multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG) High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: A chronic branch retinal artery occlusion often shows no detectable fundoscopy findings and may have a completely normal appearing fluorescein angiography. A VEP is rarely useful clinically and only shows gross deficits anywhere along the afferent visual pathway from the macula to the occipital lobe. An abnormal VEP cannot localize the site of pathology within the visual pathway. The PAM is used to assess macular vision potential through hazy media (usually a cataract). A full field ERG is best at evaluating rod function although the stimulus frequency can be altered to evaluate gross cone function. For assessing focal retinal dysfunction within the macula, such as a small BRAO, multifocal ERG is most useful. What is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy? A.autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) B.Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) C.Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) D.Behr syndrome High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: ADOA (or Kjer's syndrome) is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy with an estimated incidence of 1 in 50,000. About 50-70% of patients with the ADOA phenotype have a mutation in the OPA1 gene on chromosome 3. The OPA1 gene codes for a GTPase that appears to have a function in mitochondrial energy production and maintenance of mitochondrial membrane integrity. LHON is a maternally-inherited disease of mitochondrial dysfunction caused by point mutations in mitochondrial DNA. Wolfram syndrome is a syndrome with a unique constellation of findings including diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, and sensorineural deafness. It is generally inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion (though can be sporadic). Behr syndrome is a variant of autosomal recessive optic atrophy associated with other neurologic abnormalities including ataxia, pyramidal and extrapyramidal dysfunction, hypertonia, intellectual disability, urinary incontinence, and pes cavus. Experts believe Behr syndrome is likely a wastebasket for many different undiagnosed diseases (and is unlikely to show up on your test). Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) has all of the following characteristics EXCEPT: A.insidious bilateral vision loss over years B.known pathogenic mutations in the OPA1 gene of chromosome 3 C.focal temporal excavation of involved optic nerves D.nerve fiber bundle type visual field defects respecting the horizontal meridian High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: ADOA typically presents in the first 10 years of life but can present much later. Patients with ADOA often offer a vague family history of color blindness, progressive glaucoma, or poor vision of unknown etiology in close family members which supports the dominant inheritance (although may be a de novo mutation). Vision is typically 20/60-20/200 upon diagnosis with many patients not realizing they have a problem until obtaining a routine eye exam. Color vision is generally diminished and old literature suggests tritanopia is most characteristic of ADOA (although more recent literature found color vision deficits of all types). The optic nerves have a characteristic temporal excavation with pallor in about half of cases and diffuse pallor in other cases. Visual fields typically show central / cecocentral depression although some demonstrate global depression. Neuro-imaging of the brain / orbits should be performed prior to the diagnosis of ADOA to rule out compressive lesions. n 18-year-old girl presents to your clinic as a referral from her optometrist for "bilateral disc swelling." The patient's only complaint is a new-onset, mild headache starting 3 weeks ago. Her medical history is significant for acne vulgaris for which she is taking isotretinoin. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU, her pupillary exam is normal, she has full ductions and versions, and her static perimetry is full OU. Her dilated exam is shown above. Which of the following represents the next best course of management? A.acetaminophen or a NSAID for her mild headaches B.oral acetazolamide for her mild headaches C.lumbar puncture D.MRI / MRV High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The fundus photo depicts bilateral disc edema with tortuous retinal vessels OU. There is perhaps a peripapillary hemorrhage at 7 o'clock on the right optic disc as well as some obscuration of the vessels as they pass over the disc rim. The differential diagnosis of disc edema can be broken down according to the most frequent causes: • Most common: papilledema, optic neuritis, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, pseudopapilledema • Somewhat common: CRVO, diabetic papillopathy • Uncommon: posterior uveitis, hypotony, malignant hypertension, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, optic nerve infiltration (e.g. sarcoidosis, lymphoma) This patient most likely has papilledema given the appearance of her discs, her relatively-intact visual function, her headache symptoms, and lack of other symptoms (e.g. no pain on eye movement). As you know, the basic definition of papilledema is optic disc swelling caused by increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Though this clinical vignette wants you to jump to the diagnosis of pseudotumor cerebri, you MUST get neuro-imaging to exclude other causes of papilledema. These other causes include an intracranial tumor, hydrocephalus, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, and venous thrombosis. Though CT with contrast is sometimes used, MRI of the brain is preferred since it is more sensitive for detecting the various causes of increased ICP. MRV is also typically performed at the same time due to its convenience and ability to help rule-in/out venous sinus thrombosis. Finally, it is important to note that this patient is taking isotretinoin which is a vitamin A derivative medication and is a known cause of intracranial hypertension. In this case the work- up for probable papilledema needs to be completed but you would also want to stop isotretinoin. A patient has his right eye pharmacologically dilated while his left eye remains undilated. Assume that he has a known longstanding right afferent pupillary defect from prior exams. You know that to properly assess for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) you must hold a light indirectly on the _______ eye while a direct light is swung back and forth between the eyes. In this particular case the ______ pupil will dilate when direct light is swung from the _______ eye to the _______ eye. A.left; left; right; left B.left; left; left; right C.right; left; left; right D.It is not possible to assess for a RAPD in this scenario Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Dilation of one eye does not prevent the accurate assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). If one eye is dilated, simply hold a dim indirect light source to the side of the undilated eye (in this case the left eye) and perform the swinging flashlight test. If the undilated eye has a RAPD then it will dilate as expected when the flashlight is swung over from the dilated eye. If the dilated eye has a RAPD, the undilated eye will dilate when the flashlight is swung from the undilated eye to the dilated eye. Some refer to this as checking for a RAPD "by reverse" but others object to the use of this terminology calling it a misnomer. Misnomer or not, most ophthalmologists understand what is meant by assessing a RAPD "by reverse." Which of the following medications has been implicated as a cause of intracranial hypertension? A.cyclosporine B.furosemide (Lasix) C.sildenafil (Viagra) D.escitalopram (Lexapro) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: It is important to know the medicines that are associated with drug-induced intracranial hypertension. The more commonly implicated drugs include: vitamin A and vitamin A derivatives (isotretinoin), the tetracycline family of antibiotics, cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, prednisone (both the use and sudden withdrawal), and synthetic growth hormone. Lasix is actually a second-line treatment for IIH patients. Viagra has a questionable association with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. A 75-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol and cigarette use comes to your clinic today with a 2-month history of progressive visual loss in both eyes to 20/100 best corrected with associated prominent photopsias in both eyes. Exam one month ago by an outside ophthalmologist found 20/50 vision in both eyes with global depression on a reliable 24-2 Humphrey visual field. An electroretinogram (ERG) was performed a week ago and showed marked reduction in amplitude of both rod and cone function. Aside from his vision and mild vitritis OU, his ocular exam today is unremarkable (including normal pupils and fundus OU). What would be the next best step in diagnosis of this patient? A.optic nerve optical coherence tomography (OCT) B.thyroid function studies C.CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis D.fluorescein angiography (FA) High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient has a classic presentation for cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) although melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) is also a definite consideration. CAR and MAR are both paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndromes which share many similar features including progressive vision loss with photopsias and nyctalopia. Both diseases often have normal fundus findings until late in the disease course when retinal arterioles may become attenuated with thinning of the RPE and atrophy of the optic nerve. CAR tends to present with both Cone And Rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) and MAR Mostly Affects Rods although either can affect rods and/or cones (shout out to OQ user "Grimlock" for that memory aid. A late onset acquired retinal rod or cone dysfunction on ERG is highly suggestive of CAR or MAR. Vitritis (often mild as in this case) may or may not be present on exam in either MAR and CAR- both have been reported in the literature but vitritis is not required for the diagnosis. About 50% of patients with CAR have a known diagnosis of cancer at onset of ocular disease while the vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. The most common inciting malignancy in CAR is small cell carcinoma of the lung although other carcinomas of the lungs, breast, uterus, and cervix have also been associated. While new generation OCTs of the macula may show non-specific pathologic changes of the outer retina with CAR / MAR, an OCT of the optic nerve would expected to be normal in CAR / MAR and would not prove useful in this case. Patients with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) usually show signs of either eyelid retraction, eye muscle motility disturbance, strabismus, or proptosis on exam AND thyroid function tests can be low, high, or normal in patients with TAO so it is only a marginally useful test. A FA would not be expected to show any abnormalities that would aid diagnosis in this patient. An 80-year-old Veteran who enjoys his cigarettes, rum, and junk food presents with visual decline in both eyes over 1 year with an objective decline in serial measurements of VA and color vision bilaterally. Both eyes show a similar visual field and optic nerve appearance. In the context of a normal macular exam, which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient with the visual field shown above? A.Image A B.Image B C.Image C D.Image D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The visual field presented is a Humphrey automated 24-2 visual field of the left eye demonstrating a cecocentral scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history strongly suggestive of a combined nutritional optic neuropathy and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve but is the typical appearance associated with nutritional and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Generally this causes relatively symmetric bilateral central / cecocentral vision loss due to loss of the papillomacular bundle causing temporal atrophy of the optic nerve. While we all like clean diagnoses (e.g. vitamin B-12 deficiency or copper deficiency) many patients with this type of optic neuropathy have a "dirty diagnosis" full of both poisons (smoking and drinking) and vitamin deficiency from poor nutrition leading to mitochondrial failure of the retinal ganglion cells of the papillomacular bundle. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling or pallor is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows a severely swollen, hyperemic optic nerve with surrounding exudates that would be typical for a patient presenting with increased intracranial pressure (i.e. papilledema) (e.g. from pseudotumor cerebri, compressive tumor, or venous sinus thrombosis). Papilledema does not typically cause a cecocentral scotoma. Instead it causes enlarged blind spots and glaucomatous type field defects. End stage severe papilledema, like end-stage glaucoma, can cause central vision loss once the periphery is lost. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated cecocentral visual field defect. According to the Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial, what is the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement in patients with acute monocular non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.1-2% B.12-19% C.25-35% D.50-60% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a fact that must be memorized. For comparison, the rate of contralateral involvement in patients with untreated monocular vision loss from arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis is estimated to be 54-95% within weeks. OQ users have been frustrated by apparently different statistics in different "reputable sources" regarding the risk of contralateral NAION in a patient who suffers unilateral NAION. The current neuro BCSC states that "the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement is 15%." This is based on very good data from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study which found the rate to be 14.7% in 5 years.1 Different statistics quoted by review manuals may be looking at lifetime risk (rather than 5 year risk) or may be quoting smaller studies. OQ has researched this topic thoroughly and we are sticking with the current BCSC text on this question. Don't send us hateful comments if your review manual has a different statistic. 1Newman NJ, Scherer R, Langenberg P, Kelman S, Feldon S, Kaufman D, Dickersin K; Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial Research Group. The fellow eye in NAION: report from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study. Am J Ophthalmol. 2002 Sep;134(3):317-28. What is the term for vision which deteriorates in brighter light? A.hemeralopia B.photophobia C.metamorphopsia D.palinopsia High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Photophobia is a "fear of light" or sensitivity to light. While closely related to hemeralopia, or deterioration of vision in higher light environments, it is not the same. Hemeralopia is often described in patients with cone dystrophy. Metamorphopsia is a distortion of vision where straight objects appear wavy or crooked. Metamorphopsia typically is described by patients with macular disease. Palinopsia is an illusion marked by the preservation of images or "afterimages." Palinopsia can occur as an isolated visual phenomenon or in association with medications, hallucinogenic drugs, seizure disorders, and/or visual pathway lesions. A.Visual evoked potential (VEP) B.Full field electroretinogram (ERG) C.Potential acuity meter (PAM) D.Multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG) High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: A chronic branch retinal artery occlusion often shows no detectable fundoscopy findings and may have a completely normal appearing fluorescein angiography. A VEP is rarely useful clinically and only shows gross deficits anywhere along the afferent visual pathway from the macula to the occipital lobe. An abnormal VEP cannot localize the site of pathology within the visual pathway. The PAM is used to assess macular vision potential through hazy media (usually a cataract). A full field ERG is best at evaluating rod function although the stimulus frequency can be altered to evaluate gross cone function. For assessing focal retinal dysfunction within the macula, such as a small BRAO, multifocal ERG is most useful. What is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy? A.autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) B.Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) C.Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) D.Behr syndrome High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: ADOA (or Kjer's syndrome) is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy with an estimated incidence of 1 in 50,000.
