Experts believe Behr syndrome is likely a wastebasket for many different undiagnosed diseases (and is unlikely to show up on your test). Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) has all of the following characteristics EXCEPT: A.insidious bilateral vision loss over years B.known pathogenic mutations in the OPA1 gene of chromosome 3 C.focal temporal excavation of involved optic nerves D.nerve fiber bundle type visual field defects respecting the horizontal meridian High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: ADOA typically presents in the first 10 years of life but can present much later. Patients with ADOA often offer a vague family history of color blindness, progressive glaucoma, or poor vision of unknown etiology in close family members which supports the dominant inheritance (although may be a de novo mutation). Vision is typically 20/60-20/200 upon diagnosis with many patients not realizing they have a problem until obtaining a routine eye exam. Color vision is generally diminished and old literature suggests tritanopia is most characteristic of ADOA (although more recent literature found color vision deficits of all types). The optic nerves have a characteristic temporal excavation with pallor in about half of cases and diffuse pallor in other cases. Visual fields typically show central / cecocentral depression although some demonstrate global depression. Neuro-imaging of the brain / orbits should be performed prior to the diagnosis of ADOA to rule out compressive lesions. n 18-year-old girl presents to your clinic as a referral from her optometrist for "bilateral disc swelling." The patient's only complaint is a new-onset, mild headache starting 3 weeks ago. Her medical history is significant for acne vulgaris for which she is taking isotretinoin. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU, her pupillary exam is normal, she has full ductions and versions, and her static perimetry is full OU. Her dilated exam is shown above. Which of the following represents the next best course of management? A.acetaminophen or a NSAID for her mild headaches B.oral acetazolamide for her mild headaches C.lumbar puncture D.MRI / MRV High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The fundus photo depicts bilateral disc edema with tortuous retinal vessels OU. There is perhaps a peripapillary hemorrhage at 7 o'clock on the right optic disc as well as some obscuration of the vessels as they pass over the disc rim. The differential diagnosis of disc edema can be broken down according to the most frequent causes: • Most common: papilledema, optic neuritis, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, pseudopapilledema • Somewhat common: CRVO, diabetic papillopathy • Uncommon: posterior uveitis, hypotony, malignant hypertension, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, optic nerve infiltration (e.g. sarcoidosis, lymphoma) This patient most likely has papilledema given the appearance of her discs, her relatively-intact visual function, her headache symptoms, and lack of other symptoms (e.g. no pain on eye movement). As you know, the basic definition of papilledema is optic disc swelling caused by increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Though this clinical vignette wants you to jump to the diagnosis of pseudotumor cerebri, you MUST get neuro-imaging to exclude other causes of papilledema. These other causes include an intracranial tumor, hydrocephalus, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, and venous thrombosis. Though CT with contrast is sometimes used, MRI of the brain is preferred since it is more sensitive for detecting the various causes of increased ICP. MRV is also typically performed at the same time due to its convenience and ability to help rule-in/out venous sinus thrombosis. Finally, it is important to note that this patient is taking isotretinoin which is a vitamin A derivative medication and is a known cause of intracranial hypertension. In this case the work- up for probable papilledema needs to be completed but you would also want to stop isotretinoin. A patient has his right eye pharmacologically dilated while his left eye remains undilated. Assume that he has a known longstanding right afferent pupillary defect from prior exams. You know that to properly assess for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) you must hold a light indirectly on the _______ eye while a direct light is swung back and forth between the eyes. In this particular case the ______ pupil will dilate when direct light is swung from the _______ eye to the _______ eye. A.left; left; right; left B.left; left; left; right C.right; left; left; right D.It is not possible to assess for a RAPD in this scenario Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Dilation of one eye does not prevent the accurate assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). If one eye is dilated, simply hold a dim indirect light source to the side of the undilated eye (in this case the left eye) and perform the swinging flashlight test. If the undilated eye has a RAPD then it will dilate as expected when the flashlight is swung over from the dilated eye. If the dilated eye has a RAPD, the undilated eye will dilate when the flashlight is swung from the undilated eye to the dilated eye. Some refer to this as checking for a RAPD "by reverse" but others object to the use of this terminology calling it a misnomer. Misnomer or not, most ophthalmologists understand what is meant by assessing a RAPD "by reverse." Which of the following medications has been implicated as a cause of intracranial hypertension? A.cyclosporine B.furosemide (Lasix) C.sildenafil (Viagra) D.escitalopram (Lexapro) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: It is important to know the medicines that are associated with drug-induced intracranial hypertension. The more commonly implicated drugs include: vitamin A and vitamin A derivatives (isotretinoin), the tetracycline family of antibiotics, cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, prednisone (both the use and sudden withdrawal), and synthetic growth hormone. Lasix is actually a second-line treatment for IIH patients. Viagra has a questionable association with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. A 75-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol and cigarette use comes to your clinic today with a 2-month history of progressive visual loss in both eyes to 20/100 best corrected with associated prominent photopsias in both eyes. Exam one month ago by an outside ophthalmologist found 20/50 vision in both eyes with global depression on a reliable 24-2 Humphrey visual field. An electroretinogram (ERG) was performed a week ago and showed marked reduction in amplitude of both rod and cone function. Aside from his vision and mild vitritis OU, his ocular exam today is unremarkable (including normal pupils and fundus OU). What would be the next best step in diagnosis of this patient? A.optic nerve optical coherence tomography (OCT) B.thyroid function studies C.CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis D.fluorescein angiography (FA) High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient has a classic presentation for cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) although melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) is also a definite consideration. CAR and MAR are both paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndromes which share many similar features including progressive vision loss with photopsias and nyctalopia. Both diseases often have normal fundus findings until late in the disease course when retinal arterioles may become attenuated with thinning of the RPE and atrophy of the optic nerve. CAR tends to present with both Cone And Rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) and MAR Mostly Affects Rods although either can affect rods and/or cones (shout out to OQ user "Grimlock" for that memory aid. A late onset acquired retinal rod or cone dysfunction on ERG is highly suggestive of CAR or MAR. Vitritis (often mild as in this case) may or may not be present on exam in either MAR and CAR- both have been reported in the literature but vitritis is not required for the diagnosis. About 50% of patients with CAR have a known diagnosis of cancer at onset of ocular disease while the vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. The most common inciting malignancy in CAR is small cell carcinoma of the lung although other carcinomas of the lungs, breast, uterus, and cervix have also been associated. While new generation OCTs of the macula may show non-specific pathologic changes of the outer retina with CAR / MAR, an OCT of the optic nerve would expected to be normal in CAR / MAR and would not prove useful in this case. Patients with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) usually show signs of either eyelid retraction, eye muscle motility disturbance, strabismus, or proptosis on exam AND thyroid function tests can be low, high, or normal in patients with TAO so it is only a marginally useful test. A FA would not be expected to show any abnormalities that would aid diagnosis in this patient. An 80-year-old Veteran who enjoys his cigarettes, rum, and junk food presents with visual decline in both eyes over 1 year with an objective decline in serial measurements of VA and color vision bilaterally. Both eyes show a similar visual field and optic nerve appearance. In the context of a normal macular exam, which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient with the visual field shown above? A.Image A B.Image B C.Image C D.Image D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The visual field presented is a Humphrey automated 24-2 visual field of the left eye demonstrating a cecocentral scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history strongly suggestive of a combined nutritional optic neuropathy and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve but is the typical appearance associated with nutritional and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Generally this causes relatively symmetric bilateral central / cecocentral vision loss due to loss of the papillomacular bundle causing temporal atrophy of the optic nerve. While we all like clean diagnoses (e.g. vitamin B-12 deficiency or copper deficiency) many patients with this type of optic neuropathy have a "dirty diagnosis" full of both poisons (smoking and drinking) and vitamin deficiency from poor nutrition leading to mitochondrial failure of the retinal ganglion cells of the papillomacular bundle. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling or pallor is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows a severely swollen, hyperemic optic nerve with surrounding exudates that would be typical for a patient presenting with increased intracranial pressure (i.e. papilledema) (e.g. from pseudotumor cerebri, compressive tumor, or venous sinus thrombosis). Papilledema does not typically cause a cecocentral scotoma. Instead it causes enlarged blind spots and glaucomatous type field defects. End stage severe papilledema, like end-stage glaucoma, can cause central vision loss once the periphery is lost. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated cecocentral visual field defect. According to the Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial, what is the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement in patients with acute monocular non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.1-2% B.12-19% C.25-35% D.50-60% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a fact that must be memorized. For comparison, the rate of contralateral involvement in patients with untreated monocular vision loss from arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis is estimated to be 54-95% within weeks. OQ users have been frustrated by apparently different statistics in different "reputable sources" regarding the risk of contralateral NAION in a patient who suffers unilateral NAION. The current neuro BCSC states that "the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement is 15%." This is based on very good data from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study which found the rate to be 14.7% in 5 years.1 Different statistics quoted by review manuals may be looking at lifetime risk (rather than 5 year risk) or may be quoting smaller studies. OQ has researched this topic thoroughly and we are sticking with the current BCSC text on this question. Don't send us hateful comments if your review manual has a different statistic. 1Newman NJ, Scherer R, Langenberg P, Kelman S, Feldon S, Kaufman D, Dickersin K; Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial Research Group. The fellow eye in NAION: report from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study. Am J Ophthalmol. 2002 Sep;134(3):317-28. What is the term for vision which deteriorates in brighter light? A.hemeralopia B.photophobia C.metamorphopsia D.palinopsia High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Photophobia is a "fear of light" or sensitivity to light. While closely related to hemeralopia, or deterioration of vision in higher light environments, it is not the same. Hemeralopia is often described in patients with cone dystrophy. Metamorphopsia is a distortion of vision where straight objects appear wavy or crooked. Metamorphopsia typically is described by patients with macular disease. Palinopsia is an illusion marked by the preservation of images or "afterimages." Palinopsia can occur as an isolated visual phenomenon or in association with medications, hallucinogenic drugs, seizure disorders, and/or visual pathway lesions. A 60-year old male with no past ocular history undergoes a 6-hour cardiac bypass surgery. When he awakes from surgery he is found to have hand motion vision in both eyes. Aside from his abnormal vision, sluggish pupillary function, and pupillary light-near dissociation, his exam is unremarkable (including his dilated fundus exam). What is the most likely diagnosis? A.Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy B.Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy C.Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy D.Dorsal midbrain syndrome High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) is much rarer than anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but similarly is believed to be related to hypoperfusion of the posterior optic nerve. Usually the hypoperfusion is due to a perfect storm of contributing risk factors including anemia, hypotension, poor cardiac output, hypovolemia, and cardiopulmonary instability during surgery. Rarely PION can be related to a vasculitic process including giant cell arteritis, lupus-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa, and VZV related vasculitis. Unlike anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, PION almost always has a normal appearing optic nerve in the acute phase. Dorsal midbrain syndrome does include pupillary light-near dissociation, but has other findings not exhibited in this patient and does not typically result in sudden bilateral vision loss. As an aside, any disease process causing bilateral optic neuropathy can result in pupillary light-near dissociation. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. She reports severe left eye pain that is worse with eye movement. Her examination shows 20/20 vision in the right eye and 20/25 vision in the left eye. She has normal color vision, alignment, IOP, and motility. Her pupils show a left afferent pupillary defect. Her right eye exam is essentially normal. Confrontation fields are diffusely constricted in the left eye. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What type of optic neuropathy does this patient have? A.Demyelinating optic neuritis B.Ischemic optic neuropathy C.Optic perineuritis D.Nutritional optic neuropathy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The image shows a coronal section of a T1-weighted, fat-saturated post-contrast MRI. The MRI shows marked enhancement and slight thickening of the optic nerve sheath while the optic nerve itself shows very little enhancement. Optic nerve sheath enhancement can be seen in optic nerve sheath meningiomas and optic perineuritis (OPN). This patient’s acute presentation and pain with eye movement is suggestive of optic perineuritis. Defined by inflammation of the meninges surrounding the optic nerve, OPN is a radiologic and pathologic diagnosis. The era of MRI has enabled increased recognition of this entity while in the past these cases may have been categorized as “optic neuritis” or “atypical optic neuritis.” OPN is generally considered on the spectrum of orbital pseudotumor because in many cases there is concomitant orbital inflammation and like orbital pseudotumor it is usually idiopathic inflammation. Additional known etiologies of OPN, however, include sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, tuberculosis and syphilis. Without the MRI to aide in the diagnosis of OPN, it is virtually indistinguishable from demyelinating optic neuritis (DON). In contrast to DON, OPN has a reported slight tendency to less commonly involve the central visual field, often occurs alongside other radiographic and clinical findings of orbital inflammation, and is exquisitely steroid responsive. As we alluded to above, reasons to distinguish OPN from DON is that OPN: 1) Does not carry the same risk of future multiple sclerosis as DON; and 2) Requires a laboratory evaluation to rule-out other causes such as sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, tuberculosis and syphilis. Ingestion of which of the following substances causes an acute, bilateral toxic optic neuropathy with associated severe vision loss and disc edema? A.Ethambutol B.Ethanol C.Chloramphenicol D.Methanol High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Chronic use of ethambutol, ethanol, chloramphenicol, hydroxyquinolones, penicillamine, cisplatin, and vincristine are associated with chronic toxic optic neuropathy. Chronic toxic optic neuropathy and chronic nutritional neuropathy from B-12 / folate / thiamine classically result in diminished central visual acuity from central / cecocentral scotomas with selective loss of the papillomacular nerve fiber layer and optic nerve pallor. Methanol and ethylene glycol toxicity, however, occurs immediately with ingestion and results in devastating acute, diffuse vision loss with associated disc edema. Which of the following would be expected to result in a left afferent pupillary defect? A.A right optic nerve lesion B.A right optic tract lesion C.A right optic radiation lesion D.A right-sided lesion of the primary visual cortex High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: A lesion of the optic tract often results in an afferent pupillary defect of the contralateral eye. This is thought to occur because there are more crossed than uncrossed pupillary fibers in the optic tract. A lesion of the right optic tract results in decreased afferent input from both retinas but relatively-speaking there is a more marked reduction of afferent input from the contralateral eye. This is a simple concept yet often trips students up. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. An 80-year-old Veteran who enjoys his cigarettes, rum, and junk food presents with visual decline in both eyes over 1 year with an objective decline in serial measurements of VA and color vision bilaterally. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history strongly suggestive of a combined nutritional optic neuropathy and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve but is the typical appearance associated with nutritional and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. What is the term for vision which deteriorates in brighter light? While closely related to hemeralopia, or deterioration of vision in higher light environments, it is not the same. Hemeralopia is often described in patients with cone dystrophy. Metamorphopsia is a distortion of vision where straight objects appear wavy or crooked. Metamorphopsia typically is described by patients with macular disease. A 60-year old male with no past ocular history undergoes a 6-hour cardiac bypass surgery. When he awakes from surgery he is found to have hand motion vision in both eyes. Aside from his abnormal vision, sluggish pupillary function, and pupillary light-near dissociation, his exam is unremarkable (including his dilated fundus exam). What is the most likely diagnosis? Usually the hypoperfusion is due to a perfect storm of contributing risk factors including anemia, hypotension, poor cardiac output, hypovolemia, and cardiopulmonary instability during surgery. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. She reports severe left eye pain that is worse with eye movement. Her examination shows 20/20 vision in the right eye and 20/25 vision in the left eye. She has normal color vision, alignment, IOP, and motility. Her pupils show a left afferent pupillary defect. Her right eye exam is essentially normal. Confrontation fields are diffusely constricted in the left eye. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What type of optic neuropathy does this patient have? A.Demyelinating optic neuritis B.Ischemic optic neuropathy C.Optic perineuritis D.Nutritional optic neuropathy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The image shows a coronal section of a T1-weighted, fat-saturated post-contrast MRI. The MRI shows marked enhancement and slight thickening of the optic nerve sheath while the optic nerve itself shows very little enhancement. Optic nerve sheath enhancement can be seen in optic nerve sheath meningiomas and optic perineuritis (OPN). This patient’s acute presentation and pain with eye movement is suggestive of optic perineuritis. Defined by inflammation of the meninges surrounding the optic nerve, OPN is a radiologic and pathologic diagnosis. The era of MRI has enabled increased recognition of this entity while in the past these cases may have been categorized as “optic neuritis” or “atypical optic neuritis.” OPN is generally considered on the spectrum of orbital pseudotumor because in many cases there is concomitant orbital inflammation and like orbital pseudotumor it is usually idiopathic inflammation. Without the MRI to aide in the diagnosis of OPN, it is virtually indistinguishable from demyelinating optic neuritis (DON). In contrast to DON, OPN has a reported slight tendency to less commonly involve the central visual field, often occurs alongside other radiographic and clinical findings of orbital inflammation, and is exquisitely steroid responsive. As we alluded to above, reasons to distinguish OPN from DON is that OPN: 1) Does not carry the same risk of future multiple sclerosis as DON; and 2) Requires a laboratory evaluation to rule-out other causes such as sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, tuberculosis and syphilis. question: What is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy?
explanation: ADOA (or Kjer's syndrome) is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy with an estimated incidence of 1 in 50,000. About 50-70% of patients with the ADOA phenotype have a mutation in the OPA1 gene on chromosome 3. The OPA1 gene codes for a GTPase that appears to have a function in mitochondrial energy production and maintenance of mitochondrial membrane integrity. LHON is a maternally-inherited disease of mitochondrial dysfunction caused by point mutations in mitochondrial DNA. Wolfram syndrome is a syndrome with a unique constellation of findings including diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, and sensorineural deafness. It is generally inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion (though can be sporadic). Behr syndrome is a variant of autosomal recessive optic atrophy associated with other neurologic abnormalities including ataxia, pyramidal and extrapyramidal dysfunction, hypertonia, intellectual disability, urinary incontinence, and pes cavus. Experts believe Behr syndrome is likely a wastebasket for many different undiagnosed diseases (and is unlikely to show up on your test). Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) has all of the following characteristics EXCEPT: A.insidious bilateral vision loss over years B.known pathogenic mutations in the OPA1 gene of chromosome 3 C.focal temporal excavation of involved optic nerves D.nerve fiber bundle type visual field defects respecting the horizontal meridian High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: ADOA typically presents in the first 10 years of life but can present much later. Patients with ADOA often offer a vague family history of color blindness, progressive glaucoma, or poor vision of unknown etiology in close family members which supports the dominant inheritance (although may be a de novo mutation). Vision is typically 20/60-20/200 upon diagnosis with many patients not realizing they have a problem until obtaining a routine eye exam. Color vision is generally diminished and old literature suggests tritanopia is most characteristic of ADOA (although more recent literature found color vision deficits of all types). The optic nerves have a characteristic temporal excavation with pallor in about half of cases and diffuse pallor in other cases. Visual fields typically show central / cecocentral depression although some demonstrate global depression. Neuro-imaging of the brain / orbits should be performed prior to the diagnosis of ADOA to rule out compressive lesions. n 18-year-old girl presents to your clinic as a referral from her optometrist for "bilateral disc swelling." The patient's only complaint is a new-onset, mild headache starting 3 weeks ago. Her medical history is significant for acne vulgaris for which she is taking isotretinoin. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU, her pupillary exam is normal, she has full ductions and versions, and her static perimetry is full OU. Her dilated exam is shown above. Which of the following represents the next best course of management? A.acetaminophen or a NSAID for her mild headaches B.oral acetazolamide for her mild headaches C.lumbar puncture D.MRI / MRV High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The fundus photo depicts bilateral disc edema with tortuous retinal vessels OU. There is perhaps a peripapillary hemorrhage at 7 o'clock on the right optic disc as well as some obscuration of the vessels as they pass over the disc rim. The differential diagnosis of disc edema can be broken down according to the most frequent causes: • Most common: papilledema, optic neuritis, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, pseudopapilledema • Somewhat common: CRVO, diabetic papillopathy • Uncommon: posterior uveitis, hypotony, malignant hypertension, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, optic nerve infiltration (e.g. sarcoidosis, lymphoma) This patient most likely has papilledema given the appearance of her discs, her relatively-intact visual function, her headache symptoms, and lack of other symptoms (e.g. no pain on eye movement). As you know, the basic definition of papilledema is optic disc swelling caused by increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Though this clinical vignette wants you to jump to the diagnosis of pseudotumor cerebri, you MUST get neuro-imaging to exclude other causes of papilledema. These other causes include an intracranial tumor, hydrocephalus, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, and venous thrombosis. Though CT with contrast is sometimes used, MRI of the brain is preferred since it is more sensitive for detecting the various causes of increased ICP. MRV is also typically performed at the same time due to its convenience and ability to help rule-in/out venous sinus thrombosis. Finally, it is important to note that this patient is taking isotretinoin which is a vitamin A derivative medication and is a known cause of intracranial hypertension. In this case the work- up for probable papilledema needs to be completed but you would also want to stop isotretinoin. A patient has his right eye pharmacologically dilated while his left eye remains undilated. Assume that he has a known longstanding right afferent pupillary defect from prior exams. You know that to properly assess for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) you must hold a light indirectly on the _______ eye while a direct light is swung back and forth between the eyes. In this particular case the ______ pupil will dilate when direct light is swung from the _______ eye to the _______ eye. A.left; left; right; left B.left; left; left; right C.right; left; left; right D.It is not possible to assess for a RAPD in this scenario Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Dilation of one eye does not prevent the accurate assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). If one eye is dilated, simply hold a dim indirect light source to the side of the undilated eye (in this case the left eye) and perform the swinging flashlight test. If the undilated eye has a RAPD then it will dilate as expected when the flashlight is swung over from the dilated eye. If the dilated eye has a RAPD, the undilated eye will dilate when the flashlight is swung from the undilated eye to the dilated eye. Some refer to this as checking for a RAPD "by reverse" but others object to the use of this terminology calling it a misnomer. Misnomer or not, most ophthalmologists understand what is meant by assessing a RAPD "by reverse." Which of the following medications has been implicated as a cause of intracranial hypertension? A.cyclosporine B.furosemide (Lasix) C.sildenafil (Viagra) D.escitalopram (Lexapro) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: It is important to know the medicines that are associated with drug-induced intracranial hypertension. The more commonly implicated drugs include: vitamin A and vitamin A derivatives (isotretinoin), the tetracycline family of antibiotics, cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, prednisone (both the use and sudden withdrawal), and synthetic growth hormone. Lasix is actually a second-line treatment for IIH patients. Viagra has a questionable association with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. A 75-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol and cigarette use comes to your clinic today with a 2-month history of progressive visual loss in both eyes to 20/100 best corrected with associated prominent photopsias in both eyes. Exam one month ago by an outside ophthalmologist found 20/50 vision in both eyes with global depression on a reliable 24-2 Humphrey visual field. An electroretinogram (ERG) was performed a week ago and showed marked reduction in amplitude of both rod and cone function. Aside from his vision and mild vitritis OU, his ocular exam today is unremarkable (including normal pupils and fundus OU). What would be the next best step in diagnosis of this patient? A.optic nerve optical coherence tomography (OCT) B.thyroid function studies C.CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis D.fluorescein angiography (FA) High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient has a classic presentation for cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) although melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) is also a definite consideration. CAR and MAR are both paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndromes which share many similar features including progressive vision loss with photopsias and nyctalopia. Both diseases often have normal fundus findings until late in the disease course when retinal arterioles may become attenuated with thinning of the RPE and atrophy of the optic nerve. CAR tends to present with both Cone And Rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) and MAR Mostly Affects Rods although either can affect rods and/or cones (shout out to OQ user "Grimlock" for that memory aid. A late onset acquired retinal rod or cone dysfunction on ERG is highly suggestive of CAR or MAR. Vitritis (often mild as in this case) may or may not be present on exam in either MAR and CAR- both have been reported in the literature but vitritis is not required for the diagnosis. About 50% of patients with CAR have a known diagnosis of cancer at onset of ocular disease while the vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. The most common inciting malignancy in CAR is small cell carcinoma of the lung although other carcinomas of the lungs, breast, uterus, and cervix have also been associated. While new generation OCTs of the macula may show non-specific pathologic changes of the outer retina with CAR / MAR, an OCT of the optic nerve would expected to be normal in CAR / MAR and would not prove useful in this case. question: Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) has all of the following characteristics EXCEPT:

options.A: insidious bilateral vision loss over years
options.B: known pathogenic mutations in the OPA1 gene of chromosome 3
options.C: focal temporal excavation of involved optic nerves
options.D: nerve fiber bundle type visual field defects respecting the horizontal meridian

explanation: ADOA typically presents in the first 10 years of life but can present much later. Patients with ADOA often offer a vague family history of color blindness, progressive glaucoma, or poor vision of unknown etiology in close family members which supports the dominant inheritance (although may be a de novo mutation). Vision is typically 20/60-20/200 upon diagnosis with many patients not realizing they have a problem until obtaining a routine eye exam. Color vision is generally diminished and old literature suggests tritanopia is most characteristic of ADOA (although more recent literature found color vision deficits of all types). The optic nerves have a characteristic temporal excavation with pallor in about half of cases and diffuse pallor in other cases. Visual fields typically show central / cecocentral depression although some demonstrate global depression. Neuro-imaging of the brain / orbits should be performed prior to the diagnosis of ADOA to rule out compressive lesions. n 18-year-old girl presents to your clinic as a referral from her optometrist for "bilateral disc swelling." The patient's only complaint is a new-onset, mild headache starting 3 weeks ago. Her medical history is significant for acne vulgaris for which she is taking isotretinoin. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU, her pupillary exam is normal, she has full ductions and versions, and her static perimetry is full OU. Her dilated exam is shown above. Which of the following represents the next best course of management? A.acetaminophen or a NSAID for her mild headaches B.oral acetazolamide for her mild headaches C.lumbar puncture D.MRI / MRV High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The fundus photo depicts bilateral disc edema with tortuous retinal vessels OU. A patient has his right eye pharmacologically dilated while his left eye remains undilated. Assume that he has a known longstanding right afferent pupillary defect from prior exams. You know that to properly assess for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) you must hold a light indirectly on the _______ eye while a direct light is swung back and forth between the eyes. In this particular case the ______ pupil will dilate when direct light is swung from the _______ eye to the _______ eye. A.left; left; right; left B.left; left; left; right C.right; left; left; right D.It is not possible to assess for a RAPD in this scenario Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Dilation of one eye does not prevent the accurate assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). If one eye is dilated, simply hold a dim indirect light source to the side of the undilated eye (in this case the left eye) and perform the swinging flashlight test. If the undilated eye has a RAPD then it will dilate as expected when the flashlight is swung over from the dilated eye. If the dilated eye has a RAPD, the undilated eye will dilate when the flashlight is swung from the undilated eye to the dilated eye. Some refer to this as checking for a RAPD "by reverse" but others object to the use of this terminology calling it a misnomer. Misnomer or not, most ophthalmologists understand what is meant by assessing a RAPD "by reverse." Which of the following medications has been implicated as a cause of intracranial hypertension? A.cyclosporine B.furosemide (Lasix) C.sildenafil (Viagra) D.escitalopram (Lexapro) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: It is important to know the medicines that are associated with drug-induced intracranial hypertension. The more commonly implicated drugs include: vitamin A and vitamin A derivatives (isotretinoin), the tetracycline family of antibiotics, cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, prednisone (both the use and sudden withdrawal), and synthetic growth hormone. Lasix is actually a second-line treatment for IIH patients. Viagra has a questionable association with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. A 75-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol and cigarette use comes to your clinic today with a 2-month history of progressive visual loss in both eyes to 20/100 best corrected with associated prominent photopsias in both eyes. Exam one month ago by an outside ophthalmologist found 20/50 vision in both eyes with global depression on a reliable 24-2 Humphrey visual field. An electroretinogram (ERG) was performed a week ago and showed marked reduction in amplitude of both rod and cone function. Aside from his vision and mild vitritis OU, his ocular exam today is unremarkable (including normal pupils and fundus OU). What would be the next best step in diagnosis of this patient? A.optic nerve optical coherence tomography (OCT) B.thyroid function studies C.CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis D.fluorescein angiography (FA) High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient has a classic presentation for cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) although melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) is also a definite consideration. CAR and MAR are both paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndromes which share many similar features including progressive vision loss with photopsias and nyctalopia. Both diseases often have normal fundus findings until late in the disease course when retinal arterioles may become attenuated with thinning of the RPE and atrophy of the optic nerve. CAR tends to present with both Cone And Rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) and MAR Mostly Affects Rods although either can affect rods and/or cones (shout out to OQ user "Grimlock" for that memory aid. A late onset acquired retinal rod or cone dysfunction on ERG is highly suggestive of CAR or MAR. Vitritis (often mild as in this case) may or may not be present on exam in either MAR and CAR- both have been reported in the literature but vitritis is not required for the diagnosis. About 50% of patients with CAR have a known diagnosis of cancer at onset of ocular disease while the vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. The most common inciting malignancy in CAR is small cell carcinoma of the lung although other carcinomas of the lungs, breast, uterus, and cervix have also been associated. While new generation OCTs of the macula may show non-specific pathologic changes of the outer retina with CAR / MAR, an OCT of the optic nerve would expected to be normal in CAR / MAR and would not prove useful in this case. Patients with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) usually show signs of either eyelid retraction, eye muscle motility disturbance, strabismus, or proptosis on exam AND thyroid function tests can be low, high, or normal in patients with TAO so it is only a marginally useful test. A FA would not be expected to show any abnormalities that would aid diagnosis in this patient. An 80-year-old Veteran who enjoys his cigarettes, rum, and junk food presents with visual decline in both eyes over 1 year with an objective decline in serial measurements of VA and color vision bilaterally. Both eyes show a similar visual field and optic nerve appearance. In the context of a normal macular exam, which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient with the visual field shown above? A.Image A B.Image B C.Image C D.Image D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The visual field presented is a Humphrey automated 24-2 visual field of the left eye demonstrating a cecocentral scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history strongly suggestive of a combined nutritional optic neuropathy and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve but is the typical appearance associated with nutritional and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Generally this causes relatively symmetric bilateral central / cecocentral vision loss due to loss of the papillomacular bundle causing temporal atrophy of the optic nerve. While we all like clean diagnoses (e.g. vitamin B-12 deficiency or copper deficiency) many patients with this type of optic neuropathy have a "dirty diagnosis" full of both poisons (smoking and drinking) and vitamin deficiency from poor nutrition leading to mitochondrial failure of the retinal ganglion cells of the papillomacular bundle. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling or pallor is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows a severely swollen, hyperemic optic nerve with surrounding exudates that would be typical for a patient presenting with increased intracranial pressure (i.e. papilledema) (e.g. from pseudotumor cerebri, compressive tumor, or venous sinus thrombosis). Papilledema does not typically cause a cecocentral scotoma. Instead it causes enlarged blind spots and glaucomatous type field defects. End stage severe papilledema, like end-stage glaucoma, can cause central vision loss once the periphery is lost. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated cecocentral visual field defect. According to the Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial, what is the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement in patients with acute monocular non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.1-2% B.12-19% C.25-35% D.50-60% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a fact that must be memorized. For comparison, the rate of contralateral involvement in patients with untreated monocular vision loss from arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis is estimated to be 54-95% within weeks. The current neuro BCSC states that "the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement is 15%." This is based on very good data from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study which found the rate to be 14.7% in 5 years.1 Different statistics quoted by review manuals may be looking at lifetime risk (rather than 5 year risk) or may be quoting smaller studies. OQ has researched this topic thoroughly and we are sticking with the current BCSC text on this question. Don't send us hateful comments if your review manual has a different statistic. 1Newman NJ, Scherer R, Langenberg P, Kelman S, Feldon S, Kaufman D, Dickersin K; Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial Research Group. What is the term for vision which deteriorates in brighter light? A.hemeralopia B.photophobia C.metamorphopsia D.palinopsia High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Photophobia is a "fear of light" or sensitivity to light. While closely related to hemeralopia, or deterioration of vision in higher light environments, it is not the same. Hemeralopia is often described in patients with cone dystrophy. Metamorphopsia is a distortion of vision where straight objects appear wavy or crooked. Metamorphopsia typically is described by patients with macular disease. Palinopsia is an illusion marked by the preservation of images or "afterimages." Palinopsia can occur as an isolated visual phenomenon or in association with medications, hallucinogenic drugs, seizure disorders, and/or visual pathway lesions. A 60-year old male with no past ocular history undergoes a 6-hour cardiac bypass surgery. When he awakes from surgery he is found to have hand motion vision in both eyes. Aside from his abnormal vision, sluggish pupillary function, and pupillary light-near dissociation, his exam is unremarkable (including his dilated fundus exam). What is the most likely diagnosis? A.Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy B.Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy C.Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy D.Dorsal midbrain syndrome High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) is much rarer than anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but similarly is believed to be related to hypoperfusion of the posterior optic nerve. Unlike anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, PION almost always has a normal appearing optic nerve in the acute phase. Dorsal midbrain syndrome does include pupillary light-near dissociation, but has other findings not exhibited in this patient and does not typically result in sudden bilateral vision loss. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What type of optic neuropathy does this patient have? question: A patient has his right eye pharmacologically dilated while his left eye remains undilated. Assume that he has a known longstanding right afferent pupillary defect from prior exams. You know that to properly assess for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) you must hold a light indirectly on the _______ eye while a direct light is swung back and forth between the eyes. In this particular case the ______ pupil will dilate when direct light is swung from the _______ eye to the _______ eye.

options.D: It is not possible to assess for a RAPD in this scenario Neuro-ophthalmology

explanation: Dilation of one eye does not prevent the accurate assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). If one eye is dilated, simply hold a dim indirect light source to the side of the undilated eye (in this case the left eye) and perform the swinging flashlight test. If the undilated eye has a RAPD then it will dilate as expected when the flashlight is swung over from the dilated eye. If the dilated eye has a RAPD, the undilated eye will dilate when the flashlight is swung from the undilated eye to the dilated eye. Some refer to this as checking for a RAPD "by reverse" but others object to the use of this terminology calling it a misnomer. Misnomer or not, most ophthalmologists understand what is meant by assessing a RAPD "by reverse." Which of the following medications has been implicated as a cause of intracranial hypertension? A.cyclosporine B.furosemide (Lasix) C.sildenafil (Viagra) D.escitalopram (Lexapro) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: It is important to know the medicines that are associated with drug-induced intracranial hypertension. The more commonly implicated drugs include: vitamin A and vitamin A derivatives (isotretinoin), the tetracycline family of antibiotics, cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, prednisone (both the use and sudden withdrawal), and synthetic growth hormone. Lasix is actually a second-line treatment for IIH patients. Viagra has a questionable association with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. A 75-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol and cigarette use comes to your clinic today with a 2-month history of progressive visual loss in both eyes to 20/100 best corrected with associated prominent photopsias in both eyes. Exam one month ago by an outside ophthalmologist found 20/50 vision in both eyes with global depression on a reliable 24-2 Humphrey visual field. An electroretinogram (ERG) was performed a week ago and showed marked reduction in amplitude of both rod and cone function. Aside from his vision and mild vitritis OU, his ocular exam today is unremarkable (including normal pupils and fundus OU). What would be the next best step in diagnosis of this patient? A.optic nerve optical coherence tomography (OCT) B.thyroid function studies C.CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis D.fluorescein angiography (FA) High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient has a classic presentation for cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) although melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) is also a definite consideration. CAR and MAR are both paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndromes which share many similar features including progressive vision loss with photopsias and nyctalopia. Both diseases often have normal fundus findings until late in the disease course when retinal arterioles may become attenuated with thinning of the RPE and atrophy of the optic nerve. CAR tends to present with both Cone And Rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) and MAR Mostly Affects Rods although either can affect rods and/or cones (shout out to OQ user "Grimlock" for that memory aid. A late onset acquired retinal rod or cone dysfunction on ERG is highly suggestive of CAR or MAR. Vitritis (often mild as in this case) may or may not be present on exam in either MAR and CAR- both have been reported in the literature but vitritis is not required for the diagnosis. About 50% of patients with CAR have a known diagnosis of cancer at onset of ocular disease while the vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. The most common inciting malignancy in CAR is small cell carcinoma of the lung although other carcinomas of the lungs, breast, uterus, and cervix have also been associated. While new generation OCTs of the macula may show non-specific pathologic changes of the outer retina with CAR / MAR, an OCT of the optic nerve would expected to be normal in CAR / MAR and would not prove useful in this case. Patients with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) usually show signs of either eyelid retraction, eye muscle motility disturbance, strabismus, or proptosis on exam AND thyroid function tests can be low, high, or normal in patients with TAO so it is only a marginally useful test. A FA would not be expected to show any abnormalities that would aid diagnosis in this patient. An 80-year-old Veteran who enjoys his cigarettes, rum, and junk food presents with visual decline in both eyes over 1 year with an objective decline in serial measurements of VA and color vision bilaterally. Both eyes show a similar visual field and optic nerve appearance. In the context of a normal macular exam, which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient with the visual field shown above? A.Image A B.Image B C.Image C D.Image D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The visual field presented is a Humphrey automated 24-2 visual field of the left eye demonstrating a cecocentral scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history strongly suggestive of a combined nutritional optic neuropathy and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve but is the typical appearance associated with nutritional and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Generally this causes relatively symmetric bilateral central / cecocentral vision loss due to loss of the papillomacular bundle causing temporal atrophy of the optic nerve. While we all like clean diagnoses (e.g. vitamin B-12 deficiency or copper deficiency) many patients with this type of optic neuropathy have a "dirty diagnosis" full of both poisons (smoking and drinking) and vitamin deficiency from poor nutrition leading to mitochondrial failure of the retinal ganglion cells of the papillomacular bundle. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling or pallor is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows a severely swollen, hyperemic optic nerve with surrounding exudates that would be typical for a patient presenting with increased intracranial pressure (i.e. papilledema) (e.g. from pseudotumor cerebri, compressive tumor, or venous sinus thrombosis). Papilledema does not typically cause a cecocentral scotoma. Instead it causes enlarged blind spots and glaucomatous type field defects. End stage severe papilledema, like end-stage glaucoma, can cause central vision loss once the periphery is lost. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated cecocentral visual field defect. According to the Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial, what is the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement in patients with acute monocular non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.1-2% B.12-19% C.25-35% D.50-60% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a fact that must be memorized. For comparison, the rate of contralateral involvement in patients with untreated monocular vision loss from arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis is estimated to be 54-95% within weeks. OQ users have been frustrated by apparently different statistics in different "reputable sources" regarding the risk of contralateral NAION in a patient who suffers unilateral NAION. The current neuro BCSC states that "the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement is 15%." This is based on very good data from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study which found the rate to be 14.7% in 5 years.1 Different statistics quoted by review manuals may be looking at lifetime risk (rather than 5 year risk) or may be quoting smaller studies. OQ has researched this topic thoroughly and we are sticking with the current BCSC text on this question. question: A 75-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol and cigarette use comes to your clinic today with a 2-month history of progressive visual loss in both eyes to 20/100 best corrected with associated prominent photopsias in both eyes. Exam one month ago by an outside ophthalmologist found 20/50 vision in both eyes with global depression on a reliable 24-2 Humphrey visual field. An electroretinogram (ERG) was performed a week ago and showed marked reduction in amplitude of both rod and cone function. Aside from his vision and mild vitritis OU, his ocular exam today is unremarkable (including normal pupils and fundus OU). What would be the next best step in diagnosis of this patient?

options.C: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis

explanation: This patient has a classic presentation for cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) although melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) is also a definite consideration. CAR and MAR are both paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndromes which share many similar features including progressive vision loss with photopsias and nyctalopia. Both diseases often have normal fundus findings until late in the disease course when retinal arterioles may become attenuated with thinning of the RPE and atrophy of the optic nerve. CAR tends to present with both Cone And Rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) and MAR Mostly Affects Rods although either can affect rods and/or cones (shout out to OQ user "Grimlock" for that memory aid. A late onset acquired retinal rod or cone dysfunction on ERG is highly suggestive of CAR or MAR. Vitritis (often mild as in this case) may or may not be present on exam in either MAR and CAR- both have been reported in the literature but vitritis is not required for the diagnosis. About 50% of patients with CAR have a known diagnosis of cancer at onset of ocular disease while the vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. The most common inciting malignancy in CAR is small cell carcinoma of the lung although other carcinomas of the lungs, breast, uterus, and cervix have also been associated. While new generation OCTs of the macula may show non-specific pathologic changes of the outer retina with CAR / MAR, an OCT of the optic nerve would expected to be normal in CAR / MAR and would not prove useful in this case. Patients with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) usually show signs of either eyelid retraction, eye muscle motility disturbance, strabismus, or proptosis on exam AND thyroid function tests can be low, high, or normal in patients with TAO so it is only a marginally useful test. A FA would not be expected to show any abnormalities that would aid diagnosis in this patient. An 80-year-old Veteran who enjoys his cigarettes, rum, and junk food presents with visual decline in both eyes over 1 year with an objective decline in serial measurements of VA and color vision bilaterally. Both eyes show a similar visual field and optic nerve appearance. In the context of a normal macular exam, which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient with the visual field shown above? A.Image A B.Image B C.Image C D.Image D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The visual field presented is a Humphrey automated 24-2 visual field of the left eye demonstrating a cecocentral scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history strongly suggestive of a combined nutritional optic neuropathy and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve but is the typical appearance associated with nutritional and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Generally this causes relatively symmetric bilateral central / cecocentral vision loss due to loss of the papillomacular bundle causing temporal atrophy of the optic nerve. While we all like clean diagnoses (e.g. vitamin B-12 deficiency or copper deficiency) many patients with this type of optic neuropathy have a "dirty diagnosis" full of both poisons (smoking and drinking) and vitamin deficiency from poor nutrition leading to mitochondrial failure of the retinal ganglion cells of the papillomacular bundle. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling or pallor is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows a severely swollen, hyperemic optic nerve with surrounding exudates that would be typical for a patient presenting with increased intracranial pressure (i.e. papilledema) (e.g. from pseudotumor cerebri, compressive tumor, or venous sinus thrombosis). Papilledema does not typically cause a cecocentral scotoma. Instead it causes enlarged blind spots and glaucomatous type field defects. End stage severe papilledema, like end-stage glaucoma, can cause central vision loss once the periphery is lost. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated cecocentral visual field defect. According to the Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial, what is the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement in patients with acute monocular non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.1-2% B.12-19% C.25-35% D.50-60% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a fact that must be memorized. For comparison, the rate of contralateral involvement in patients with untreated monocular vision loss from arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis is estimated to be 54-95% within weeks. OQ users have been frustrated by apparently different statistics in different "reputable sources" regarding the risk of contralateral NAION in a patient who suffers unilateral NAION. The current neuro BCSC states that "the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement is 15%." This is based on very good data from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study which found the rate to be 14.7% in 5 years.1 Different statistics quoted by review manuals may be looking at lifetime risk (rather than 5 year risk) or may be quoting smaller studies. OQ has researched this topic thoroughly and we are sticking with the current BCSC text on this question. question: A patient comes to you as a second opinion with limited medical records from her prior care providers. Which of the following findings or symptoms would make you question the diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension in a 30-year-old obese female with bilateral disc edema on examination and a two-year history of headaches?
explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) frequently presents with severe headaches, nausea/vomiting, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations (lasting seconds), and *horizontal* binocular diplopia due to cranial nerve VI dysfunction from increased intracranial pressure. Typical exam findings include papilledema (present in over 90%), enlargement of the blind spot (present in most patients with papilledema), glaucoma-like visual field defects, and cranial nerve VI palsy (can be unilateral or bilateral). Pulsatile tinnitus is a nonspecific symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure and is very common with IIH. *Vertical* binocular diplopia would suggest possible impairment of either cranial nerve III or IV and should not occur in IIH. There are case reports of cranial nerve III or IV impairment associated with IIH but they are very few. Aside from cranial nerve VI dysfunction, any other cranial nerve deficits should raise serious doubts about the diagnosis of IIH and prompt further evaluation. According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), which of the following was found to be a benefit of IV methylprednisolone followed by PO prednisone in the treatment of optic neuritis? A.Faster visual recovery in the affected eye B.Improved visual acuity outcome in the affected eye C.Improved visual field outcome in the affected eye D.A reduced risk of multiple sclerosis (MS) development at 10 years High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The ONTT showed that IV corticosteroid treatment (methylprednisolone 250 mg every 6 hours x 3 days) followed by oral prednisone (1 mg / kg / day x 11 days) resulted in a quicker recovery by 1-2 weeks but did not change long-term outcome compared to placebo. It did find that IV followed by PO steroids reduced the rate of progression to MS for the first 2 years in high risk patients with 2 or more suspicious white matter lesions on MRI. By 3 years after the initial event, however, this effect diminished to become equivalent to placebo. Oral prednisone alone in the treatment of optic neuritis was found to nearly double the rate of recurrent optic neuritis compared to placebo and the IV steroid / PO steroid treatment group. For that reason, oral steroids alone are never utilized in the treatment of an initial bout of optic neuritis. There is no good data on the treatment of oral steroids for subsequent bouts of optic neuritis. Most neuro- ophthalmologists extrapolate from the ONTT data, however, and choose to abstain from using prednisone alone for the treatment of optic neuritis. A 25-year-old type I diabetic with poor blood sugar control (last HgbA1c = 9.5) presents as a referral from his optometrist after bilateral disc edema was found on routine examination. His vision is 20/25 OU and exam is remarkable for moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy and moderate disc edema bilaterally with fine disc surface telangiectatic vessels. What other finding on history or exam would dissuade you from the diagnosis of diabetic papillopathy? A.the absence of an afferent pupillary defect (APD) B.leakage from the optic disc telangiectasias on fluorescein angiography (FA) C.superior arcuate visual field defects on Humphrey visual field (HVF) testing OU D.no subjective visual complaints High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: Diabetic papillopathy is usually a mild optic neuropathy with minimal visual manifestations. While it is was originally described in type 1 diabetics, it is considered to be more common in older type 2 diabetics. The exact mechanism is unknown but thought to be due to ischemia of the optic nerve head with resultant swelling. Typically, it resolves in 2-10 months with minimal optic nerve damage and ultimately visual acuity outcome depends more on the extent of concomitant diabetic retinopathy than optic nerve pathology. Visual fields may show enlargement of the blind spot but should not show any other major defects (if other defects are present the diagnosis is highly unlikely). The optic disc may have telangiectasias on the surface which look similar to neovascularization of the disc (NVD) and often leak on FA. Unlike NVD, however, these telangiectasias should not be seen rising into the vitreous or leaking into the vitreous on FA. When bilateral diabetic papillopathy appears to be present, neuro-imaging and a lumbar puncture should be performed to rule out papilledema. Which of the following is not associated with acute optic disc edema? A.impaired axoplasmic flow in ganglion cell axons B.chorioretinal folds C.macular edema D.loss of the capillary net on the optic disc surface High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Optic disc edema can occur from any process which hinders axoplasmic flow in ganglion cells including optic nerve compression, increased intracranial pressure, ischemia, and inflammation. Findings associated with disc edema include an elevated appearance of the optic nerve head, blurring of the optic nerve head margins and blood vessels as they traverse the border of the optic nerve due to nerve fiber layer edema, retinal venous dilation and tortuosity, peripapillary hemorrhages and exudates, macular edema and chorioretinal folds. Loss of disc surface capillaries is a finding of optic nerve atrophy and acute optic disc edema actually causes prominent "hyperemic" vasculature of the optic nerve head. Which of the following features favors the diagnosis of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy as opposed to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.4 in the contralateral eye B.pallid swelling of the affected optic nerve C.patchy choroidal filling on fluorescein angiography (FA) in the affected eye D.visual acuity better than 20/200 in the affected eye High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The most important first step in diagnosis of patients with anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is distinguishing the cases of arteritic (from giant cell arteritis) from non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is often more visually-devastating than its non-arteritic counterpart with 60% of patients with less than 20/200 vision. GCA damages vision by vasculitic occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries that supply the optic nerve head and choroid; therefore, it is common to see "pallid" disc edema due to severe ischemia along with patchy choroidal filling on FA in the affected eye (and sometimes even the seemingly unaffected contralateral eye). Optic disc swelling can make it difficult to judge a patient's baseline cup-to-disc ratio in the affected eye prior to the ischemic event. Based on the fact that most people have symmetric optic nerves, a small cup-to-disc ratio in the contralateral eye is suggestive of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy in the affected eye. How long after injury to the retinal ganglion cells or their axons does it take for optic nerve atrophy to appear? A.1-2 days B.1-2 weeks C.4-6 weeks D.10-12 weeks High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: This fact simply needs to be memorized. Optic atrophy does not occur in the acute phase of optic nerve or retinal damage but rather requires 4-6 weeks to appear. Optic atrophy will occur with significant damage, ranging from the retina to the lateral geniculate body, where the majority of retinal ganglion cells synapse. Of the tests provided, which of the following tests would be the best test to distinguish between arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy and non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.Spectral domain OCT B.ERG C.Humphrey visual field D.Fluorescein angiography High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: D Explanation: While CRP, ESR, platelet counts, and a detailed history often help in making the diagnosis of arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis (GCA), a fluorescein angiography (FA) can also be a very useful test. While non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy likely stems from diminished perfusion to the optic nerve head, artertic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is due to a vasculitis of posterior ciliary arteries supplying the optic nerve head and the adjacent choroid. Therefore, cases of arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy often demonstrate patchy choroidal perfusion on FA. Occasionally patients with vision loss from GCA may infarct a posterior ciliary artery that does not supply the optic nerve head in which case the patient may have vision loss with a completely normal fundus exam. In that scenario the vision loss would not be due to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but rather choroidal ischemia / infarction. The fundus photo and FA series below is an excellent example of what that would look like. Notice the large dark region devoid of choroidal filling temporally despite normal filling of the nasal choroid, cilio- retinal artery, and retinal vasculature. In the correct clinical context, this FA finding is highly suggestive of GCA (and high yield for standardized tests).

Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is often more visually-devastating than its non-arteritic counterpart with 60% of patients with less than 20/200 vision. How long after injury to the retinal ganglion cells or their axons does it take for optic nerve atrophy to appear? A.1-2 days B.1-2 weeks C.4-6 weeks D.10-12 weeks High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: This fact simply needs to be memorized. Optic atrophy does not occur in the acute phase of optic nerve or retinal damage but rather requires 4-6 weeks to appear. Optic atrophy will occur with significant damage, ranging from the retina to the lateral geniculate body, where the majority of retinal ganglion cells synapse. In that scenario the vision loss would not be due to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but rather choroidal ischemia / infarction. Notice the large dark region devoid of choroidal filling temporally despite normal filling of the nasal choroid, cilio- retinal artery, and retinal vasculature. question: Approximately how much (measured posteriorly from the anterior tip) of the temporal lobe can be resected without causing a visual field deficit?
explanation: The optic radiations extend from the lateral geniculate nucleus to the ipsilateral primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. The fibers corresponding to the contralateral superior quadrant visual field from both eyes pass anteriorly into the temporal lobe in a path known as the "loop of Meyer". This becomes important when neurosurgeons excise tissue from the temporal lobe because depending on how much tissue is excised, surgery may cause a contralateral "pie in the sky" type visual field defect by violating the loop of Meyer. s a general rule of retro-chiasmal optic pathway pathology (lesions located posterior to the optic chiasm), which of the following is true? A.More anteriorly-located lesions result in monocular visual field deficits. B.More posteriorly-located lesions result in monocular visual field deficits. C.More anteriorly-located lesions result in more congruous visual field deficits. D.More posteriorly-located lesions result in more congruous visual field deficits. High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Unilateral pathology posterior to the chiasm ("retro-chiasmal") virtually always results in binocular visual field deficits. The one exception to this rule is that in theory a small occipital lobe lesion in the far anterior aspect of the primary visual cortex could result in a contralateral loss of the far temporal crescent. This far temporal crescent of the visual field is located 60-90 degrees from fixation and projects to only the contralateral occipital lobe. Otherwise, it is a general rule that a more posteriorly located lesion of the retro-chiasmal optic pathways is more likely to result in a congruous visual field deficit. A congruous visual field defect is one in which the deficits in each corresponding hemifield are very similar. Occipital lobe lesions, therefore, are more likely to result in a congruous (or similar) contralateral hemianopia (in both eyes). A parietal lobe lesion, however, may result in an incongruous hemianopia where one eye has a complete hemi-field cut and the other eye has only partial hemi-field loss. This is not a strict rule but rather describes a tendency. There are plenty of exceptions to this "rule." A 70-year-old male presents for consideration of strabismus surgery. He undergoes MRI of the brain and orbits which demonstrates a T2 hyperintense lesion in the left cavernous sinus shown in the image. Given the location of the lesion, what is the most likely examination finding?
