A 60-year-old female presents with anisocoria which she noticed one week prior to presentation while looking in the mirror. Her right pupil is significantly smaller than her left. She also noticed drooping of her right eyelid for the past year. She feels like her vision is slightly blurry in her left eye for the past 6 months although admits that her current glasses are 2 years old. She has a history of migraine headaches for about 35 years which are usually left sided and last for several hours before subsiding. There is a strong family history of migraines. The patient denies any headaches in the last week. If your exam confirms the presence of anisocoria, what single finding is the most important in elucidating the underlying etiology of her anisocoria? A.The presence of ptosis B.The effect of lighting conditions on her anisocoria C.The presence of visual blurring D.The location of her headache High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This may seem like a silly question but it is important conceptually. The most important step in distinguishing the cause of anisocoria is whether the anisocoria is greater in light or dark. Anisocoria which is greater in dark is indicative of a failure to dilate in the more miotic pupil and may signify an number of different entities including Horner's syndrome, old chronic Adies pupil, pharmacologic miosis, or posterior synechiae. Anisocoria which is greater in light is indicative of a failure to constrict in the more mydriatic pupil and may occur with a tonic pupil, CN3 palsy, or pharmacologic mydriasis. Ptosis in the setting of anisocoria is important, but it can occur in association with miosis (Horner's syndrome) or mydriasis (CN3 palsy); so it is key to figure out whether the smaller pupil or the larger pupil is the abnormal pupil. Furthermore, ptosis is extremely common in older patients due to an age-related dehiscence of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle so it could be entirely unrelated to the anisocoria. Visual blurring, likewise, should be noted but is a common complaint and may or may not be related to the underlying anisocoria. Finally, headache is another symptom that may be related to anisocoria but is an extremely common complaint among all patients. The first and most important step to elucidating the cause of anisocoria is figuring out which pupil is abnormal and that starts by comparing the degree of anisocoria in light and dark. 30-year-old nurse presents with a dilated left pupil for the last 2 days. She denies any associated headache, diplopia, or ptosis. She also denies any recent eye drops and takes no medications. On examination, she has 20/20 vision OU with no evidence of an afferent pupillary defect. Her right pupil measures 5 mm in the dark and 3 mm in the light while her left pupil is perfectly round, measures 8 mm in the dark, and is non-reactive to light (confirmed with the slit lamp). The remainder of her examination is unremarkable (including alignment and motility testing. There is no constriction of the left pupil with near gaze. You suspect that the patient has placed dilating drops in her left eye. Which of the following would definitively confirm the diagnosis of pharmacologic dilation? A.No pupillary response to pilocarpine 0.125% in the left eye B.Dramatic pupillary constriction to pilocarpine 0.125% in the left eye C.No pupillary response to pilocarpine 1% in the left eye D.Dramatic pupillary constriction to pilocarpine 1% in the left eye High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Fortunately the differential for a poorly reactive or non-reactive dilated pupil is limited. Possible causes include tonic pupil (sometimes referred to as Adies tonic pupil), trauma, CN3 palsy, and pharmacologic dilation (intended or unintended). Tonic pupils demonstrate denervation hypersensitivity by constricting with dilute pilocarpine 0.125%. A normal pupil and pupil involving 3rd nerve palsy will both constrict to full strength pilocarpine 1% while a pharmacologically dilated pupil will not. A severely injured iris from trauma may not constrict well in response to full strength pilocarpine but usually there are obvious signs of iris trauma on examination in addition to a history of trauma. Pharmacologic dilation may be intentional in patients seeking attention or other secondary gains or it may be unintentional in patients using scopolamine patches or "get the red out" artificial tears. Farmers / gardeners may be exposed to plant materials with dilation properties (e.g. the deadly nightshade plant). Which of the following is true regarding Horner syndrome? A.Sympathetic pathway lesions are always ipsilateral to the side of the Horner syndrome B.Pancoast tumors are a common cause of third order Horner syndrome C.The most common cause of congenital Horner syndrome is neuroblastoma D.In the cavernous sinus the sympathetics travel in closest proximity to CN4 High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The sympathetic pathway to the eye is complex and involves three interconnected neuron segments (first order, second order, and third order). Throughout the entire sympathetic pathway, axons never decussate meaning that causative lesions are always ipsilateral to the Horner syndrome. The cell bodies of the first order neuron lies in the posterior lateral hypothalamus and descends through the brainstem to the intermediolateral cell column between C7 and T2 where they synapse with cell bodies of the second order neurons. Wallenberg (or lateral medullary syndrome) usually arises from a stroke and causes a first order Horner syndrome. Other causes of first order Horner syndrome include thalamic hemorrhage / stroke and tumors, cervical disc disease, demyelination, and other pathology of the cervical spinal cord. Second order sympathetic neurons project from the intermediolateral cell column between C7 and T2 to the paravertebral sympathetic chain where fibers ascend to the superior cervical ganglion and synapse with third order neurons. Causes of a second order Horner syndrome include apical lung malignancies ("Pancoast syndrome"), thoracic aortic aneurysms, brachial plexus injuries, and thoracic surgery with disruption of the superior portion of the paravertebral sympathetic chain. Third order neuron cell bodies lie in the superior cervical ganglion and pass superiorly into the cranial cavity with the internal carotid artery (ICA) in a fine web of nerves along the wall of the artery known as the carotid plexus. The ocular sympathetics continue with the internal carotid as it passes through the cavernous sinus. While in the cavernous sinus, the third order neuron axons travel from the ICA to the abducens nerve before joining the nasociliary branch of V1. The sympathetics then travel with the nasociliary branch of V1 into the orbit and through the ciliary ganglion (without synapsing) to extend to the dilator muscle of the eye. Causes of third order Horner syndrome include internal carotid artery pathology (including dissection), cavernous sinus compressive / inflammatory lesions, and trigeminal autonomic cephalgia type headaches (e.g. cluster headache, SUNCT, etc). A 45-year-old female with chronic back and neck pain presents with a drooping of her right upper eyelid for the last 2 weeks. She first noted the problem after a visit to her chiropractor for manipulation. She also notes an associated moderate right sided headache although she has a history of migraines in the past. Her vision is 20/20 OU with no afferent pupillary defect. She has anisocoria that is greater in dark and the right pupil is smaller than the left. The remainder of her neurological and ophthalmic examination is normal aside from 2 mm of right upper eyelid ptosis. Apraclonidine 0.5% applied to both eyes resulted in reversal of anisocoria and resolution of her right upper eyelid ptosis. What is the most appropriate next step in the care of this patient? A.MRI / MRA of the head and neck B.Immediate anticoagulation C.Reassurance D.Tensilon test High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This patient has right upper eyelid ptosis with miosis suggestive of Horner syndrome. Drop testing with apraclonidine showed reversal of anisocoria which confirms the diagnosis. Her history of recent chiropractic manipulation and an ipsilateral headache is very concerning for carotid artery dissection which is considered a neuro-ophthalmic emergency due to the risk for CVA. MRI / MRA of the head and neck is the appropriate study to assess for carotid dissection. The treatment of carotid dissection is controversial and depends on clinician preference and the acuteness of onset. Some experts advocate anticoagulation for stroke prevention but anticoagulation is not the correct answer choice because the diagnosis of carotid dissection should be confirmed prior to initiating treatment. There are multiple types of primary headache disorders such as migraine, cluster headache, and paroxysmal hemicrania that can cause headache and Horner syndrome. Patients with these primary headache disorders would not require anticoagulation for this issue. physiologic anisocoria classically demonstrates a difference in pupil size that is equal in light and dark and the difference between the pupils measures less than how many millimeters? In cases of anisocoria greater than 1 mm, alternative diagnoses should be carefully considered. Approximately 20% of healthy individuals have anisocoria so it is often not a harbinger of "badness." A.Duane syndrome B.Dominant optic atrophy C.Best disease D.Congenital achromatopsia Topic: The Patient with Pupillary Abnormalities High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: For unknown reasons, early onset (usually congenital) disease of optic nerve or retinal disease can result in a paradoxical pupillary reaction. Affected patients will have immediate pupillary constriction instead of dilation upon turning the exam room lights off. The finding is most significant clinically in young children with poor vision of unknown etiology. Paradoxical pupillary reaction is highly suggestive of optic nerve or retinal pathology. The full differential diagnosis for paradoxical pupillary reaction should be memorized and includes: • congenital stationary night blindness • congenital achromatopsia • Best disease • dominant optic atrophy • optic nerve hypoplasia • Leber congenital amaurosis • Albinism • retinitis pigmentosa A 30-year-old female presents with a dilated left pupil that she first noticed while applying make-up one week ago. She denies any associated diplopia or ptosis. She denies any recent eye drops, takes no medications, and has suffered no ocular trauma in the past. On examination, she has 20/20 vision OU at distance with no evidence of an afferent pupillary defect. Her right pupil measures 5 mm in the dark and 3 mm in the light while her left pupil is slightly irregular (oval), measures about 8 mm in the dark, and is sluggishly reactive to light to 7 mm. The remainder of her examination is unremarkable (including alignment and motility testing). Pilocarpine 0.125% is applied to both eyes and 30 minutes following drop administration there is no response in the right eye but dramatic constriction in the left eye to 3 mm. Which of the following findings / symptoms would NOT be expected in association with this patient's pupil disorder? A.Blurred near vision in the left eye B.Headache / periorbital pain C.Spontaneous segmental oscillations of the iris musculature in the left eye D.Light-near dissociation in the left eye High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: A tonic pupil is caused by disruption of post-ganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers from the ciliary ganglion. While tonic pupils can rarely be associated with orbital tumors, VZV infection, orbital trauma, giant cell arteritis, diabetes, amyloidosis, and syphilis, the vast majority of the cases are idiopathic and isolated. Common findings of a tonic pupil include sluggish pupillary reactivity to light, more prominent pupillary constriction on near gaze than to light (light-near dissociation), segmental constriction (parts of iris reactive while others are not), and hypersensitivity to dilute pilocarpine (0.1% or 0.125%). Other features of tonic pupils include loss of accommodation (which is usually temporary with resolution over months) and "vermiform" spontaneous segmental oscillations of the iris musculature. Over many years, tonic pupils often "shrink" and may eventually become more miotic than the normal contralateral eye. Tonic pupils are more common in females (70% of cases) and are usually unilateral at onset (80%). The risk of contralateral tonic pupil development, however, is about 1-4% per year in unilateral cases. Tonic pupils are generally not associated with headache. Bilateral tonic pupils can occur along with diminished deep tendon reflexes as part of a syndrome known as Adies syndrome. While a this is a popular test question and pimp question, there is little clinical significance to the presence of diminished deep tendon reflexes. What is the primary mechanism of action of apraclonidine? A.Beta adrenergic receptor agonist (beta 1 > beta 2) B.Alpha adrenergic receptor agonist (alpha 2 > alpha 1) C.Alpha adrenergic receptor antagonist (alpha 1 > alpha 2) D.Beta adrenergic receptors antagonist (beta 2 > beta 1) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Apraclonidine is an alpha-adrenergic receptor agonist that has more effect on alpha-2 receptors than alpha-1 receptors. It is not completely clear how it functions in the diagnosis of Horner syndrome, but the current theory revolves around up-regulation of post-synaptic alpha-1 receptors in Horner syndrome. The belief is that as early as 36 hours following disruption of sympathetic fibers to the eye, the pupillary dilator muscle experiences up-regulation of alpha-1 receptors in response to sympathetic denervation. A normal pupillary response to apraclonidine 0.5% (trade name Iopidine) is mild constriction due to action of the medication on pre-synaptic alpha-2 receptors which act to decrease release of norepinephrine to the dilator muscle. In patients with Horner syndrome, however, the action of apraclonidine on up-regulated alpha-1 receptors predominates over the alpha-2 effect resulting in dilation. In an individual with unilateral Horner syndrome who has apraclonidine drops applied bilaterally, the sympathetically denervated eye dilates and the normal eye constricts leading to reversal of anisocoria.

What is the primary mechanism of action of apraclonidine? In an individual with unilateral Horner syndrome who has apraclonidine drops applied bilaterally, the sympathetically denervated eye dilates and the normal eye constricts leading to reversal of anisocoria.

The remainder of her neurological and ophthalmic examination is normal aside from 2 mm of right upper eyelid ptosis. Apraclonidine 0.5% applied to both eyes resulted in reversal of anisocoria and resolution of her right upper eyelid ptosis. What is the most appropriate next step in the care of this patient? Affected patients will have immediate pupillary constriction instead of dilation upon turning the exam room lights off. The full differential diagnosis for paradoxical pupillary reaction should be memorized and includes: • congenital stationary night blindness • congenital achromatopsia • Best disease • dominant optic atrophy • optic nerve hypoplasia • Leber congenital amaurosis • Albinism • retinitis pigmentosa A 30-year-old female presents with a dilated left pupil that she first noticed while applying make-up one week ago. She denies any associated diplopia or ptosis. She denies any recent eye drops, takes no medications, and has suffered no ocular trauma in the past. On examination, she has 20/20 vision OU at distance with no evidence of an afferent pupillary defect. Her right pupil measures 5 mm in the dark and 3 mm in the light while her left pupil is slightly irregular (oval), measures about 8 mm in the dark, and is sluggishly reactive to light to 7 mm. The remainder of her examination is unremarkable (including alignment and motility testing). Pilocarpine 0.125% is applied to both eyes and 30 minutes following drop administration there is no response in the right eye but dramatic constriction in the left eye to 3 mm. Which of the following findings / symptoms would NOT be expected in association with this patient's pupil disorder? A.Blurred near vision in the left eye B.Headache / periorbital pain C.Spontaneous segmental oscillations of the iris musculature in the left eye D.Light-near dissociation in the left eye High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: A tonic pupil is caused by disruption of post-ganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers from the ciliary ganglion. While tonic pupils can rarely be associated with orbital tumors, VZV infection, orbital trauma, giant cell arteritis, diabetes, amyloidosis, and syphilis, the vast majority of the cases are idiopathic and isolated. Bilateral tonic pupils can occur along with diminished deep tendon reflexes as part of a syndrome known as Adies syndrome. While a this is a popular test question and pimp question, there is little clinical significance to the presence of diminished deep tendon reflexes. What is the primary mechanism of action of apraclonidine? A.Beta adrenergic receptor agonist (beta 1 > beta 2) B.Alpha adrenergic receptor agonist (alpha 2 > alpha 1) C.Alpha adrenergic receptor antagonist (alpha 1 > alpha 2) D.Beta adrenergic receptors antagonist (beta 2 > beta 1) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Apraclonidine is an alpha-adrenergic receptor agonist that has more effect on alpha-2 receptors than alpha-1 receptors. It is not completely clear how it functions in the diagnosis of Horner syndrome, but the current theory revolves around up-regulation of post-synaptic alpha-1 receptors in Horner syndrome. The belief is that as early as 36 hours following disruption of sympathetic fibers to the eye, the pupillary dilator muscle experiences up-regulation of alpha-1 receptors in response to sympathetic denervation. A normal pupillary response to apraclonidine 0.5% (trade name Iopidine) is mild constriction due to action of the medication on pre-synaptic alpha-2 receptors which act to decrease release of norepinephrine to the dilator muscle. In patients with Horner syndrome, however, the action of apraclonidine on up-regulated alpha-1 receptors predominates over the alpha-2 effect resulting in dilation. In an individual with unilateral Horner syndrome who has apraclonidine drops applied bilaterally, the sympathetically denervated eye dilates and the normal eye constricts leading to reversal of anisocoria.

question: A patient comes in to your office for decreased peripheral vision in both eyes and you order a Goldmann visual field (GVF). The GVF in the left eye is shown above and results in the right eye are essentially identical. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The GVF displayed above is a classic example of overlapping or crossing isopters indicative of functional vision loss. In patients with organic disease resulting in a small central island of vision such as severe glaucoma or severe papilledema, there would be no crossing of the various isopters. The fact that isopters cross indicates variability in testing results that is not compatible with real disease. For instance, the purple lines in this GVF outline where the patient can see the V4E stimulus and the light brown lines outline where the patient can see the III4E stimulus. The V4E stimulus is larger than the III4E stimulus and should ALWAYS have a larger field than the III4E. When the purple lines pass inside of the light brown lines (see arrows), that would mean that the patient was able to see the smaller stimulus in an area where he/she could not see the larger stimulus with the same intensity. No real pathology would ever cause crossing of the isopters. Considering that many functional vision loss patients have concomitant organic pathology, it is important to perform a careful examination of the eyes and sometimes other ancillary tests (neuro-imaging, FA, ERG, etc) to prove that the patient has no other visual issues.

question: A 20-year-old otherwise healthy male comes in with a complaint of sudden loss of color vision in both eyes for the last 3 weeks. He had a head CT in the ER about a week ago which was normal. His neuro-ophthalmic examination shows 20/20 vision in both eyes with normal pupillary testing and no afferent pupillary defect. He identified 3/9 Ishihara color plates OU but in both eyes missed the color plates shown above. His confrontation visual fields were full. Motility and alignment were normal. Slit lamp examination and dilated fundus examination were normal with healthy appearing optic nerves in both eyes. Based on his history and examination, what is the next best step in management?

options.A: Reassurance that his color vision will return
options.B: MRI of the orbits and brain
options.D: More detailed color testing with the Farnsworth Munsell 100 test

explanation: Color vision loss can be acquired in association with macular disease, parietal lobe lesions, and / or optic neuropathy although seldom is color vision loss isolated without visual acuity loss or visual field loss. In patients who have recovered from optic neuritis, color vision loss can be present in isolation with normal acuity and visual fields, but the acuity or visual field were almost certainly impaired during the active bout of optic neuritis. This patient's complaint is not physiologic which should raise red flags for functional vision loss. The patient only saw 3/9 color plates which would suggest a real impairment of color vision in both eyes although the color plate with the number 16 shown above is the control plate (meaning that it does not test color vision). Any patient with 20/400 or better vision should be able to see the number 16 regardless of the status of their color vision. Completely color blind patients can see the control plate on Ishihara testing. Therefore, this patient's color vision loss is clearly functional. Since his acuity and visual fields are otherwise normal, there is no need to perform further testing to look for organic disease underlying his functional color vision loss. While approaches to functional patients differ some from clinician to clinician, most experts agree that a non-confrontational and supportive approach is best (answer choice A). The control plate does not require color vision because it contains a luminance signal by which you can detect the number (i.e. the foreground digit is brighter than the background). In other plates any luminance signal is masked by luminance noise so that the numbers can only be detected on the basis of a chromatic signal. Which of the following visual fields is most suggestive of functional vision loss? A.Figure A B.Figure B C.Figure C D.Figure D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The GVF displayed above in Figure D is a classic example of overlapping or crossing isopters indicative of functional vision loss. In patients with organic disease resulting in a small central island of vision such as severe glaucoma or severe papilledema, there would be no crossing of the various isopters. The fact that isopters cross indicates variability in testing results that is not compatible with real disease. For instance, the purple lines in this GVF outline where the patient can see the V4E stimulus and the light brown lines outline where the patient can see the III4E stimulus. The V4E stimulus is larger than the III4E stimulus and should ALWAYS have a larger field than the III4E. When the purple lines pass inside of the light brown lines (see arrows in image below), that would mean that the patient was able to see the smaller stimulus in an area where he/she could not see the larger stimulus with the same intensity. No real pathology would ever cause crossing of the isopters such as in this GVF. Considering that many functional vision loss patients have concomitant organic pathology, it is important to perform a careful examination of the eyes and sometimes order other ancillary tests (neuro-imaging, FA, ERG, etc) to prove that the patient has no other visual issues. Visual field A is a Humphrey visual field (HVF) showing a superonasal defect abiding by both the vertical and horizontal meridian along with a small paracentral visual field defect. There is nothing in particular about this visual field to suggest functional vision loss. Visual field B is a HVF showing diffuse peripheral constriction compatible with both organic and functional peripheral vision loss. An argument could be made that visual field B may slightly resemble a cloverleaf defect. Even classic cloverleaf defects are not specific for functional vision loss and are very commonly seen in poor test takers with organic eye disease. Visual field C is a GVF showing a small central scotoma with a mild superotemporal contraction and is not suspicious for functional vision loss.

question: The fundus photo and two fluorescein angiography (FA) images shown above were taken from a patient with giant cell arteritis (GCA) and vision loss in the left eye. In this patient, occlusion of which specific vessel is responsible for her vision loss.
explanation: The majority of GCA cases present with arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy although less common presentations include posterior ischemic optic neuropathy, central retinal artery occlusion, branch retinal artery occlusion, choroidal infarction, ocular ischemia, central nervous system stroke, and diplopia from ischemia of the extraocular muscles and/or ocular motor nerves. While GCA can present with a wide array of symptoms, the pathophysiology is the same in all cases: vasculitis of elastin containing large and medium-sized arteries of the head and neck. The symptoms of presentation in any given GCA case depend on which particular vessels are occluded and what structures are damaged. The optic nerve head is supplied primarily by the posterior ciliary arteries which are a favorite target of GCA. If vasculitis causes occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery supplying the optic nerve head then arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy develops. If vasculitis occludes the posterior ciliary artery supplying the temporal choroid (but not the optic nerve) then there may be NO fundus findings but the fluorescein angiography will show dramatic filling delay as seen in this case (see FA above). In the context of an elderly patient with vision loss, findings of profound choroidal filling delay are HIGHLY suggestive of GCA. A 75-year-old female with a past medical history of mild heartburn only presents with 1 week of progressive and fluctuating binocular diplopia. At times the images seem vertical to one another and at other times horizontal. She also reports a 2-month history of progressive headaches and several episodes of transient vision loss in the left eye lasting seconds. Her exam shows mild left upper eyelid ptosis and a complex strabismus pattern with both a right hypertropia and an esotropia in primary gaze. Motility is full in the right eye but shows a -2 elevation and -2 abduction deficit in the left eye. Despite a normal appearing fundus exam (left eye color photo shown above), you order a fluorescein angiography (select images shown above). What is the most likely diagnosis? A.Giant cell arteritis B.Orbital involvement by varicella zoster virus C.Ocular myasthenia gravis D.Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a source of anxiety for ophthalmologists because it has a wide assortment of presentations and is often visually devastating if not diagnosed and treated early. The majority of GCA cases present with arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy although less common presentations include posterior ischemic optic neuropathy, central retinal artery occlusion, branch retinal artery occlusion, choroidal infarction, and diplopia from ischemia of the extraocular muscles and/or ocular motor nerves. GCA is a high yield topic for standardized tests and should always be on your radar when test taking (or seeing patients in clinic for that matter). Any elderly patient with new onset headaches and transient vision loss episodes should be evaluated carefully for GCA. In such a patient, findings of profound choroidal filling abnormalities (shown in FA above) are HIGHLY suggestive of GCA. Varicella zoster virus is a great mimicker and can cause ocular motor palsies, choroidopathy with choroidal filling abnormalities, and anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. The vast majority of VZV-related ocular and orbital sequelae occur in concert with or following an ipsilateral, painful vesicular facial rash, however. Case reports of VZV vasculitis without rash mimicking GCA exist in the literature but are exceedingly rare and would be unlikely to show up on a standardized test. Myasthenia gravis is a consideration in any elderly patient with fluctuating binocular diplopia and multiple motility deficits but should NEVER be associated with transient vision loss or choroidal filling abnormalities. Thyroid associated ophthalmopathy commonly causes hypertropia and esotropia but would be unlikely to occur so rapidly, would be more likely to present with eyelid retraction than ptosis, and is NOT a cause of choroidal hypoperfusion.

question: A 75-year-old smoker with a history of hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia presents with acute onset oscillopsia, disequilibrium, face / body numbness, and difficulty walking. The patient had an MRI performed (MRI slices shown above include a T2 sequence on left and a diffusion weighted image shown on the right) confirming the diagnosis. Which ophthalmic finding might you expect to see in this patient?
explanation: The MRI images provided above demonstrate a T2 hyperintense region in the left dorsal lateral region of the medulla (see green arrow in explanation image- just ventral to the arrow tip is the body of the lateral medulla while just dorsal to the arrow tip is the inferior cerebellar peduncle). The diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) sequence (the image on the right) shows hyperintensity in the same region indicating restricted diffusion. Together these findings support the diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke of the left dorso-lateral medulla which is also known clinically as Wallenberg syndrome (WS). The medulla is full of important pathways including many that affect the eyes and eyelids. WS is classically characterized by a loss of pain and temperature sensation on the contralateral side of the body (due to impairment of the lateral spinothalamic tract) and ipsilateral side of the face (due to impairment of the spinal trigeminal tract). There is also ipsilateral Horner syndrome due to loss of ipsilateral descending sympathetic fibers. The sympathetic pathway involves a series of three orders of neurons and is quite complicated. It is important, however, to remember that the sympathetic fibers throughout their 3 neuron system NEVER decussate. Therefore a lesion affecting the sympathetic pathway will ALWAYS be ipsilateral to the Horner syndrome it causes. Damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle as it enters the medulla results in ipsilateral ataxia (of the limbs) and ipsilateral axial lateropulsion (falling to the same side of the lesion when walking). Damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle and the vestibular nuclei results in nystagmus. Other associated features include vertigo (from vestibular dysfunction), diplopia (from skew deviation), and uncontrollable hiccups (from vagal nerve dysfunction). The oculomotor nuclei and CN IV nuclei are located in the midbrain and should not be impaired by a medullary stroke. A lateral gaze palsy can occur due to a lesion of the CN6 nucleus or the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) which are both located in the pons. It possible for a stroke in the dorsolateral medulla to extend into the pons and cause a lateral gaze palsy. If this particular left medullary stroke were to extend into the pons, however, it would involve the left side of the pons which would cause a left gaze palsy (and not a right gaze palsy). • What optic nerve appearance would you expect at the time of diagnosis (2 weeks after symptom onset) in a patient with the imaging study shown above? A.Photo A B.Photo B C.Photo C D.Photo D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: The figure above shows a coronal source image (left) and a 3D-reconstructed image (right) from a magnetic resonance venography (MRV) study. It demonstrates a classic example of a dural venous sinus thrombosis (DVST) with a flow void (a filling defect in the venous sinus where hyperintense flow should be seen) in the right transverse sinus. Aneurysms occur in arteries and would not typically be seen on an MRV. DVST is one of the more common mimickers of pseudotumor cerebri and often presents acutely with one or more of the following: headache, blurred vision, papilledema, transient visual obscurations, and unilateral / bilateral sixth nerve palsy. Before the advent of non-invasive venography (MRV and CTV), many patients with DVST were misdiagnosed as having pseudotumor cerebri. For this reason, an MRI and MRV have become standard of care in patients with presumed papilledema who are not overweight females of child bearing age (the typical demographic of pseudotumor cerebri). Patients with hypercoaguable risk factors and bilateral presumed papilledema should also have an MRI and MRV due to increased risk for DVST. Of the pictures shown, image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). Image B shows a severely swollen, hyperemic optic nerve with surrounding exudates that would be typical for a patient presenting with DVST. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Image D shows mild to moderate temporal pallor. Of note, once papilledema has resolved following resolution of DVST, there may be mild to severe optic nerve pallor but this would not be expected for a minimum of 4-6 weeks. Typically the exam findings would transition from hyperemic swelling to pallid swelling to pallor without swelling over many months. A.75-year-old male with a history of moderate hypertension B.25-year-old female with a history of lupus and a recent ear infection C.18-year-old female with a history of chronic migraine headaches D.44-year-old male with a history of head trauma at age 20 High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: B Explanation: The figure above shows a coronal source image (left) and a 3D-reconstructed image (right) from a magnetic resonance venography (MRV) study. It demonstrates a classic example of a dural venous sinus thrombosis (DVST) with a flow void (a filling defect in the venous sinus where hyperintense flow should be seen) in the right transverse sinus. DVST is one of the more common mimickers of pseudotumor cerebri and often presents acutely with one or more of the following: headache, blurred vision, papilledema, transient visual obscurations, and unilateral / bilateral sixth nerve palsy. More rarely, DVST can cause intracranial hemorrhage and stroke. Before the advent of non-invasive venography (MRV and CTV), many patients with DVST were misdiagnosed as having pseudotumor cerebri. In fact, an MRV or CTV (in addition to a brain CT or MRI) should be performed in any patient with bilateral papilledema who does not fit the typical pseudotumor cerebri profile (overweight female of childbearing age). DVST, similar to deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, can be precipitated by acquired or hereditary hypercoaguability. The common DVST associated hypercoaguable states include pregnancy (and the peripartum period), oral contraceptive use, lupus, inherited coagulopathies, infection, dehydration, and acute head injury (not a remote history). Any infection will increase the risk for DVST although middle / inner ear infections and meningitis are among the more common precipitating infections. Patients with DVST but without a clear hypercoaguable risk factor should be considered for a hypercoaguable laboratory evaluation and/or referral to a hematologist. 55-year-old French Canadian woman presents for ptosis evaluation. The patient reports a progressive history of bilateral ptosis that is now interfering with her vision. She notes that several other family members have had a similar problem. Examination demonstrates bilateral ptosis, slowed saccades, and limited extraocular movements in all gazes. Alternate cover testing is normal in primary position. Fundoscopic examination is normal. Review of systems reveals difficulty swallowing and proximal limb weakness. Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following additional findings are expected in this patient? A.PABPN1 gene mutation B.Ragged red fibers on muscle biopsy C.Serum GQ1b IgG autoantibodies D."Christmas tree" cataracts High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The patient has oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy. This autosomal dominant condition is more common in French Canadian and Bukhara Jewish populations. The condition most often presents in middle-age with bilateral progressive ptosis and dysphagia. Other clinical findings include an external ophthalmoplegia (similar to myotonic dystrophy or chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia), facial weakness, proximal limb weakness, slowed saccades, and ocular misalignments. The gene mutation has been mapped to chromosome 14q11.2-13 (PABPN1 gene) with a triplet repeat expansion of guanine-cytosine-guanine (GCG). Pathology shows filamentous intranuclear inclusion in affected muscles. WRONG ANSWERS: • Choice B: Chronic progression external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) and Kearns- Sayre Syndrome (KSS) are disorders most commonly due to sporadic mitochondrial DNA deletions. Less commonly, there are familial inherited forms of CPEO which can be autosomal dominant or recessive. CPEO symptoms can start at any age with slowly progressive ptosis due to levator dysfunction, ophthalmoplegia, and asymptomatic orbicularis, neck, and limb weakness. The ophthalmoplegia is usually symmetric without ocular misalignment and there is no pupillary involvement. KSS has a younger onset (<20 years of age) and is characterized by CPEO, pigmentary retinopathy, and either heart block, CSF protein above 100 mg/dl, or ataxia. KSS may also lead to sensorineural hearing loss and dementia. Pathology shows “ragged red fibers” on muscle biopsy. • Choice C: Miller Fisher Syndrome is considered an ocular variant of Guillain- Barré Syndrome and is primarily characterized by ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and areflexia. The ophthalmoplegia is the prominent feature and can mimic any cranial nerve dysfunction, causing diplopia. Some patients have complete loss of movement and pupillary involvement can occur. Additionally, facial nerve dysfunction is usually present. The symmetric, ascending motor weakness of the limbs that is classic of GBS is typically less prominent but other findings such as areflexia, cytoalbuminal dissociation in the CSF, and an antecedent C. jejuni infection can be present. Greater than 90% of patients with Miller Fisher syndrome will have GQ1b IgG autoantibodies in the serum. The clinical course and treatment are similar to GBS with excellent prognosis over months with IVIG and plasmapheresis. • Choice D: Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant muscular disorder with ocular findings which include ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, pigmentary retinopathy, miotic poorly reactive pupils, and polychromatic lens deposits referred to as “Christmas tree” cataracts. The myopathy leads to atrophy of the muscles of the face and extremities with distal muscle weakness predominating initially. The facial muscle atrophy causes lack of facial expressions and a characteristic “hatchet face” due to temporalis muscle wasting. This myopathy is distinguished by muscle myotonia causing continued contraction of muscles despite attempted relaxation. Patients therefore have difficulty releasing grasp if shaking hands. The condition affects multiple systems with other findings including cognitive delay, testicular atrophy, cardiac abnormalities/arrhythmias, and heart failure. What diagnosis is apparent in the imaging study shown above? A.Arterial venous malformation B.Stroke C.Dural venous sinus thrombosis D.Aneurysm High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The figure above shows a coronal source image (left) and a 3D-reconstructed image (right) from a magnetic resonance venography (MRV) study. It demonstrates a classic example of a dural venous sinus thrombosis with a flow void (a filling defect in the venous sinus where hyperintense flow should be seen) in the right transverse sinus. Aneurysms occur in arteries and would not typically be seen on an MRV. In stroke, a large arterial filling defect may sometimes be present when there is occlusion of a large artery although the most characteristic magnetic resonance changes in stroke occur in the brain parenchyma. An arterial venous malformation would be demonstrated when there is abnormal early filling of a tangled cluster of venous structures in the arterial phase of a vascular imaging study (MRA, CTA, or traditional catheter angiography).

The common DVST associated hypercoaguable states include pregnancy (and the peripartum period), oral contraceptive use, lupus, inherited coagulopathies, infection, dehydration, and acute head injury (not a remote history). Any infection will increase the risk for DVST although middle / inner ear infections and meningitis are among the more common precipitating infections. Patients with DVST but without a clear hypercoaguable risk factor should be considered for a hypercoaguable laboratory evaluation and/or referral to a hematologist. 55-year-old French Canadian woman presents for ptosis evaluation. The patient reports a progressive history of bilateral ptosis that is now interfering with her vision. She notes that several other family members have had a similar problem. Examination demonstrates bilateral ptosis, slowed saccades, and limited extraocular movements in all gazes. Alternate cover testing is normal in primary position. Fundoscopic examination is normal. Review of systems reveals difficulty swallowing and proximal limb weakness. Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following additional findings are expected in this patient? A.PABPN1 gene mutation B.Ragged red fibers on muscle biopsy C.Serum GQ1b IgG autoantibodies D."Christmas tree" cataracts High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The patient has oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy. This autosomal dominant condition is more common in French Canadian and Bukhara Jewish populations. The condition most often presents in middle-age with bilateral progressive ptosis and dysphagia. Other clinical findings include an external ophthalmoplegia (similar to myotonic dystrophy or chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia), facial weakness, proximal limb weakness, slowed saccades, and ocular misalignments. The gene mutation has been mapped to chromosome 14q11.2-13 (PABPN1 gene) with a triplet repeat expansion of guanine-cytosine-guanine (GCG). Pathology shows filamentous intranuclear inclusion in affected muscles. Less commonly, there are familial inherited forms of CPEO which can be autosomal dominant or recessive. CPEO symptoms can start at any age with slowly progressive ptosis due to levator dysfunction, ophthalmoplegia, and asymptomatic orbicularis, neck, and limb weakness. The ophthalmoplegia is usually symmetric without ocular misalignment and there is no pupillary involvement. KSS has a younger onset (<20 years of age) and is characterized by CPEO, pigmentary retinopathy, and either heart block, CSF protein above 100 mg/dl, or ataxia. Pathology shows “ragged red fibers” on muscle biopsy. • Choice C: Miller Fisher Syndrome is considered an ocular variant of Guillain- Barré Syndrome and is primarily characterized by ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and areflexia. The ophthalmoplegia is the prominent feature and can mimic any cranial nerve dysfunction, causing diplopia. Some patients have complete loss of movement and pupillary involvement can occur. Additionally, facial nerve dysfunction is usually present. The symmetric, ascending motor weakness of the limbs that is classic of GBS is typically less prominent but other findings such as areflexia, cytoalbuminal dissociation in the CSF, and an antecedent C. jejuni infection can be present. Greater than 90% of patients with Miller Fisher syndrome will have GQ1b IgG autoantibodies in the serum. The myopathy leads to atrophy of the muscles of the face and extremities with distal muscle weakness predominating initially. The facial muscle atrophy causes lack of facial expressions and a characteristic “hatchet face” due to temporalis muscle wasting. This myopathy is distinguished by muscle myotonia causing continued contraction of muscles despite attempted relaxation. Patients therefore have difficulty releasing grasp if shaking hands. The condition affects multiple systems with other findings including cognitive delay, testicular atrophy, cardiac abnormalities/arrhythmias, and heart failure. What diagnosis is apparent in the imaging study shown above? A.Arterial venous malformation B.Stroke C.Dural venous sinus thrombosis D.Aneurysm High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The figure above shows a coronal source image (left) and a 3D-reconstructed image (right) from a magnetic resonance venography (MRV) study. It demonstrates a classic example of a dural venous sinus thrombosis with a flow void (a filling defect in the venous sinus where hyperintense flow should be seen) in the right transverse sinus. Aneurysms occur in arteries and would not typically be seen on an MRV. question: The Patient with Eyelid Or Facial Abnormalities What is considered the definition of normal levator function (as measured by upper eyelid excursion in clinic)?
explanation: The single most important clinic test in assessment of the cause of ptosis is the measurement of levator function (LF). While there is usually no upper limit of normal in textbooks, there is a well- established lower limit of normal. LF < 12 mm is suggestive of a myopathic or neurogenic cause of ptosis as opposed to age- related levator dehiscence. In Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome, if the affected ptotic upper eyelid elevates upon forced closure of the mouth, then there are synkinetic connections between the ______ muscle and the levator palpebrae superioris. If the affected ptotic upper eyelid elevates upon opening of the mouth, then there are synkinetic connections between the ______ muscle and the levator palpebrae superioris. A.Internal pterygoid; external pterygoid B.Masseter; external pterygoid C.Masseter; internal pterygoid D.Masseter; temporalis High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: This question must simply be memorized. Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome is a synkinetic phenomena caused by congenital "miswiring" of the innervation to the levator palpebrae superioris. Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome is a variant of congenital ptosis with fibrosis and poor function of the levator palpebrae superioris. If the affected ptotic upper eyelid elevates upon opening of the mouth, movement of the mandible to the contralateral side, or jaw protrusion then there are aberrant connections between the external pterygoid muscle and the levator palpebrae superioris leading to synkinetic movements. If the affected ptotic upper eyelid elevates upon closure of the mouth, then there are aberrant connections between the internal pterygoid muscle and the levator palpebrae superioris leading to synkinetic movments.

question: A 44-year-old gentleman is referred to you by his perplexed primary eye care provider for "atypical Bell's palsy." You review the referring provider's clinical notes which detail that the patient has been experiencing recurrent bouts of left-sided facial weakness and bilateral perioral as well as eyelid swelling. During your external exam, you notice his tongue does not look normal (see photo above). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
explanation: All of the answer choices listed can be associated with CN VII palsy. However, only Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome (MRS) syndrome is characterized by the clinical triad of recurrent facial paralysis (~30% of cases), orofacial edema (usually the lips; "cheilitis"), and lingua plicata (i.e. fissured tongue). A lip biopsy can be helpful in the diagnosis of MRS and would demonstrate a typical granulomatous infiltration. The exact cause of MRS is not known and there is no well-defined treatment for this disorder. Some clinicians will inject corticosteroid to reduce the lip swelling. Others have tried a wide variety of immunomodulatory agents to suppress the swelling episodes. (Image credit: Wikimedia Commons; http://commons.wikimedia.org). 70-year-old with a four year history of difficulty walking and postural instability presents with a complaint of difficulty opening his eyelids. The patient notes that at times when he closes his eyes, he can not re-open them easily. He is able to reproduce his symptoms in clinic and you clearly see that the patient is struggling using frontalis contraction to open his eyelids. Once open, his superior eyelids are only slightly ptotic. The remainder of his ocular examination, including motility and saccades ,is unremarkable aside from numerous (>20 per minute) square wave jerks. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient? A.Vascular dementia B.Progressive supranuclear palsy C.Parkinson disease D.Functional disorder High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient exhibits apraxia of eyelid opening. This is a feature of some patients with extra- pyramidal disease including Parkinson disease, Huntington disease, Wilson disease, and progressive supranuclear palsy. Other findings on this patient's history and exam suggest Parkinson disease including numerous square wave jerks and difficulty with balance and gait. Other neuro-ophthalmic features seen in Parkinson disease include convergence insufficiency, blepharospasm (which can occur along with and be difficulty to distinguish from apraxia of eyelid opening), dry eye, and decreased blink rate. Progressive supranuclear palsy can appear similar to Parkinson disease but would be expected to affect vertical saccades as a predominate early feature of the disease. What of the following is the most commonly involved cranial nerve in neurosarcoidosis? A.CN 3 B.CN 4 C.CN 6 D.CN 7 High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Sarcoidosis is a systemic inflammatory syndrome of unknown etiology. The eye is frequently involved in the form of uveitis. Neurosarcoidosis develops in a minority (5-10%) of sarcoid patients and frequently involves the facial nerve. Neuro-sarcoid also very commonly involves the optic nerve (cranial nerve 2) via a number of different mechanisms including papilledema due to meningeal infiltration around the brain OR optic nerve perineuritis related to optic nerve sheath infiltration OR optic nerve infiltration. The combination of uveitis and facial nerve palsy should always raise concern for Lyme disease and sarcoidosis.

question: Millard-Gubler syndrome is NOT associated with which of the following findings?
explanation: Millard-Gubler syndrome is another confusing brainstem syndrome that must be memorized. Understanding the brainstem anatomy will help to remember the features of the syndrome. It is caused by a lesion in the ventral pons that disrupts: 1) the 6th nerve fasciculus resulting in an ipsilateral abduction deficit; 2) the corticospinal tract before decussation in the medulla causing contralateral spastic hemiplegia; and 3) the 7th nerve fasciculus resulting in an ipsilateral facial weakness. Ataxia is not associated with Millard-Gubler but can occur in Claude syndrome caused by damage to the dorsal midbrain affecting the superior cerebellar peduncle and 3rd nerve fasciculus. Claude syndrome results in ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and contralateral ataxia. A 70-year-old male with diabetes and hypertension develops binocular diplopia immediately following uncomplicated cataract surgery in the left eye. There was no strabismus noted on preoperative examination. The diplopia improves slightly over several months but still remains. Examination two months following surgery reveals 20/20 vision in both eyes. There is a -2 elevation deficit in the left eye. Alignment testing reveals a moderate right hypertropia in primary gaze which increases on upgaze and resolves on downgaze. What is the most likely cause of this patient's strabismus? A.Retrobulbar injection B.Thyroid associated ophthalmopathy C.Microvascular partial CN III palsy D.Brainstem stroke High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Binocular diplopia is a rare complication of cataract surgery associated with retrobulbar anesthetic injection. The diplopia is typically present immediately following surgery and is thought to occur due to hemorrhage or nerve damage of the inferior rectus muscle from mechanical needle trauma. It may resolve over time although it may result in chronic fibrosis of the inferior rectus. While thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) can result in a similar clinical picture as seen in this case of inferior rectus restriction, there are usually other associated features of TAO such as eyelid retraction, proptosis, or conjunctival injection not mentioned in this case and the diplopia would not be expected to present acutely following cataract surgery. Which of the following is NOT characteristic of a "microvascular" or "vasculopathic" 6th nerve palsy? A.Horizontal binocular diplopia B.Diplopia worse at near C.Resolution in 3 months D.Normal appearance on MRI High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: "Microvascular" or "vasculopathic" 6th nerve palsies behave similarly to vasculopathic 4th and 3rd nerve palsies in that they usually occur in patients over the age of 50 with known vasculopathic risk factors, resolve over 3 months, and are isolated in nature without other associated neurologic deficits. They may or may not be associated with eye pain or ipsilateral periorbital headache. The classic teaching (what you should use on the test) is that neuro-imaging is not necessary in these patients assuming the aforementioned features are present because the yield is very low. There is now, however, controversy on the issue because some clinicians will immediately perform neuro-imaging on patients with isolated 3rd, 4th, or 6th nerve palsies that are clinically consistent with microvascular palsy. The MRI is expected to be normal in all patients with 3rd, 4th, or 6th microvascular palsies but some argue that observing clinically apparent microvascular palsies will result in missed diagnoses in 10-14% of cases. In general, 6th nerve palsies cause horizontal binocular diplopia that is worse at distance. This makes sense considering the eyes converge at near so less abduction is necessary to maintain alignment. Which of the following is NOT a manifestation of aberrant regeneration seen following damage to the 3rd nerve? A.Eyelid retraction upon abduction B.Eyelid retraction upon depression C.Miosis upon adduction D.Miosis upon depression a High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Aberrant regeneration can occur after nerve damage to the third nerve from compression or trauma. It is a "high yield" topic for testing because it never occurs following vasculopathic 3rd nerve palsies and can therefore serve to catch compressive 3rd nerve palsies that were previously misdiagnosed as vasculopathic in origin. The strange findings exhibited in aberrant regeneration are a form of synkinesis. Following axonal damage to the 3rd nerve, aberrant re-routing of regenerating fibers causes co-contraction of muscles that typically share innervation. Because the lateral rectus is not innervated by the 3rd nerve, aberrant regeneration linking abduction (lateral rectus) to eyelid retraction (levator palpebrae superioris) is not possible. Addendum 2/7/16: In response to an OQ user question, "Don't understand how you can say synkinesis occurs with co-contraction of muscles sharing innervation when jaw winking (pterygoids & levator) are clearly not sharing original innervation..." There is an important distinction between aberrant regeneration and synkinesis. Synkinesis involves the abnormal co-contraction of muscles that would not typically occur. This may be congenital, in which case the "miswiring of nerves" may bridge normal cranial nerve anatomy by involving fibers from DIFFERENT cranial nerves. For instance, Duane syndrome occurs due to synkinesis of the oculomotor nerve fibers (CN3) and the abducens nerve fibers (CN6). MRI and cadaver histopathological evidence show that the abducens nucleus is often absent and the lateral rectus is innervated by the oculomotor nerve. In the setting of NORMAL development of the brainstem and cranial nerve pathways, damage to the oculomotor cranial nerve or facial cranial nerve can lead to an acquired miswiring of fibers within the SAME cranial nerve during regeneration, known as aberrant regeneration. In conclusion, aberrant regeneration causes synkinesis BUT synkinesis can also occur due to congenital maldevelopment in which case the synkinesis may span across 2 different cranial nerves innervation distributions. Which of the following syndromes does not involve a palsy of the 3rd nerve nucleus or fasciculus? A.Raymond syndrome B.Weber syndrome C.Benedikt syndrome D.Claude syndrome High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation:As annoying as it may be, it is necessary to memorize the various syndromes of the brain stem. Fortunately, learning the syndromes also reinforces one's knowledge of the location of important structures within the brainstem. Raymond syndrome is a 6th nerve palsy with a contralateral hemiparesis due to a lesion in the mid-pons affecting the 6th nerve fasciculus along with the corticospinal tract. Weber syndrome is the 3rd nerve correlate of Raymond syndrome. Weber syndrome is due to a midbrain lesion causing a fascicular 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral hemiparesis. Benedikt syndrome is due to a lesion of the midbrain affecting the 3rd nerve fascicle and the red nucleus which causes an ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral "rubral" tremor (a slow tremor present with activity and rest). Claude syndrome is caused by damage to the dorsal midbrain affecting the superior cerebellar peduncle and 3rd nerve fasiculus typically resulting in ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and contralateral ataxia. A 45-year-old female with schizophrenia and severe anxiety presents with a complaint of acute onset of double vision. She states that when she covers her right eye, she sees double. Similarly when she covers her left eye, she sees double. With both eyes open she sees a similar "doubling" of images. How would you characterize her double vision? A.Cerebral polyopia B.Bilateral monocular diplopia C.Binocular diplopia D.Unilateral monocular polyopia High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: The single most important historical element in the assessment of double vision is whether the symptoms occur under monocular or binocular conditions because the underlying etiology differs greatly between these two groups. Binocular diplopia is almost always a result of misalignment of the visual axis of the two eyes while monocular diplopia is usually the result of optical problems such as dry eye, cataract, refractive error, or a displaced IOL. Bilateral monocular diplopia (or diplopia present in BOTH eyes under monocular conditions) likewise is either an optical problem or functional. Polyopia is technically defined as seeing multiple images but in practice the term is used to mean seeing 3 or more images. Polyopia can be unilateral monocular, in which case the underlying cause is either functional or optical, or bilateral monocular which can result rarely from migraine, epilepsy, or stroke (aka "cerebral polyopia"). Polyopia is often a functional visual disorder, but when there is an organic cause (super rare) it usually occurs due to disturbance of the occipital lobes and is generally accompanied by a homonymous visual field defect.

A 45-year-old female with schizophrenia and severe anxiety presents with a complaint of acute onset of double vision. She states that when she covers her right eye, she sees double. Similarly when she covers her left eye, she sees double. With both eyes open she sees a similar "doubling" of images. How would you characterize her double vision? question: Which of the following is NOT characteristic of a "microvascular" or "vasculopathic" 6th nerve palsy?
explanation: "Microvascular" or "vasculopathic" 6th nerve palsies behave similarly to vasculopathic 4th and 3rd nerve palsies in that they usually occur in patients over the age of 50 with known vasculopathic risk factors, resolve over 3 months, and are isolated in nature without other associated neurologic deficits. They may or may not be associated with eye pain or ipsilateral periorbital headache. The classic teaching (what you should use on the test) is that neuro-imaging is not necessary in these patients assuming the aforementioned features are present because the yield is very low. There is now, however, controversy on the issue because some clinicians will immediately perform neuro-imaging on patients with isolated 3rd, 4th, or 6th nerve palsies that are clinically consistent with microvascular palsy. The MRI is expected to be normal in all patients with 3rd, 4th, or 6th microvascular palsies but some argue that observing clinically apparent microvascular palsies will result in missed diagnoses in 10-14% of cases. In general, 6th nerve palsies cause horizontal binocular diplopia that is worse at distance. This makes sense considering the eyes converge at near so less abduction is necessary to maintain alignment. Which of the following is NOT a manifestation of aberrant regeneration seen following damage to the 3rd nerve? A.Eyelid retraction upon abduction B.Eyelid retraction upon depression C.Miosis upon adduction D.Miosis upon depression a High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Aberrant regeneration can occur after nerve damage to the third nerve from compression or trauma. It is a "high yield" topic for testing because it never occurs following vasculopathic 3rd nerve palsies and can therefore serve to catch compressive 3rd nerve palsies that were previously misdiagnosed as vasculopathic in origin. The strange findings exhibited in aberrant regeneration are a form of synkinesis. Following axonal damage to the 3rd nerve, aberrant re-routing of regenerating fibers causes co-contraction of muscles that typically share innervation. Because the lateral rectus is not innervated by the 3rd nerve, aberrant regeneration linking abduction (lateral rectus) to eyelid retraction (levator palpebrae superioris) is not possible. Addendum 2/7/16: In response to an OQ user question, "Don't understand how you can say synkinesis occurs with co-contraction of muscles sharing innervation when jaw winking (pterygoids & levator) are clearly not sharing original innervation..." There is an important distinction between aberrant regeneration and synkinesis. Synkinesis involves the abnormal co-contraction of muscles that would not typically occur. This may be congenital, in which case the "miswiring of nerves" may bridge normal cranial nerve anatomy by involving fibers from DIFFERENT cranial nerves. For instance, Duane syndrome occurs due to synkinesis of the oculomotor nerve fibers (CN3) and the abducens nerve fibers (CN6). MRI and cadaver histopathological evidence show that the abducens nucleus is often absent and the lateral rectus is innervated by the oculomotor nerve. In the setting of NORMAL development of the brainstem and cranial nerve pathways, damage to the oculomotor cranial nerve or facial cranial nerve can lead to an acquired miswiring of fibers within the SAME cranial nerve during regeneration, known as aberrant regeneration. In conclusion, aberrant regeneration causes synkinesis BUT synkinesis can also occur due to congenital maldevelopment in which case the synkinesis may span across 2 different cranial nerves innervation distributions.
