A.Skew deviation B.Bilateral CN IV palsy C.unilateral complete CN III palsy D.Bilateral inferior rectus restriction High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Skew deviation (SD) is admittedly confusing, but a few simple concepts will help clarify the entity. SD is a supranuclear disorder caused by a disruption of vestibular input (from the utricle and semicircular canals) to the brainstem nuclei responsible for vertical eye movement (CN III and IV). SD arises from either cerebellar or brainstem pathology but is difficult to more accurately localize. SD can result in comitant or incomitant vertical deviations which can complicate diagnosis. For unclear reasons, SD often manifests as weakness of the inferior rectus muscle(s). Skew deviation presenting with bilateral inferior rectus weakness presents with alternating hypertropia as detailed in the question, often localizes to the cervicomedullary junction, and can be associated with downbeat nystagmus. Alternating hypertropia can occur in bilateral CN IV palsies but in that case there would be hypertropia of the adducting eye (not abducting eye) so that there is a right hypertropia in left gaze and a left hypertropia in right gaze. This occurs because superior oblique weakness is most evident in the adducted position while inferior rectus weakness is most evident in the abducted position. CN III palsy (especially a partial CN III palsy with superior and inferior rectus weakness) can result in a hypertropia that alternates with up-gaze and down-gaze. With a partial right CN III palsy, for instance, there may be a left hypertropia on up-gaze and a right hypertropia on down-gaze. Bilateral inferior rectus restriction can occur with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy and would cause a left hypertropia on right gaze and a right hypertropia on left gaze. A 40-year-old female with Graves disease and confirmed thyroid-associated orbitopathy (TAO) suffers from binocular diplopia greatest on upgaze. Motility testing reveals a -2 upgaze deficiency in the right eye and a -1 upgaze deficiency in left eye. How could her particular case of strabismus be described? A.Paretic and comitant B.Paretic and incomitant C.Restrictive and comitant D.Restrictive and incomitant High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Comitant strabismus is defined as strabismus where the degree of misalignment is equal in all gaze directions. Congenital strabismus is generally comitant in nature while paretic or restrictive strabismus is by definition incomitant. In this clinical scenario the patient has known TAO in which extraocular muscles become enlarged and fibrotic. Generally, the inferior rectus and medial rectus are the most commonly and worse affected muscles in TAO. The fibrotic changes in the muscle lead to a restrictive effect that prevents antagonist muscles from functioning properly. In this case, inferior rectus restriction prevents the superior rectus from elevating the eye properly. A lesion isolated to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the pons or midbrain frequently results in which of the following? A.Skew deviation B.A contralateral gaze palsy C.Divergence insufficiency D.An up-gaze palsy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Most people know that a lesion of the MLF causes an ipsilateral INO. You must also know, however, that a lesion of the MLF often causes a skew deviation in addition to an INO. Vestibular and cerebellar input (through the vestibular nuclei) project to the 3rd and 4th nerve nuclei to coordinate vertical gaze. This vestibular / cerebellar input also travels through the MLF (along with the interneurons connecting CN III and 6). A lesion of the MLF, therefore, often causes both INO and a skew deviation. In case you are unclear on the topic, a skew deviation is a vertical strabismus that can be comitant or incomitant. There are many different presentations of skew deviations but when caused by a MLF lesion, the hypertropic eye is USUALLY located on the side of the lesion. Some OQ customers in the past have been unsure of the meaning of "gaze palsy" leading to a wrong answer. A gaze palsy to one side means that BOTH eyes have limited motility to that side. For instance, a complete left gaze palsy means that the right eye is unable to adduct past midline and the left eye is unable to abduct past midline. A lesion of the CN6 nucleus or PPRF would be expected to cause an ipsilateral gaze palsy. A severe INO often causes an inability to adduct the eye on the same side as the lesion; the lack of adduction in one eye is NOT the same as a gaze palsy. A pupil-involving third nerve palsy is assumed to caused by an aneurysm until proven otherwise by neuro-imaging. Where is the most common location of the causative aneurysm? A.At the tip of the basilar artery B.At the junction of the basilar artery and the posterior cerebral artery C.In the posterior cerebral artery after the posterior communicating artery branches off D.At the junction of the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: One of the most feared and deadly neuro-ophthalmic emergencies, acute 3rd nerve palsy from aneurysm is frequently tested on standardized exams. While saccular aneurysms can occur virtually anywhere in the cerebral circulation, aneurysms at the junction of the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery often present with a pupil involving 3rd nerve palsy by compressing the 3rd nerve as it passes by in the subarachnoid space. The parasympathetic fibers responsible for contraction of the pupillary sphincter muscle (and therefore miosis) travel in the peripheral segment of the nerve and are therefore very vulnerable to external compression. Microvascular 3rd nerve palsies can have pupil involvement but it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after a thorough evaluation to rule out an aneurysm. ADDENDUM (2/14/16): One OQ user has suggested other users reference this wikipedia link showing the anatomy of the circle of willis and the location of common berry aneurysms: Intracranial aneurysms link which of the following is NOT associated with Brown syndrome? A.Idiopathic orbital inflammation B.Rheumatoid arthritis C.A congenitally short superior oblique tendon D.Migraine disorder Topic: The Patient with Diplopia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Brown syndrome is a special form of restrictive strabismus marked by inability to elevate the eye when adducted. It may be unilateral or bilateral. Severity of the elevation deficits in adduction vary greatly from mild to severe. Severe unilateral cases can even lead to an ipsilateral hypotropia in primary gaze. Usually Brown syndrome is congenital in which case it is thought to occur due to a short superior oblique tendon. Acquired cases are due to pathology of the trochlea such as trauma, inflammation from idiopathic orbital inflammation, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome, or neoplasm (rare). What is the best test to precisely measure incyclotorsion or excyclotorsion? A.Double Maddox rod B.Alternate cover testing C.Worth 4-dot test D.Bagolini glasses High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This fact must be memorized. The double Maddox rod is performed by placing two differently colored Maddox rods in front of each eye using a trial frame. While testing procedures may vary, generally a red Maadox rod lens with ridges oriented vertically is placed over the right eye and a clear Maadox rod lens with ridges oriented vertically is placed over the left eye. When both eyes are open and a light stimulus provided, the patient will see two horizontal lines extending from left to right. An eye with no torsional deviation will see its respective line as parallel to the floor while any torsional deviation results in a slanted line. To measure the exact amount of torsional deviation, the patient is directed to rotate the trial frame knob responsible for clockwise/counter clockwise rotation of the lens until the tilted line is parallel to the other horizontal line in the unaffected eye (and parallel to the floor). The examiner can then read on the trial frame how many degrees of rotation were required to normalize the slanted line. While it is more difficult to measure precise degrees of rotation, assessing fundus torsion on indirect ophthalmoscopy is another acceptable means to diagnose ocular torsion.

question: A 50-year-old female with a history of hypothyroidism diagnosed 15 years prior presents with 1 month of progressive binocular diplopia, tearing, and bilateral ocular injection. Her external examination is shown above. There is normal orbicularis strength bilaterally. When the right superior eyelid is manually elevated, the left superior eyelid appearance remains unchanged. Her motility exam is marked by a -1 elevation deficit in the right eye along with a -2 elevation deficit and -1 abduction deficit in the left eye. Of the options provided, which is the most helpful test in this patient to confirm your suspected diagnosis?
explanation: The picture shows two hallmarks of thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) including a vertical strabismus and upper eyelid retraction. The two diseases that should ALWAYS come to mind when ocular motility suggests multiple cranial neuropathies are TAO and myasthenia gravis (MG). Based on this picture alone it would be difficult to distinguish between TAO and MG but the exam details in the question stem aide in diagnosis. Myasthenia gravis can cause "pseudo eyelid retraction" which is actually a consequence of Herring's law of equal innervation. In a patient with pseudo eyelid retraction, the apparently normal superior eyelid is actually ptotic. In an effort to elevate a weak, ptotic eyelid, both eyelids provide additional innervational input. The increased effort raises the ptotic eyelid to a normal level while raising the normal eyelid to a retracted position. If this patient had pseudo retraction of the left eye then manually elevating the right eye would cause the left eye to drop down to a normal or ptotic position ("eye lid curtaining" sign). Ocular irritation and injection are a characteristic finding of TAO but are not typically found with MG unless there is incomplete eyelid closure. This patient also failed to show any orbicularis weakness which is a common finding in MG. We have established why this patient has TAO and not MG; the next question is how do we establish that this is a case of hypothyroid associated TAO and not some other process such as multiple cranial nerve palsies? Since TAO can occur in association with hyperthyroidism (85% of the time), hypothyroidism (10%), or euthyroidism (5%) then thyroid function tests are NOT helpful in securing the diagnosis. The reality is that they are always ordered because thyroid levels need to be managed in TAO but abnormal thyroid function studies do not prove the diagnosis. Orbital ultrasounds are not available at all ophthalmic centers but are an excellent imaging study to show enlargement of the extraocular muscles and hyper-reflectivity of the muscles expected in TAO. A hypothyroid patient without TAO would be expected to have a normal orbital ultrasound. A 40-year-old male presents with a 1-year history of intermittent binocular diplopia that is becoming more frequent and more bothersome. Initially, it occurred only late in the evening when he was tired but now it takes great effort at all times to fuse the two diagonal images. There is no associated ptosis or anisocoria. Examination is remarkable for a comitant 10 prism diopter right hypertropia. A review of old pictures reveals that the patient had a previously unrecognized left head tilt in all of his childhood photos although it does not appear in photos taken in the last 20 years. A recent MRI of the brain is unremarkable and the patient is diagnosed with a congenital CN IV palsy. What principle explains the alignment measurements in this patient which at first glance don't seem to fit a unilateral superior oblique palsy? A.Spread of comitance B.Hering's Law C.Sherington's law D.Inhibitional paresis of the contralateral antagonist High Yield: Yes Your Answer: C Correct Answer: A Explanation: The general rule is that paretic strabismus is incomitant. This case of a chronic CN IV palsy demonstrates the exception to that rule. When paresis of an extraocular muscle(s) is chronic, a poorly understood phenomena known as spread of comitance can occur. Over many years, the mind recalibrates the neural input to individual extraocular muscles allowing an incomitant paretic strabismus to become comitant. This represents a direct violation of Hering's law which states that equal and simultaneous innervation runs to yoke muscles. Sherington's law is an unrelated law of extraocular muscles which states that increased contraction / innervation of one muscle results in an equal relaxation in that muscles antagonist (in the same eye). A simple way to remember the difference between these two Laws is that Sherington's law is a monocular principle of how extraocular muscles "share" an eye. Hering's law, in contrast, is a rule dictating interaction of yoke muscles under binocular conditions. Inhibitional paresis of the contralateral antagonist is closely related to Hering's law and is best explained by example. In a right CN IV palsy, the affected eye has a tendency to elevate when in adduction due to superior oblique (SO) weakness. If a patient fixates with the paretic eye (rather than the unaffected left eye) it requires a great deal more innervational input to the right superior oblique to maintain fixation. This leads to a reduced required tone of the right inferior oblique muscle due to Sherington's law. Then due to Hering's law, the left superior rectus muscle (the yolk muscle of the right inferior oblique) will have reduced innervational tone and the left superior rectus will appear weak. This apparent weakness is known as inhibitional paresis of the contralateral antagonist. A patient with a right hypertropia from a right CN IV palsy has Maddox rod testing performed. A red Maddox rod is placed in front of the right eye with the lens ridges oriented vertically in the 90 / 270 degree axis (no lens is placed in front of the left eye). If a Fenhoff pupillary light is held 5 feet in front of the patient, what would you expect the patient to see? A.A tilted red line above a white light with the right end higher than the left end B.A tilted red line above a white light with the left end higher than the right end C.A tilted red line below a white light with the right end higher than the left end D.A tilted red line below a white light with the left end higher than the right end High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Maddox rod testing is an excellent tool to dissociate vision and test/measure strabismus. If you are not accustomed to using the Maddox rod then these types of questions can be very confusing. To simplify, vertically oriented ridges on a Maddox rod produce a horizontal line and horizontal ridges produce a vertical line. To test for vertical deviations the glass ridges should be placed vertically as they are in this question. In strabismus the hypertropic (or higher eye) will always see its image as lower than the other eye because the more superiorly an image projects on the retina, the more inferiorly the image is perceived. Therefore, in this example the red Maddox rod over the hypertropic eye (and nothing over the left eye) results in the patient experiencing a horizontal red line (seen by the right eye) below the white light (seen by the left eye). The second trickier portion of the question involves ocular torsion. A CN IV palsy is expected to cause excyclotorsion of the affected eye. An excylotorted eye with a Maddox rod oriented so the ridges are perfectly vertical (90 / 270 degrees) will perceive the line as slanted as though the line were actually incyclotorted with the right side higher than the left. Which of the following is definitely NOT consistent with an isolated, "microvascular" cranial mononeuropathy of cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 and should prompt a thorough evaluation? A.Failure to recover within 3 weeks B.Age less than 70 C.Eye pain D.Progression of deficits after 2 weeks High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Idiopathic or so called "microvascular" cranial mononeuropathies of cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 are thought to be due to microvascular disease of the vasa nervorum, or blood supply to the peripheral nerves. Eye or periorbital pain is very common in these microvascular cranial neuropathies. In theory, this infarct of the nerve results in focal demyelination without permanent damage to the nerve axons allowing for full resolution with time. It is by far the most common etiology for acute onset cranial mononeuropathies of cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 in patients with microvascular risk factors. Such risk factors include HTN, DM, peripheral vascular disease, coronary artery disease, hypercholesterolemia, smoking, and age. The classic teaching is that patients over the age of 50 (or 55 depending on the source) who develop an acute onset, isolated peripheral cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 palsy can be observed without requiring an extensive work-up. Any cranial mononeuropathy in patients less than 50 (or 55) must be imaged and worked up. One caveat to this traditional rule is that in order to observe a 3rd nerve palsy there must be no pupil involvement and a complete CN3 palsy. The definition of pupil involvement varies but includes a larger ipsilateral pupil ( > 1-2 mm of anisocoria depending on the source is the definition) that responds poorly to light due to impaired parasympathetic innervation. Anisocoria greater than 2 mm is extremely concerning for a compressive mass of the 3rd nerve (most often an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery). A complete CN3 palsy means that all muscles innervated by the 3rd cranial nerve are maximally (100%) paretic. Microvascular cranial mononeuropathies are either resolved or mostly resolved by 3 months. Improvement can be seen for up to 6 months. The onset is usually acute although there can be progression of the motility deficit / alignment over the first 7 days after initial onset. A progressive worsening of diplopia, motility, or alignment after the first week of symptoms is certainly an indication for a complete work-up including neuro-imaging. The aforementioned "rules" are the classic teaching although the standard of care is changing. Most experts now suggest imaging ALL patients with CN3 palsy undergo urgent imaging including non-invasive vascular imaging (CTA or MRA). Some experts (controversial) recommend imaging all cranial nerve 4 and 6 mononeuropathies in part due to the availability, accuracy, and affordability of neuro-imaging. The data suggests that approximately 5% of clinically apparent microvascular CN4 and CN6 palsies actually have another more sinister cause visible on MRI. For the purposes of standardized testing follow the classic rules for neuro-imaging of cranial nerve palsies. A 65-year-old male poor historian who reports a vague past medical history of hypertension is referred to you after suffering a right 6th nerve palsy 2 months ago. The patient states that he awoke one morning with severe horizontal binocular diplopia and his right eye was "stuck in." The patient has no primary care provider (PCP) so he went to the emergency department (ED). The ED physician diagnosed him at the time with a right 6th nerve palsy and told him to patch either eye for diplopia relief and follow-up with you. The patient reports that his diplopia improved over about a month following onset and is now almost completely resolved except for occasional double vision on far right gaze. His visual acuity is normal and the remainder of his exam (including slit lamp and fundoscopy) is remarkable for a 2 diopter esophoria in primary gaze, orthophoria in left gaze, and an 8 diopter intermittent esotropia in right gaze. What is the most appropriate next step? A.Send the patient to a general internist / primary care physician B.Prescribe Fresnel prisms for his intermittent esotropia C.Reassure the patient and suggest follow-up as needed D.Obtain an MRI of the brain High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This question describes what is most likely a "vasculopathic" or "microvascular" 6th nerve palsy based on the patient's age (over 50) and the fact that his deficit has virtually resolved over 2 months (based on history provided by the patient). Two issues persist, however. While no neuro-imaging is required at this time, it is prudent to have the patient follow-up again in 4-8 weeks to ensure that his esotropia has resolved. The vast majority of microvascular 3rd, 4th, and 6th nerve palsies resolve entirely by 3 months so if there is not more improvement at this patient;s next visit then imaging may be warranted to exclude other more serious causes of 6th nerve palsy such as a neoplasm. Secondly, the ophthalmologist's job does not end after the diagnosis of vasculopathic nerve palsy. The risk factors for vasculopathic 3rd, 4th, and 6th nerve palsies are DM, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, etc. Patients should be advised that they need to control their vasculopathic risk factors (smoking, cholesterol, HTN, elevated blood sugars) to avoid numerous other serious diseases such as stroke, peripheral vascular disease, coronary artery disease, and renal failure. A patient without a PCP has likely not addressed these issues in the recent past and needs to immediately. Finally, prisms are generally not prescribed in microvascular nerve palsies considering the natural course of the disease is resolution. With an ocular deviation that is constantly improving, it would require weekly visits to keep the correct Fresnel stick-on prism. That said some physicians will choose to offer Fresnel prisms to select patients with microvascular nerve palsies. In this case it is definitely not warranted because the patient has only a small esophoria in primary gaze that he easily fuses and is only intermittently diplopic on right gaze. Usually prisms are prescribed to maintain single vision in primary gaze (and occasionally for down gaze) but virtually never for lateral gaze or up gaze. Which of the following syndromes results in an ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral tremor? A.Raymond syndrome B.Weber syndrome C.Benedikt syndrome D.Claude syndrome High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Raymond syndrome is a 6th nerve palsy with a contralateral hemiparesis due to a lesion in the mid-pons affecting the 6th nerve fasciculus along with the corticospinal tract. Weber syndrome is the 3rd nerve correlate of Raymond syndrome. Weber syndrome is due to a midbrain lesion causing a fascicular 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral hemiparesis. Benedikt syndrome is due to a lesion of the midbrain affecting the 3rd nerve fascicle and the red nucleus which causes an ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral "rubral" tremor (a slow tremor present with activity and rest). Claude syndrome is caused by damage to the dorsal midbrain affecting the superior cerebellar peduncle and 3rd nerve fasciculus typically resulting in ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and contralateral ataxia. What is the eponym for idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus? A.Wallenberg syndrome B.Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon C.Miller Fisher syndrome D.Tolosa-Hunt syndrome High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Standardized tests have been known to ask easy questions and then list obscure eponyms for answers instead of descriptive disease names so it is a good idea to familiarize yourself with as many eponyms as possible. Wallenberg syndrome is also known as lateral medullary syndrome and is a constellations of findings (not all features necessary for diagnosis) associated with damage to the lateral medulla including an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain / temperature in the face, contralateral loss of pain / temperature in the body, and ipsilateral ataxia. Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon is a monocular vertical pendular nystagmus that occurs in poorly seeing eyes (often in children). It can occur following vision loss from low-grade pediatric optic nerve gliomas, amblyopia, trauma, and many other causes of vision loss. Because of the possibility of an optic nerve glioma, any child with monocular nystagmus (in clinic or on standardized tests) should have neuro-imaging performed if the cause of their vision loss has not already been elucidated in the past. Miller Fisher syndrome is an oculomotor predominant variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome that affects eye muscle movements first. After extraocular muscle involvement it can then progress to cause systemic motor and/or sensory neuropathy typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus marked by severe ipsilateral periorbital pain along with deficits of any or all of the nerves passing through the affected cavernous sinus (CN 3,4,V1,V2,6 and the sympathetics). It is a diagnosis of exclusion after infectious causes of inflammation, lymphoma, and carcinoma have been excluded. Many patients who were previously given the diagnosis of Tolosa-Hunt are later found to have malignancies leading some experts to regard Tolosa-Hunt as a "waste basket" term used for other undiagnosed pathology. Which of the following diseases is NOT associated with agenesis of one or more cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem? A.Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles B.Superior oblique myokymia C.Duane syndrome D.Mobius syndrome High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles is thought to be caused by congenital agenesis of the 3rd nerve central levator palebrae superioris subnucleus and the bilateral 3rd nerve superior rectus subnuclei. Duane syndrome similarly is thought to be due to agenesis or dysgenesis of the 6th nerve nucleus and cranial nerve resulting in failure to abduct and/or adduct (depending on the subtype of Duane syndrome). Mobius syndrome occurs due to agenesis of the 6th and 7th cranial nerves producing failure of abduction bilaterally, esotropia, and facial diplegia. Superior oblique myokymia is an acquired disorder of irritation of the CN IV resulting in intermittent, high-frequency, low- amplitude contractions of the superior oblique muscle. The majority of these cases are idiopathic although very rarely there may be an inciting compressive lesion such as a neoplasm or vascular anomaly. There are no brainstem nuclei abnormalities associated with superior oblique myokymia. A 20-year-old female complains of intermittent binocular diplopia when she is reading late at night. Review of old photographs reveals a chronic right head tilt since early childhood. Alignment testing shows a left hypertropia that is worse on downgaze and right gaze. When testing each eye individually, eye movements appear full. When testing eye movements under binocular conditions there is a prominent up shoot of the left eye on far right gaze. Which of the following accurately describes her eye movement examination? A.Abnormal ductions and versions B.Normal ductions and versions C.Abnormal ductions with normal versions D.Normal ductions with abnormal versions High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: A good careful motility examination includes both ductions testing and versions testing. Ductions describe testing of ocular motility under monocular conditions (in other words, covering one eye and testing the other eye) while versions are tested under binocular conditions (both eyes open). Why does it matter? Sometimes, as in this case, a subtle motility deficit may not be appreciated under monocular ductions testing but is obvious when testing versions. In this case, the patient suffers from a classic case of a left congenital 4th nerve palsy with overaction of the inferior oblique. The inferior oblique "overaction" is a result of a weak antagonistic superior oblique muscle. The inferior oblique overaction effect is always most evident in adduction where the muscle has its greatest elevation effect. A 60-year-old woman presents with horizontal diplopia of recent onset. On exam, her visual acuity is 20/20 OU and her pupillary exam is normal. On testing of her versions, she appears to have no horizontal movement of her left eye and her right eye can only abduct. Her vertical gaze movements are normal. Her medical history is significant for a recent stroke. This patient's syndrome is most likely caused by a lesion of what structure? A.cerebellum B.midbrain C.pons D.thalamus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient displays the classic signs of one-and-a-half syndrome which combines the features of internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) with a ipsilateral gaze palsy. In this case, there is a LEFT one-and-a-half syndrome since there is impaired adduction OS (due to the left INO) as well as impaired abduction OS and impaired adduction OD (due to the left gaze palsy). The only horizontal eye movement remaining ("the half") is abduction of the RIGHT (contralateral) eye. This contralateral eye would classically display an abduction nystagmus as typically occurs in an INO. This syndrome is classically caused by a stroke or other lesion of the pontine region which contains the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) and paramedian pontine reticular formation (and CN VI nucleus). Vertical gaze is unaffected in this syndrome. What is the best test to precisely measure incyclotorsion or excyclotorsion? A.Double Maddox rod B.Alternate cover testing C.Worth 4-dot test D.Bagolini glasses High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This fact must be memorized. The double Maddox rod is performed by placing two differently colored Maddox rods in front of each eye using a trial frame. question: A 40-year-old male presents with a 1-year history of intermittent binocular diplopia that is becoming more frequent and more bothersome. Initially, it occurred only late in the evening when he was tired but now it takes great effort at all times to fuse the two diagonal images. There is no associated ptosis or anisocoria. Examination is remarkable for a comitant 10 prism diopter right hypertropia. A review of old pictures reveals that the patient had a previously unrecognized left head tilt in all of his childhood photos although it does not appear in photos taken in the last 20 years. A recent MRI of the brain is unremarkable and the patient is diagnosed with a congenital CN IV palsy. What principle explains the alignment measurements in this patient which at first glance don't seem to fit a unilateral superior oblique palsy?

options.D: Inhibitional paresis of the contralateral antagonist

explanation: The general rule is that paretic strabismus is incomitant. This case of a chronic CN IV palsy demonstrates the exception to that rule. When paresis of an extraocular muscle(s) is chronic, a poorly understood phenomena known as spread of comitance can occur. Over many years, the mind recalibrates the neural input to individual extraocular muscles allowing an incomitant paretic strabismus to become comitant. This represents a direct violation of Hering's law which states that equal and simultaneous innervation runs to yoke muscles. Sherington's law is an unrelated law of extraocular muscles which states that increased contraction / innervation of one muscle results in an equal relaxation in that muscles antagonist (in the same eye). A simple way to remember the difference between these two Laws is that Sherington's law is a monocular principle of how extraocular muscles "share" an eye. Hering's law, in contrast, is a rule dictating interaction of yoke muscles under binocular conditions. Inhibitional paresis of the contralateral antagonist is closely related to Hering's law and is best explained by example. In a right CN IV palsy, the affected eye has a tendency to elevate when in adduction due to superior oblique (SO) weakness. If a patient fixates with the paretic eye (rather than the unaffected left eye) it requires a great deal more innervational input to the right superior oblique to maintain fixation. This leads to a reduced required tone of the right inferior oblique muscle due to Sherington's law. Then due to Hering's law, the left superior rectus muscle (the yolk muscle of the right inferior oblique) will have reduced innervational tone and the left superior rectus will appear weak. This apparent weakness is known as inhibitional paresis of the contralateral antagonist. A patient with a right hypertropia from a right CN IV palsy has Maddox rod testing performed. A red Maddox rod is placed in front of the right eye with the lens ridges oriented vertically in the 90 / 270 degree axis (no lens is placed in front of the left eye). If a Fenhoff pupillary light is held 5 feet in front of the patient, what would you expect the patient to see? A.A tilted red line above a white light with the right end higher than the left end B.A tilted red line above a white light with the left end higher than the right end C.A tilted red line below a white light with the right end higher than the left end D.A tilted red line below a white light with the left end higher than the right end High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Maddox rod testing is an excellent tool to dissociate vision and test/measure strabismus. If you are not accustomed to using the Maddox rod then these types of questions can be very confusing. To simplify, vertically oriented ridges on a Maddox rod produce a horizontal line and horizontal ridges produce a vertical line. To test for vertical deviations the glass ridges should be placed vertically as they are in this question. In strabismus the hypertropic (or higher eye) will always see its image as lower than the other eye because the more superiorly an image projects on the retina, the more inferiorly the image is perceived. Therefore, in this example the red Maddox rod over the hypertropic eye (and nothing over the left eye) results in the patient experiencing a horizontal red line (seen by the right eye) below the white light (seen by the left eye). The second trickier portion of the question involves ocular torsion. A CN IV palsy is expected to cause excyclotorsion of the affected eye. An excylotorted eye with a Maddox rod oriented so the ridges are perfectly vertical (90 / 270 degrees) will perceive the line as slanted as though the line were actually incyclotorted with the right side higher than the left. Which of the following is definitely NOT consistent with an isolated, "microvascular" cranial mononeuropathy of cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 and should prompt a thorough evaluation? A.Failure to recover within 3 weeks B.Age less than 70 C.Eye pain D.Progression of deficits after 2 weeks High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Idiopathic or so called "microvascular" cranial mononeuropathies of cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 are thought to be due to microvascular disease of the vasa nervorum, or blood supply to the peripheral nerves. Eye or periorbital pain is very common in these microvascular cranial neuropathies. In theory, this infarct of the nerve results in focal demyelination without permanent damage to the nerve axons allowing for full resolution with time. It is by far the most common etiology for acute onset cranial mononeuropathies of cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 in patients with microvascular risk factors. Such risk factors include HTN, DM, peripheral vascular disease, coronary artery disease, hypercholesterolemia, smoking, and age. The classic teaching is that patients over the age of 50 (or 55 depending on the source) who develop an acute onset, isolated peripheral cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 palsy can be observed without requiring an extensive work-up. Any cranial mononeuropathy in patients less than 50 (or 55) must be imaged and worked up. One caveat to this traditional rule is that in order to observe a 3rd nerve palsy there must be no pupil involvement and a complete CN3 palsy. The definition of pupil involvement varies but includes a larger ipsilateral pupil ( > 1-2 mm of anisocoria depending on the source is the definition) that responds poorly to light due to impaired parasympathetic innervation. Anisocoria greater than 2 mm is extremely concerning for a compressive mass of the 3rd nerve (most often an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery). A complete CN3 palsy means that all muscles innervated by the 3rd cranial nerve are maximally (100%) paretic. Microvascular cranial mononeuropathies are either resolved or mostly resolved by 3 months. Improvement can be seen for up to 6 months. The onset is usually acute although there can be progression of the motility deficit / alignment over the first 7 days after initial onset. A progressive worsening of diplopia, motility, or alignment after the first week of symptoms is certainly an indication for a complete work-up including neuro-imaging. The aforementioned "rules" are the classic teaching although the standard of care is changing. Most experts now suggest imaging ALL patients with CN3 palsy undergo urgent imaging including non-invasive vascular imaging (CTA or MRA). Some experts (controversial) recommend imaging all cranial nerve 4 and 6 mononeuropathies in part due to the availability, accuracy, and affordability of neuro-imaging. The data suggests that approximately 5% of clinically apparent microvascular CN4 and CN6 palsies actually have another more sinister cause visible on MRI. For the purposes of standardized testing follow the classic rules for neuro-imaging of cranial nerve palsies. A 65-year-old male poor historian who reports a vague past medical history of hypertension is referred to you after suffering a right 6th nerve palsy 2 months ago. The patient states that he awoke one morning with severe horizontal binocular diplopia and his right eye was "stuck in." The patient has no primary care provider (PCP) so he went to the emergency department (ED). The ED physician diagnosed him at the time with a right 6th nerve palsy and told him to patch either eye for diplopia relief and follow-up with you. The patient reports that his diplopia improved over about a month following onset and is now almost completely resolved except for occasional double vision on far right gaze. His visual acuity is normal and the remainder of his exam (including slit lamp and fundoscopy) is remarkable for a 2 diopter esophoria in primary gaze, orthophoria in left gaze, and an 8 diopter intermittent esotropia in right gaze. What is the most appropriate next step? A.Send the patient to a general internist / primary care physician B.Prescribe Fresnel prisms for his intermittent esotropia C.Reassure the patient and suggest follow-up as needed D.Obtain an MRI of the brain High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This question describes what is most likely a "vasculopathic" or "microvascular" 6th nerve palsy based on the patient's age (over 50) and the fact that his deficit has virtually resolved over 2 months (based on history provided by the patient). Two issues persist, however. While no neuro-imaging is required at this time, it is prudent to have the patient follow-up again in 4-8 weeks to ensure that his esotropia has resolved. The vast majority of microvascular 3rd, 4th, and 6th nerve palsies resolve entirely by 3 months so if there is not more improvement at this patient;s next visit then imaging may be warranted to exclude other more serious causes of 6th nerve palsy such as a neoplasm. Secondly, the ophthalmologist's job does not end after the diagnosis of vasculopathic nerve palsy. The risk factors for vasculopathic 3rd, 4th, and 6th nerve palsies are DM, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, etc. Patients should be advised that they need to control their vasculopathic risk factors (smoking, cholesterol, HTN, elevated blood sugars) to avoid numerous other serious diseases such as stroke, peripheral vascular disease, coronary artery disease, and renal failure. A patient without a PCP has likely not addressed these issues in the recent past and needs to immediately. Finally, prisms are generally not prescribed in microvascular nerve palsies considering the natural course of the disease is resolution. With an ocular deviation that is constantly improving, it would require weekly visits to keep the correct Fresnel stick-on prism. That said some physicians will choose to offer Fresnel prisms to select patients with microvascular nerve palsies. In this case it is definitely not warranted because the patient has only a small esophoria in primary gaze that he easily fuses and is only intermittently diplopic on right gaze. Usually prisms are prescribed to maintain single vision in primary gaze (and occasionally for down gaze) but virtually never for lateral gaze or up gaze. Which of the following syndromes results in an ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral tremor? A.Raymond syndrome B.Weber syndrome C.Benedikt syndrome D.Claude syndrome High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Raymond syndrome is a 6th nerve palsy with a contralateral hemiparesis due to a lesion in the mid-pons affecting the 6th nerve fasciculus along with the corticospinal tract. Weber syndrome is the 3rd nerve correlate of Raymond syndrome. Weber syndrome is due to a midbrain lesion causing a fascicular 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral hemiparesis. Benedikt syndrome is due to a lesion of the midbrain affecting the 3rd nerve fascicle and the red nucleus which causes an ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral "rubral" tremor (a slow tremor present with activity and rest). Claude syndrome is caused by damage to the dorsal midbrain affecting the superior cerebellar peduncle and 3rd nerve fasciculus typically resulting in ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and contralateral ataxia. What is the eponym for idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus? A.Wallenberg syndrome B.Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon C.Miller Fisher syndrome D.Tolosa-Hunt syndrome High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Standardized tests have been known to ask easy questions and then list obscure eponyms for answers instead of descriptive disease names so it is a good idea to familiarize yourself with as many eponyms as possible. Wallenberg syndrome is also known as lateral medullary syndrome and is a constellations of findings (not all features necessary for diagnosis) associated with damage to the lateral medulla including an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain / temperature in the face, contralateral loss of pain / temperature in the body, and ipsilateral ataxia. Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon is a monocular vertical pendular nystagmus that occurs in poorly seeing eyes (often in children). It can occur following vision loss from low-grade pediatric optic nerve gliomas, amblyopia, trauma, and many other causes of vision loss. Because of the possibility of an optic nerve glioma, any child with monocular nystagmus (in clinic or on standardized tests) should have neuro-imaging performed if the cause of their vision loss has not already been elucidated in the past. Miller Fisher syndrome is an oculomotor predominant variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome that affects eye muscle movements first. After extraocular muscle involvement it can then progress to cause systemic motor and/or sensory neuropathy typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus marked by severe ipsilateral periorbital pain along with deficits of any or all of the nerves passing through the affected cavernous sinus (CN 3,4,V1,V2,6 and the sympathetics). It is a diagnosis of exclusion after infectious causes of inflammation, lymphoma, and carcinoma have been excluded. Many patients who were previously given the diagnosis of Tolosa-Hunt are later found to have malignancies leading some experts to regard Tolosa-Hunt as a "waste basket" term used for other undiagnosed pathology. Which of the following diseases is NOT associated with agenesis of one or more cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem? A.Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles B.Superior oblique myokymia C.Duane syndrome D.Mobius syndrome High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles is thought to be caused by congenital agenesis of the 3rd nerve central levator palebrae superioris subnucleus and the bilateral 3rd nerve superior rectus subnuclei. Duane syndrome similarly is thought to be due to agenesis or dysgenesis of the 6th nerve nucleus and cranial nerve resulting in failure to abduct and/or adduct (depending on the subtype of Duane syndrome). Mobius syndrome occurs due to agenesis of the 6th and 7th cranial nerves producing failure of abduction bilaterally, esotropia, and facial diplegia. Superior oblique myokymia is an acquired disorder of irritation of the CN IV resulting in intermittent, high-frequency, low- amplitude contractions of the superior oblique muscle. The majority of these cases are idiopathic although very rarely there may be an inciting compressive lesion such as a neoplasm or vascular anomaly. There are no brainstem nuclei abnormalities associated with superior oblique myokymia. A 20-year-old female complains of intermittent binocular diplopia when she is reading late at night. Review of old photographs reveals a chronic right head tilt since early childhood. Alignment testing shows a left hypertropia that is worse on downgaze and right gaze. When testing each eye individually, eye movements appear full. When testing eye movements under binocular conditions there is a prominent up shoot of the left eye on far right gaze. Which of the following accurately describes her eye movement examination? A.Abnormal ductions and versions B.Normal ductions and versions C.Abnormal ductions with normal versions D.Normal ductions with abnormal versions High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: A good careful motility examination includes both ductions testing and versions testing. Ductions describe testing of ocular motility under monocular conditions (in other words, covering one eye and testing the other eye) while versions are tested under binocular conditions (both eyes open). Why does it matter? Sometimes, as in this case, a subtle motility deficit may not be appreciated under monocular ductions testing but is obvious when testing versions. In this case, the patient suffers from a classic case of a left congenital 4th nerve palsy with overaction of the inferior oblique. The inferior oblique "overaction" is a result of a weak antagonistic superior oblique muscle. The inferior oblique overaction effect is always most evident in adduction where the muscle has its greatest elevation effect. A 60-year-old woman presents with horizontal diplopia of recent onset. On exam, her visual acuity is 20/20 OU and her pupillary exam is normal. On testing of her versions, she appears to have no horizontal movement of her left eye and her right eye can only abduct. Her vertical gaze movements are normal. Her medical history is significant for a recent stroke. This patient's syndrome is most likely caused by a lesion of what structure? A.cerebellum B.midbrain C.pons D.thalamus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient displays the classic signs of one-and-a-half syndrome which combines the features of internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) with a ipsilateral gaze palsy. In this case, there is a LEFT one-and-a-half syndrome since there is impaired adduction OS (due to the left INO) as well as impaired abduction OS and impaired adduction OD (due to the left gaze palsy). The only horizontal eye movement remaining ("the half") is abduction of the RIGHT (contralateral) eye. This contralateral eye would classically display an abduction nystagmus as typically occurs in an INO. This syndrome is classically caused by a stroke or other lesion of the pontine region which contains the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) and paramedian pontine reticular formation (and CN VI nucleus). Vertical gaze is unaffected in this syndrome. As an aside, other interesting syndromes involving the MLF: • Raymond-Cestan syndrome: damage to MLF and corticospinal tracts; leads to INO + contralateral hemiparesis • "Eight-and-a-half syndrome": one-and-a-half syndrome + ipsilateral facial palsy (i.e. 1.5 + 7) Alternating hypertropia is a somewhat unusual but localizable finding marked by hypertropia alternating with hypotropia depending on gaze direction. An alternating hypertropia in which a right hypertropia is seen in right gaze and a left hypertropia is seen in left gaze indicates what diagnosis? A.Skew deviation B.Bilateral CN IV palsy C.unilateral complete CN III palsy D.Bilateral inferior rectus restriction High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Skew deviation (SD) is admittedly confusing, but a few simple concepts will help clarify the entity. SD is a supranuclear disorder caused by a disruption of vestibular input (from the utricle and semicircular canals) to the brainstem nuclei responsible for vertical eye movement (CN III and IV). SD arises from either cerebellar or brainstem pathology but is difficult to more accurately localize. SD can result in comitant or incomitant vertical deviations which can complicate diagnosis. For unclear reasons, SD often manifests as weakness of the inferior rectus muscle(s). Skew deviation presenting with bilateral inferior rectus weakness presents with alternating hypertropia as detailed in the question, often localizes to the cervicomedullary junction, and can be associated with downbeat nystagmus. Alternating hypertropia can occur in bilateral CN IV palsies but in that case there would be hypertropia of the adducting eye (not abducting eye) so that there is a right hypertropia in left gaze and a left hypertropia in right gaze. This occurs because superior oblique weakness is most evident in the adducted position while inferior rectus weakness is most evident in the abducted position. CN III palsy (especially a partial CN III palsy with superior and inferior rectus weakness) can result in a hypertropia that alternates with up-gaze and down-gaze. With a partial right CN III palsy, for instance, there may be a left hypertropia on up-gaze and a right hypertropia on down-gaze. Bilateral inferior rectus restriction can occur with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy and would cause a left hypertropia on right gaze and a right hypertropia on left gaze. A 40-year-old female with Graves disease and confirmed thyroid-associated orbitopathy (TAO) suffers from binocular diplopia greatest on upgaze. Motility testing reveals a -2 upgaze deficiency in the right eye and a -1 upgaze deficiency in left eye. How could her particular case of strabismus be described? A.Paretic and comitant B.Paretic and incomitant C.Restrictive and comitant D.Restrictive and incomitant High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Comitant strabismus is defined as strabismus where the degree of misalignment is equal in all gaze directions. Congenital strabismus is generally comitant in nature while paretic or restrictive strabismus is by definition incomitant. In this clinical scenario the patient has known TAO in which extraocular muscles become enlarged and fibrotic. Generally, the inferior rectus and medial rectus are the most commonly and worse affected muscles in TAO. The fibrotic changes in the muscle lead to a restrictive effect that prevents antagonist muscles from functioning properly. In this case, inferior rectus restriction prevents the superior rectus from elevating the eye properly. A lesion isolated to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the pons or midbrain frequently results in which of the following? A.Skew deviation B.A contralateral gaze palsy C.Divergence insufficiency D.An up-gaze palsy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Most people know that a lesion of the MLF causes an ipsilateral INO. You must also know, however, that a lesion of the MLF often causes a skew deviation in addition to an INO. Vestibular and cerebellar input (through the vestibular nuclei) project to the 3rd and 4th nerve nuclei to coordinate vertical gaze. This vestibular / cerebellar input also travels through the MLF (along with the interneurons connecting CN III and 6). A lesion of the MLF, therefore, often causes both INO and a skew deviation. In case you are unclear on the topic, a skew deviation is a vertical strabismus that can be comitant or incomitant. There are many different presentations of skew deviations but when caused by a MLF lesion, the hypertropic eye is USUALLY located on the side of the lesion. Some OQ customers in the past have been unsure of the meaning of "gaze palsy" leading to a wrong answer. A gaze palsy to one side means that BOTH eyes have limited motility to that side. For instance, a complete left gaze palsy means that the right eye is unable to adduct past midline and the left eye is unable to abduct past midline. A lesion of the CN6 nucleus or PPRF would be expected to cause an ipsilateral gaze palsy. A severe INO often causes an inability to adduct the eye on the same side as the lesion; the lack of adduction in one eye is NOT the same as a gaze palsy. The majority of these cases are idiopathic although very rarely there may be an inciting compressive lesion such as a neoplasm or vascular anomaly. There are no brainstem nuclei abnormalities associated with superior oblique myokymia. A 20-year-old female complains of intermittent binocular diplopia when she is reading late at night. Review of old photographs reveals a chronic right head tilt since early childhood. Alignment testing shows a left hypertropia that is worse on downgaze and right gaze. When testing each eye individually, eye movements appear full. When testing eye movements under binocular conditions there is a prominent up shoot of the left eye on far right gaze. Which of the following accurately describes her eye movement examination? A.Abnormal ductions and versions B.Normal ductions and versions C.Abnormal ductions with normal versions D.Normal ductions with abnormal versions High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: A good careful motility examination includes both ductions testing and versions testing. Ductions describe testing of ocular motility under monocular conditions (in other words, covering one eye and testing the other eye) while versions are tested under binocular conditions (both eyes open). Why does it matter? Sometimes, as in this case, a subtle motility deficit may not be appreciated under monocular ductions testing but is obvious when testing versions. In this case, the patient suffers from a classic case of a left congenital 4th nerve palsy with overaction of the inferior oblique. The inferior oblique "overaction" is a result of a weak antagonistic superior oblique muscle. The inferior oblique overaction effect is always most evident in adduction where the muscle has its greatest elevation effect. A 60-year-old woman presents with horizontal diplopia of recent onset. On exam, her visual acuity is 20/20 OU and her pupillary exam is normal. On testing of her versions, she appears to have no horizontal movement of her left eye and her right eye can only abduct. Her vertical gaze movements are normal. Her medical history is significant for a recent stroke. This patient's syndrome is most likely caused by a lesion of what structure? A.cerebellum B.midbrain C.pons D.thalamus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient displays the classic signs of one-and-a-half syndrome which combines the features of internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) with a ipsilateral gaze palsy. In this case, there is a LEFT one-and-a-half syndrome since there is impaired adduction OS (due to the left INO) as well as impaired abduction OS and impaired adduction OD (due to the left gaze palsy). The only horizontal eye movement remaining ("the half") is abduction of the RIGHT (contralateral) eye. This contralateral eye would classically display an abduction nystagmus as typically occurs in an INO. An alternating hypertropia in which a right hypertropia is seen in right gaze and a left hypertropia is seen in left gaze indicates what diagnosis? SD arises from either cerebellar or brainstem pathology but is difficult to more accurately localize. SD can result in comitant or incomitant vertical deviations which can complicate diagnosis. For unclear reasons, SD often manifests as weakness of the inferior rectus muscle(s). A 40-year-old female with Graves disease and confirmed thyroid-associated orbitopathy (TAO) suffers from binocular diplopia greatest on upgaze. Motility testing reveals a -2 upgaze deficiency in the right eye and a -1 upgaze deficiency in left eye. How could her particular case of strabismus be described? Congenital strabismus is generally comitant in nature while paretic or restrictive strabismus is by definition incomitant. In this clinical scenario the patient has known TAO in which extraocular muscles become enlarged and fibrotic. Generally, the inferior rectus and medial rectus are the most commonly and worse affected muscles in TAO. The fibrotic changes in the muscle lead to a restrictive effect that prevents antagonist muscles from functioning properly. A lesion isolated to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the pons or midbrain frequently results in which of the following? For instance, a complete left gaze palsy means that the right eye is unable to adduct past midline and the left eye is unable to abduct past midline. A lesion of the CN6 nucleus or PPRF would be expected to cause an ipsilateral gaze palsy. A severe INO often causes an inability to adduct the eye on the same side as the lesion; the lack of adduction in one eye is NOT the same as a gaze palsy. A pupil-involving third nerve palsy is assumed to caused by an aneurysm until proven otherwise by neuro-imaging. Where is the most common location of the causative aneurysm? A.At the tip of the basilar artery B.At the junction of the basilar artery and the posterior cerebral artery C.In the posterior cerebral artery after the posterior communicating artery branches off D.At the junction of the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: One of the most feared and deadly neuro-ophthalmic emergencies, acute 3rd nerve palsy from aneurysm is frequently tested on standardized exams. The parasympathetic fibers responsible for contraction of the pupillary sphincter muscle (and therefore miosis) travel in the peripheral segment of the nerve and are therefore very vulnerable to external compression. Microvascular 3rd nerve palsies can have pupil involvement but it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after a thorough evaluation to rule out an aneurysm. ADDENDUM (2/14/16): One OQ user has suggested other users reference this wikipedia link showing the anatomy of the circle of willis and the location of common berry aneurysms: Intracranial aneurysms link which of the following is NOT associated with Brown syndrome? A.Idiopathic orbital inflammation B.Rheumatoid arthritis C.A congenitally short superior oblique tendon D.Migraine disorder Topic: The Patient with Diplopia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Brown syndrome is a special form of restrictive strabismus marked by inability to elevate the eye when adducted. It may be unilateral or bilateral. Severity of the elevation deficits in adduction vary greatly from mild to severe. Severe unilateral cases can even lead to an ipsilateral hypotropia in primary gaze. Usually Brown syndrome is congenital in which case it is thought to occur due to a short superior oblique tendon. Acquired cases are due to pathology of the trochlea such as trauma, inflammation from idiopathic orbital inflammation, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome, or neoplasm (rare). What is the best test to precisely measure incyclotorsion or excyclotorsion? A.Double Maddox rod B.Alternate cover testing C.Worth 4-dot test D.Bagolini glasses High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This fact must be memorized. The double Maddox rod is performed by placing two differently colored Maddox rods in front of each eye using a trial frame. While testing procedures may vary, generally a red Maadox rod lens with ridges oriented vertically is placed over the right eye and a clear Maadox rod lens with ridges oriented vertically is placed over the left eye. When both eyes are open and a light stimulus provided, the patient will see two horizontal lines extending from left to right. An eye with no torsional deviation will see its respective line as parallel to the floor while any torsional deviation results in a slanted line. To measure the exact amount of torsional deviation, the patient is directed to rotate the trial frame knob responsible for clockwise/counter clockwise rotation of the lens until the tilted line is parallel to the other horizontal line in the unaffected eye (and parallel to the floor). The examiner can then read on the trial frame how many degrees of rotation were required to normalize the slanted line. While it is more difficult to measure precise degrees of rotation, assessing fundus torsion on indirect ophthalmoscopy is another acceptable means to diagnose ocular torsion.

question: Which of the following is definitely NOT consistent with an isolated, "microvascular" cranial mononeuropathy of cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 and should prompt a thorough evaluation?
explanation: Idiopathic or so called "microvascular" cranial mononeuropathies of cranial nerve 3, 4, or 6 are thought to be due to microvascular disease of the vasa nervorum, or blood supply to the peripheral nerves. In theory, this infarct of the nerve results in focal demyelination without permanent damage to the nerve axons allowing for full resolution with time. Such risk factors include HTN, DM, peripheral vascular disease, coronary artery disease, hypercholesterolemia, smoking, and age. A complete CN3 palsy means that all muscles innervated by the 3rd cranial nerve are maximally (100%) paretic. question: A 65-year-old male poor historian who reports a vague past medical history of hypertension is referred to you after suffering a right 6th nerve palsy 2 months ago. The patient states that he awoke one morning with severe horizontal binocular diplopia and his right eye was "stuck in." The patient has no primary care provider (PCP) so he went to the emergency department (ED). The ED physician diagnosed him at the time with a right 6th nerve palsy and told him to patch either eye for diplopia relief and follow-up with you. The patient reports that his diplopia improved over about a month following onset and is now almost completely resolved except for occasional double vision on far right gaze. His visual acuity is normal and the remainder of his exam (including slit lamp and fundoscopy) is remarkable for a 2 diopter esophoria in primary gaze, orthophoria in left gaze, and an 8 diopter intermittent esotropia in right gaze. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Send the patient to a general internist / primary care physician
options.B: Prescribe Fresnel prisms for his intermittent esotropia
options.C: Reassure the patient and suggest follow-up as needed
options.D: Obtain an MRI of the brain

explanation: This question describes what is most likely a "vasculopathic" or "microvascular" 6th nerve palsy based on the patient's age (over 50) and the fact that his deficit has virtually resolved over 2 months (based on history provided by the patient). Two issues persist, however. While no neuro-imaging is required at this time, it is prudent to have the patient follow-up again in 4-8 weeks to ensure that his esotropia has resolved. The vast majority of microvascular 3rd, 4th, and 6th nerve palsies resolve entirely by 3 months so if there is not more improvement at this patient;s next visit then imaging may be warranted to exclude other more serious causes of 6th nerve palsy such as a neoplasm. Secondly, the ophthalmologist's job does not end after the diagnosis of vasculopathic nerve palsy. The risk factors for vasculopathic 3rd, 4th, and 6th nerve palsies are DM, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, etc. Patients should be advised that they need to control their vasculopathic risk factors (smoking, cholesterol, HTN, elevated blood sugars) to avoid numerous other serious diseases such as stroke, peripheral vascular disease, coronary artery disease, and renal failure. A patient without a PCP has likely not addressed these issues in the recent past and needs to immediately. Finally, prisms are generally not prescribed in microvascular nerve palsies considering the natural course of the disease is resolution. With an ocular deviation that is constantly improving, it would require weekly visits to keep the correct Fresnel stick-on prism. That said some physicians will choose to offer Fresnel prisms to select patients with microvascular nerve palsies. In this case it is definitely not warranted because the patient has only a small esophoria in primary gaze that he easily fuses and is only intermittently diplopic on right gaze. Usually prisms are prescribed to maintain single vision in primary gaze (and occasionally for down gaze) but virtually never for lateral gaze or up gaze. Which of the following syndromes results in an ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral tremor? A.Raymond syndrome B.Weber syndrome C.Benedikt syndrome D.Claude syndrome High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Raymond syndrome is a 6th nerve palsy with a contralateral hemiparesis due to a lesion in the mid-pons affecting the 6th nerve fasciculus along with the corticospinal tract. Weber syndrome is the 3rd nerve correlate of Raymond syndrome. Weber syndrome is due to a midbrain lesion causing a fascicular 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral hemiparesis. Benedikt syndrome is due to a lesion of the midbrain affecting the 3rd nerve fascicle and the red nucleus which causes an ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and a contralateral "rubral" tremor (a slow tremor present with activity and rest). Claude syndrome is caused by damage to the dorsal midbrain affecting the superior cerebellar peduncle and 3rd nerve fasciculus typically resulting in ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and contralateral ataxia. What is the eponym for idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus? A.Wallenberg syndrome B.Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon C.Miller Fisher syndrome D.Tolosa-Hunt syndrome High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Standardized tests have been known to ask easy questions and then list obscure eponyms for answers instead of descriptive disease names so it is a good idea to familiarize yourself with as many eponyms as possible. Wallenberg syndrome is also known as lateral medullary syndrome and is a constellations of findings (not all features necessary for diagnosis) associated with damage to the lateral medulla including an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain / temperature in the face, contralateral loss of pain / temperature in the body, and ipsilateral ataxia. Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon is a monocular vertical pendular nystagmus that occurs in poorly seeing eyes (often in children). It can occur following vision loss from low-grade pediatric optic nerve gliomas, amblyopia, trauma, and many other causes of vision loss. Because of the possibility of an optic nerve glioma, any child with monocular nystagmus (in clinic or on standardized tests) should have neuro-imaging performed if the cause of their vision loss has not already been elucidated in the past. Miller Fisher syndrome is an oculomotor predominant variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome that affects eye muscle movements first. After extraocular muscle involvement it can then progress to cause systemic motor and/or sensory neuropathy typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus marked by severe ipsilateral periorbital pain along with deficits of any or all of the nerves passing through the affected cavernous sinus (CN 3,4,V1,V2,6 and the sympathetics). It is a diagnosis of exclusion after infectious causes of inflammation, lymphoma, and carcinoma have been excluded. Many patients who were previously given the diagnosis of Tolosa-Hunt are later found to have malignancies leading some experts to regard Tolosa-Hunt as a "waste basket" term used for other undiagnosed pathology. There are no brainstem nuclei abnormalities associated with superior oblique myokymia. A 20-year-old female complains of intermittent binocular diplopia when she is reading late at night. Review of old photographs reveals a chronic right head tilt since early childhood. Alignment testing shows a left hypertropia that is worse on downgaze and right gaze. In this case, the patient suffers from a classic case of a left congenital 4th nerve palsy with overaction of the inferior oblique. The inferior oblique overaction effect is always most evident in adduction where the muscle has its greatest elevation effect. A 60-year-old woman presents with horizontal diplopia of recent onset. On exam, her visual acuity is 20/20 OU and her pupillary exam is normal. On testing of her versions, she appears to have no horizontal movement of her left eye and her right eye can only abduct. question: What is the eponym for idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus?
explanation: Standardized tests have been known to ask easy questions and then list obscure eponyms for answers instead of descriptive disease names so it is a good idea to familiarize yourself with as many eponyms as possible. Wallenberg syndrome is also known as lateral medullary syndrome and is a constellations of findings (not all features necessary for diagnosis) associated with damage to the lateral medulla including an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain / temperature in the face, contralateral loss of pain / temperature in the body, and ipsilateral ataxia. Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon is a monocular vertical pendular nystagmus that occurs in poorly seeing eyes (often in children). It can occur following vision loss from low-grade pediatric optic nerve gliomas, amblyopia, trauma, and many other causes of vision loss. Because of the possibility of an optic nerve glioma, any child with monocular nystagmus (in clinic or on standardized tests) should have neuro-imaging performed if the cause of their vision loss has not already been elucidated in the past. Miller Fisher syndrome is an oculomotor predominant variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome that affects eye muscle movements first. After extraocular muscle involvement it can then progress to cause systemic motor and/or sensory neuropathy typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus marked by severe ipsilateral periorbital pain along with deficits of any or all of the nerves passing through the affected cavernous sinus (CN 3,4,V1,V2,6 and the sympathetics).
